speechtext: Hon. S. F. TOLMIE (Minister of Agriculture) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 78, to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Explain, please.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
' The Bill proposes an amendment of that section of the Act which refers to compensation. Under the present Act, where an animal which is killed on account of contagious disease is not badly enough diseased to be entirely destroyed and is sold as fit for food, it is quite possible

for the owner to obtain more for the animal so destroyed than he could have obtained for it had it been in healthy condition. An amendment is being made in that respect. Then, the amount of the fine is being changed from a maximum of $200 to range from $50 up to $500.

speechtext: Resuming the adjourned debate on the motion of Hon. N. W. Rowell (Minister of Health) for the second reading of Bill No. 20, to amend the Opium and Drug Act.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
On Friday evening when this Order was called, I gave to the House certain amendments which I intended to incorporate in the Bill when the House went into committee, and it is not my intention this afternoon to discuss the Bill at length on the second reading. When the resolution upon which the Bill is founded, was before the House, I outlined the steps which led up to an agreement upon the terms of the International Opium 1041
Convention and the proceedings which had been taken since 1912 to secure the assent of the Powers to its terms and its final ratification. It is not needful that I should repeat that history this afternoon.
I shall, therefore, limit my observations to pointing out the importance and the necessity of the proposed legislation and to a few words with reference to its general character in an endeavour to facilitate the consideration of the matter in Committee of the Whole House.
I may say that the Bill is necessary for two purposes, one to carry out the obligations we have assumed under the International Opium Convention, and the other in the interest of public health and the welfare of the people. The first legislation in Canada in fconnection with the prohibition of the importation of opium was the Act of 1908 introduced by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), then Minister of Labour. That legislation grew out of an investigation carried on by the present leader of the Opposition (Mr. King) when Deputy Minister of Labour, into certain anti-Asiatic riots in the city of Vancouver, which disclosed the extent to which the manufacture and sale of opium were being carried on in the Dominion of Canada. One of the effects of that legislation was greatly to decrease the importation of opium into Canada, and I shall give the House in a few minutes some statistics which are most interesting as indicating the effects of that legislation.
Following that was the Act of 1911, which went very much further than the Act of 1908. The Act of 1911 followed what was known as the Shanghai Conference, and was intended to give effect to some of the important decisions of that conference. It was introduced and carried through the House by the present leader of the Opposition, then the Minister of Labour. That legislation continued on the statute books unaltered until last year, when a Bill was passed through the House which provided for licensing import into Canada and prohibiting import except under license. That is the condition of the legislation at the present time.
In reference to the character of the traffic itself, it is not necessary that I should speak. The Act of 1908 dealt only with opium. The Act of 1911 went further and dealt with certain derivates of opium-morphine, heroin and codeine as well as with cocaine. At the time of the conference in Shanghai, it was deemed essential to the successful control of these habit-forming
1630	,

drugs that cocaine should be dealt with as well as morphine, heroin and codeine. The members of the House are aware that morphine and codeine are derivates of opium. Heroin, I believe, is a derivative of morphine, so they are all derived from opium, except cocaine, the morphine 'being the most important and valuable of them all. The morphine content of opium is about 10 per cent. I am sure the House will be interested in the importation figures. Starting in the year 1900 with an importation of 56,630 lbs. of opium gum crude, the amount went up to 81,302 lbs. the next year, and then went up and down until in the year 1908 the amount imported was 88,013 lbs. Following the legislation of 1908, the importation in the next year came down to 41,638 lbs. Then it dropped to 3,000 pounds. The figures are as follows: 1910, 3,576 lbs.;	1911,	6,418	lbs.;	1912,	5,017	lbs.;1913, 5,117	lbs.;	1914,	4,436	lbs.;	1915,	7,243lbs.; 1916,	1,741	lbs.	Then	it takes a	sudden jump	to 15,423 lbs. in	1917;	12,471	lbs.
in 1918, and 34,263 lbs. in 1919.
In the year 1918 a very Stringent law was passed in the United States. What is known as the Harrison Act was passed in 1914. That Act was amended in 1918 and made much more stringent. The United States Government took almost complete control of the traffic in these drugs by reason of that legislation and the regulations passed thereunder. One of the results appears to have been that those interested in the trade imported these drugs into Canada, and then by smuggling gained access to the American market. In fact that- was complained of by a committee appointed by the United States Government to investigate the matter. In Canada last session the licensing system was introduced, first by Order in Council to meet the situation, and subsequently confirmed by legislation. While the Order in Council was in force and before the Department of Health was organized, the licensing system was1 carried on by the Department of Trade and Commerce. Subsequently, and since the department was organized, It has been carried on by the Department of Health, with this very interesting result: The importation of 34,263 pounds of opium in 1919 dropped to 13,626 pounds in 1920; that is for the fiscal year ending March 31. The importation of cocaine, which in 1919 amounted to 12,333 ounces, dropped to 6,968 ounces in 1920, showing the great decrease in the importation of these drugs under the Order in Council and the legislation passed last session.
I am sure the House would be interested in a comparison of the importations during the ten months ending March 31, 1919, of unrestricted importation, except for the limitation that the drugs were to be used for medicinal purposes, with the ten months ending March 31, 1920, during which time the importation was under Government license. For the ten months ending March 31, 1919, the importation was 32,247 lbs., as compared with 7,995 lbs. for the ten months ending March 31, 1920, or a diminution of 24,252 pounds. Cocaine, for the same periods, dropped from 11,770 ounces to 5,250 ounces, and morphine from 25,677 ounces to 19,938 ounces.
The opium figures are in pounds, and cocaine and morphine in ounces?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. These figures will indicate to the House how great a reduction has been made in the past nine months. I think I should say to the House that I do not for one moment assume, and the department does not assume, that the great increase in the importation of opium, morphine and cocaine into Canada, which reached its high water mark in 1919 indicates that there was anything like a corresponding increase in the consumption of these drugs in Canada. The evidence we have would lead us to believe/ corresponding with the information which the American authorities have gathered, that by reason of the very stringent regulations adopted in the United States, those who are interested in getting the high prices which they could get for these drugs in the United States, but who were not able to import them through the regular channels, imported them through Canada. We had no limitation on import except a declaration that the drugs were required for medicinal purposes, and after once getting these drugs into Canada they succeeded in getting them into the American market. As to the figures I have given, it is anticipated that the results will be better as the months go by, because in the early days of the Government licensing system it took some time to get the system in thorough working order and to discover the bona fide importers as distinguished from the importers who were simply bringing these drugs, in for the purpose of getting them across the border into the United States.

Is the Department of Health in a position to say whether there has been a large amount of these drugs smuggled into Canada from the United
[Mr. Rowell.1

States. I understand it is rather an easy matter to smuggle through the border large quantities of morphine and cocaine.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am sure that hon.
members -will realize that it is with gTeat difficulty that smuggling of these drugs is stopped, because they are high-priced and are carried in small bulk. But our information would not lead us to think that there had been as large quantities of these drugs smuggled into Canada from the United States as from the United States into Canada, for the reason that up to the passing of the legislation of last session the United States had in operation a stricter law than ours and were able better to trace and follow up men who were violating the law than we were. Under the legislation of last session no man can import any of these drugs into Canada without obtaining a license to do so. In that license he must declare that the drugs are required only for medicinal purposes, and he must undertake to account for the disposition of the entire quantity. I may add that the depart ment does call upon every licensee to account for the manner in which he has disposed of these drugs, and by following up the information thus secured the department is able to check up that which is used for legitimate purposes and to trace that which is being used for illegitimate purposes or which is being disposed of to be smuggled into the United States. Better results are being secured every day in connection with this work, and with the legislation now before the House it is confidently anticipated that there will be a still greater improvement in enforcement of the law. The legislation of 1911 covers these drugs, and section five of the Act of that year provides that they shall not be sold except upon a doctor's prescription. It is not necessary this afternoon that I should enter Into a discussion of the effect of that section. There may be differences of opinion as to whether that section prohibited the sale of any preparations that contained any quantity of these drugs, or simply prohibited the sale of the drugs as such. I think that a fair interpretation of the Act of 1911 would be that it prohibited not only the drugs but preparations from them. Whatever may be the interpretation of the section, that matter is dealt with in the Bill now before the House. The important changes introduced into the legislation by the new Bill may be summarized briefly. First of all, in the definition of "drugs" itself, it is made perfectly clear that the prohibitions of the Act apply not only to the drug itself but to any preparations of it, subject to the exceptions provided in the Bill. Secondly, under the International Opium Convention, it is required-in order to limit the extent of this traffic as much as it is possible to do by legislation and regulation-that not only shall there be a limit to the purposes for which drugs may be imported, and for which they may be exported to other countries that have adopted regulations, but also that the ports of import or export shall be named so that it may be possible to check up what is coming in and going out; and it is also required that the packages which contain 'these drugs shall also be marked in such a way as to indicate their character. These are some of the requirements of the International Convention, and this legislation provides for such regulations.

Will the
minister be good enough to giye us an explanation regarding the International Convention to which he has referred? Is it intended that there shall be an international regulation with regard to these narcotic drugs, and particularly with regard to opium?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This convention provides for international regulation, and this legislation is to enable the 'Government of Canada to carry out the obligation it has assumed under the International Convention. As my hon. friend was not here, perhaps I may give just a word of explanation with regard to that Convention, although I explained that aspect of the subject when the resolution was before the committee.
Following an international conference held in Shanghai in 1909 to consider steps to be taken either to prohibit or to limit the trade in opium, at which conference Canada was represented by the present leader of the Opposition (Hon. Mackenzie King), then Deputy Minister of Labour, it was decided to call an international convention with a view to securing an international agreement to limit and control the trade in opium and similar drugs. That convention was held at The Hague in 1912. The International Convention of which I now speak was agreed upon at The Hague in 1912, but up to the beginning of the war it had not been found possible to obtain the assent of all the nations that were interested in the production of opium or in the growth of the poppy, and it was not

deemed fair to prohibit the trade of those countries [DOT]which were engaged in it and which were willing to sign the agreement, so long as other countries also engaged in the traffic would not come in. What they desired to do was to stop the trade, and if only some of the countries eneaued in it were willing to stop it, while others continued, it simply meant that the business would be transferred from the countries which were willing to stop to those which were not. That is why the convention had not been .fully signed and put into effect prior to the war. Among the chief countries which did not come in and which were interested in the trade were Austria, Turkey, (Germany to some extent, and Greece also to a limited extent; and the Allied and Associated Powers at the Peace Conference incorporated a provision in the Treaty of Peace with each of these countries requiring their adherence to the International Opium Convention, and stipulating that when the Treaty of Peace was ratified and carried into effect it carried with it the ratification of the International Opium Convention. As the Treaty of Peace with Germany has gone into effect by deposit of ratifications in the month of January of the present year, this convention is now in effect with Tespect to the powers that were parties to that Treaty. I think that this statement covers the (question raised by the hon. member.
Is it true that practically all the powers had agreed to the convention of 1912 prior to its discussion at the Peace Conference?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sorry I cannot answer my hon. friend this afternoon as I have not my papers in connection with the earlier proceedings.
Is it not a fact that the United States w.as the only power that had ratified the treaty.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend may be
correct in that but many had signed it and ( were only waiting a general agreement of the powers to ratify before ratifying. Great Britain, Canada and France were in that position. I think the powers interested were prepared to go on with the exception of the powers I have mentioned.

Can the minister
advise the House as to whether Turkey will accept the provision in the Peace Treaty to which he has referred?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That involves a very
much larger question than the Opium Con-

vention. I imagine that finally a Treaty of Peace with Turkey will be concluded and this certainly will be in the Treaty; so that I think we may proceed on the assumption that Turkey will be bound by this, provision. I was going on to remark that representations have been made to the Government that we should not absolutely prohibit the sale of preparations containing a limited quantity of these drugs except upon a prescription by a medical doctor. The Government in the amendment which I read to the House Friday night is prepared to meet that view to the extent indicated in the amendment. I think there is nothing to be gained by discussing the general terms of the amendment at the present time. We can discuss the matter with greater advantage when the Bill goes into committee. Therefore I move the second reading.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1, subsection 1-definition of " drug " :

What is the object of
striking out the words " imports, manufactures, sells, offers,for sale, has in his possession, or"? Would it be possible for the minister to read a list of the drugs contained in the schedule?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The drugs contained in
the schedule are cocaine, and any salts or compound's thereof; morphine and any salts or compounds thereof, and opium and eucaine and any salts or compounds thereof. Under section 14 of the Act of 1911 provision was made for adding to the schedule by Order in Council any other drugs, alkaloids, derivatives or preparations of the drugs named in the schedule, and by an Order in Council passed during the early part of the present year the schedule was amended by adding to it, after the word " opium " the words " or its preparations or any opium alkaloids or derivatives or salts, or preparation of opium alkaloids or derivatives." The schedule as it now stands would be as I have read it with these words added.
Would the minister be in a position to state in a few words the effect of striking out these words referred to in subsection 2 of section 1 and also in subsection 3 of section 1.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
Will these changes have
any connection with the requests made by the druggists to the minister last week?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, that comes in a later section.
On section 1, subsection 4-prescriptions. Mr. BUREAU: I desire to supplement the question put by my hon. friend to the minister in regard to the new section proposed to be substituted for subsection (4) of section 5. I understand that the introduction of this section, which the minister gave notice of on Friday evening last, was the result of communications that were received from various parties iwhoi are interested in the Act. Now I find something here that to my judgment ought to be carefully considered. In the latter part of the proposed section it is provided that a druggist cannot, without the consent of a physician, sell any drug upon a prescription already given without incurring a penalty of $1,000 and not less than $500 and imprisonment. If I read the section correctly that is what it contemplates; it applies to:
Any druggist who, without the authority of the prescribing physician, veterinary surgeon, or dentist uses any prescription to sell any drug on more than 6ne occasion.
Cases might arise in which such a provision would not only cause great inconvenience but great hardship. Take for instance the case of a man who is undergoing treatment from a doctor. He gets a prescription from his medical attendant but the latter goes away for a time. The prescription is exhausted, and the patient cannot go to another physician who has not treated him to get the same prescription-the other physician does not know anything about the circumstances. Therefore the man goes to his druggist and says "I had on such a date a prescription from Dr. So-and-So. Would you kindly renew it?" The druggist agrees to do so, and in so doing performs what I would consider a service not only to the sick man but to the community. Yet under this section as I read i't he is liable to a fine of not less than $500.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The section in that respect does not change the law as it has been since 1911 and no particular hardship has arisen out of it, so far as I am aware. The object of this provision, of course, is to prevent abuse. A doctor gives a prescription on a particular occasion and, unless there is a limit, the druggist might go on
selling indefinitely, whether the patient needed the drug or. not.

Notwithstanding that
such is the law I think it results in hardship and ought to be corrected. I quite appreciate the abuse that my hon. friend wants to reach; but the section could be so framed as to prevent that result and at the same time not impose hardship upon anybody. 'The section, as framed, is made general in its application. Why not limit its effect, or have the provision so worded that a prescription given by a medical man Ito ia patient in -a particular case may 'be renewed without exposing the druggist to this heavy penalty? My hon. friend states that no hardship has resulted from the operation of the law; but we know that drug stores these days and other places are filled with fellows trying to induce people to break the law in order to have a chance to lay a complaint against them and have them fined.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The difficulty is the one I have already mentioned: The change proposed would make possible the refilling of the prescription as frequently as a man might apply for it; and one knows how persistent is the Tequest for refilling prescriptions by men who are at all addicted to the use of these drugs. I am also under the impression-although in this I speak subject to correction-that most of the provincial Acts Tegulating the practice of pharmacy contain similar provisions; they require that these drugs shall be sold under certain restricted conditions, and I think that when a prescription is required it can only be used once.
I have no objection to the definition as laid down in 'the interpretation clause but this provision makes the law applicable to all drugs.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, it only deals with those habit-forming drugs which contain opium, morphine, heroin, and so forth. The definition clause reads as follows:
"Drug" means and includes any substance (whether alone or in conjunction with any other substance) mentioned in the schedule to this Act or which may be added to such schedule under the authority of this Act.
Now drugs can only be added to the schedule under the authority of the Act in case they are of a character I have already mentioned, viz:-that they are derivatives or alkaloids of those particular drugs referred to in the schedule, that is under section 14 of the Act of 1911.

I a.m not quite clear as to 'what is meant. I would like to ask the minister what is the meaning of the proposed new section 4. It reads that:
Any person who deals in any drug, who gives, sells or furnishes any drug to any person-
And so on. Does that apply to the ordinary drugs that are in daily use-for example in the practice of a veterinary-such [DOT]as carbolic acid, tincture of iron, sulphate of iron, and so on, things that are commonly used as disinfectants in case of sickness? Would it be an infraction of the law for these to be sold by a druggist for any particular purpoise?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. My hon. friend evidently did not hear the explanation I gave to my hon. friend from Three Rivers. This could only apply to the drugs referred to in the schedule-that is the group of habit-forming drugs such as opium, heroin, codeine, cocaine, and so forth. The Act is limited to drugs containing any of these preparations.
According to -this clause the physicians are themselves permitted to sell these drugs direct. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
Is there any restriction whatever upon the physician? Does the physician himself have-to keep a record of the sales which he makes of these habitforming drugs?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
Is there no check whatever upon the physician?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He is not compelled to keep a record of sales, but he is prohibited from prescribing except for the purposes mentioned in the Act. But when we come to another section of the Bill I intend to introduce an amendment requiring the physician to supply to the department any information which the department may require in regard to the use or sale of any of these drugs. '
What is the proposed amendment?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is set out in Hansard of Friday: It reads:
(4) Section 5, subsection 1, of the said Act is hereby repealed and the following substituted therefor:
" Any person who deals in any drug, who gives, sells or furnishes any drug to any person other than a duly authorized and practising physician, veterinary surgeon or dentist, or to a bona fide wholesale druggist, or to a druggist carrying on business in a bona fide drug store, and any druggist who gives, sells or furnishes any drug except upon a written order or prescription signed by a duly authorized and practising physician, veterinary surgeon or dentist, or who, without the authority of the prescribing physician, veterinary surgeon, or dentist, uses any prescription to sell any drug on more than one occasion, shall be guilty of a criminal offence and shall he liable, upon summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars and costs and not less than five hundred dollars and costs, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or to both fine and imprisonment."
That is the clause to which my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) has referred.

It is provided by this Bill that any retailer or manufacturer of drugs may sell to a practising physician any of these drugs. The seller has to keep a record of what he buys and of what he sells, but the doctor may obtain these drugs and dispense them to1 whomever he sees fit, without keeping any record. If any abuse occurs, there is no provision for suspending his license as practising physician or for the imposition of any other penalty. My opinion is that there ought to be some check on the physician-even if that view should bring down the thunders of the medical profession.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I suggest that we leave the discussion of that until we come to (5-A), in which'the question of keeping records is dealt with.

'This is a prohibitive
clause; if we are going to prohibit the handling of drugs by anybody, we ought to enumerate here all those who will be subject to that restriction.
Does this mean that the authority of the prescribing physician must be obtained in every case before the druggist may refill a prescription?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

Must the authority be
written, or may it be verbal? Can it be obtained by telephone, for instance?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This law as it stood since 1911 requires that the prescription shall be a written one.
For refilling?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The original prescription must be written; then it is provided that the prescription shall not be filled more than once.
It will work a great hardship in the western country, where we sometimes have to depend on physicians who reside from thirty to sixty miles away, if that restriction is imposed.

Suppose I had
a prescription filled in Ottawa and then travelled to my home in Saskatchewan: I might want to have that prescription refilled when I got home. Why should I not be able to do so?

My interpretation of that section is that the physician may write a prescription, and that subsequently, if the patient intends to leave for another part of the country, the physician may give the patient written authority for the refilling of the prescription as many times as the patient shall require. The words " without the authority of the prescribing physician" are used in the clause, and further down it is provided that the druggist shall not fill the prescription more than once. You must read also with that last provision the phrase " without the authority of the prescribing physician." I do not consider this clause as meaning that the physician shall have to write the prescription out every time that the bottle has to be refilled. It means that-every time the druggist refills a prescription he shall be authorized to do so by the prescribing physician.
But if he is away?

My hon. friend asks, "If he is away." The member for Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) wants to know what will happen if he leaves his home, where he had obtained a prescription, and comes to Ottawa. Well, if he is a sick man he will be as particular about his health and about taking the prescription to Ottawa as he is about
taking along with him the clothes he needs. If he comes tp live in Ottawa in winter, he will bring some winter clothing with him. If he leaves his home as a sick man and knows that he will require some drugs when he is in the capital city, he will certainly take heed and go to his physician before he leaves home in order to procure the necessary authority for the druggist in Ottawa to fill the prescription. It seems elementary that a man has as much concern about his health as he has about his clothing in cold or warm weather. If you read the clause from the first line to the last, you will see that it is not necessary, as I take it, for the physician each time to write down a prescription; it is only essential for the druggist to have from the prescribing physician the necessary authority to refill the prescription.
Has it not been a long standing practice for people to have prescriptions filled several times, without having new ones made out by the physician?

I think it has; but it
should not be so, and I will tell my hon. friend why. The drugs that are referred to in this clause are the drugs included in the schedule which are poisonous, deleterious, dangerous drugs. Let me give an illustration. My hon. friend will get a prescription for a case of bronchitis and this prescription will very likely contain some narcotic. He will have a four ounce bottle filled on this prescription; he will leave the prescription with the druggist, take the bottle home and drink the contents; and when the bottle is empty, instead of being dead, he will be better.
Strange.

He will have entirely recovered; but his neighbour who has some kind of a disease of the chest and who does not know anything about it pays a visit to my hon. friend and says: "1 am coughing very badly." My hon. friend replies: "Oh, here is my bottle; go to the druggist he will fill it; you need not go to a doctor." His friend goes to the druggist; gets the narcotic, drinks it and dies, because the drug that has been prescribed for my hon. friend is not intended for his neighbour. It is to prevent such abuses taking place and such dangerous risks being taken by people who do not consult a proper medical authority, that this clause has been framed.

My hon. friend surely does not think for a minute that I am as little concerned about my health as

about my old suit of clothes. When I go to a physician and that physician prescribes a prescription for me, that prescription is mine; and if I choose to use that prescription several times, that should be my business. I certainly object to this provision that prevents a patient from having a prescription refilled without going back to his physician every time he wants the prescription refilled. I think that is an injustice and an imposition.

In such a case, there is
a remedy for the situation. Supposing my hon. friend has contracted a chronic disease. He gets a prescription from his doctor, and he may easily at the same time obtain from his doctor authority to have it refilled as many times as he likes. But he must have that authority, and if he has an acute disease, my hon. friend is going to have almost a daily call from his physician.

I do not know the custom in other parts of Canada; but in most cities in Ontario, the custom in regard to prescriptions is that if a doctor gives a prescription which contains no harmful drug, the druggist will fill it as many times as the patient requires without the necessity of the patient obtaining a new prescription from the doctor, and I presume that is also the custom in the other provinces of Canada. But where a prescription contains drugs such as morphine or opium or cocaine or chloral, which may be harmful, the druggist would refuse to refill the prescription without an order from the doctor, and he would be quite right in so doing. As regards a question of the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) regarding the authorization of refilling prescriptions, any druggist in the country, once he knows that he is dealing with a responsible doctor, would accept a telephone order from the doctor to refill a prescription and let the doctor send the written prescription by mail. As regards the case he mentions of a man ten or thirty miles away from a doctor,, the man would get a prescription from the doctor, and when the man wanted it refilled, and the doctor thought it was proper to have it refilled, the doctor could easily telephone the necessary authorization to the druggist, and then the doctor could send the written authorization by mail.

Supposing the doctor is
overseas and not within reach.

Then the patient would have to consult another doctor. If the pre-

scription did not contain harmful drugs, there would be no difficulty about having it refilled.

It seems rather strange that on the one hand you will permit prescriptions being sold containing a certain quantity of the harmful drugs which the hon. member mentions, and yet, on the other hand, you cannot get a prescription refilled even if it does not contain any of these drugs.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken. There is nothing to prevent a prescription being refilled as often as you like unless it contains some of these drugs. This Act is absolutely limited to these particular drugs and preparations containing them; it does not deal with any other drugs at all.
I cannot read that into this clause.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will see that the description of the "drug" is referred to in the schedule.
I understand that.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The schedule in the Act of 1911 is absolutely limited to these drugs. There is no power to add to the schedule drugs of a different character.
I quite understand that, but this clause deals with prescriptions specifically, not with drugs.
With any drugs.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will see that the word "drug" in this Act, Wherever it applies, means drug as defined in the schedule, and that is the object of having an interpretation clause. If my hon. friend will turn to the interpretation clause, he will see that subclause (a) says that the word "drug," wherever used in this Act, is limited by the definition of "drug" contained in the interpretation clause.
The term "any drug" seems to extend the meaning beyond the interpretation clause.

A restriction of this nature is absolutely essential to dangerous drugs, because a patient in getting a prescription does not know what it contains. The doctor does not tell him what is in that prescription. The patient may not consult the doctor again for a considerable time, and if he is having a prescription refilled, he may' be injuring his health. I have known certain cases of that kind. For

instance, a man got a prescription containing a considerable quantity of aconite for some acute trouble. The doctor met him on the road .some months afterwards, and the man stopped him and asked how much longer he should go on taking the prescription, telling the doctor that he had been taking it ever since. It is a wonder the man was still alive. He did not realize the dangerous character of the drug, so that it is quite evident that a restriction of this kind is .absolutely essential in -connection with the dangerous drugs mentioned in the schedule in this Act. The general public are not cognizant of the drugs which they are taking, and it is not the place of a doctor to tell them exactly what they are taking, because even if he did, they would not know anything about it anyway.
And they might not come back for a new prescription.
No competent druggist would refill a prescription containing drugs that were deleterious to human life.

I think the minister could get over the difficulty by limiting the number of drugs in respect of which the prescription can only be filled once. The minister was good enough to meet the wishes of the druggists, and I think the people are just as worthy of consideration.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not see how you *could define what should be in a prescription, and what should not, before it can be refilled. I woud draw my hon. friend's attention to the provincial legislation on this question. I do not know what the law is in Saskatchewan, but these drugs are so thoroughly recognized throughout the country as being poisonous and dangerous to health that I think every provincial legislature, with the possible exception of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, has legislated with reference to some or all of these drugs. I have before me the Ontario Act. It has since been amended. I have not the amendment before me, but the amendment extends the scope of the provisions dealing with these particular drugs. The Ontario Act absolutely prohibits a druggist from filling more than once a prescription containing any admixture of cocaine or eucaine. It goes further and says: "No copy thereof shall be taken by or given to any person by the person who has the custody or control thereof." That was no doubt to meet the point raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Beland).
Does the Ontario Act deal only with the two drugs mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That particular section deals with only these two drugs, but my recollection is that the Act was amended in 1917 to cover opium and other drugs. I speak subject to correction because I have not the amendment before me.

The law now provides that the prescription of the physician must be in writing. The proposed amendment provides that with the consent of the prescribing physician the prescription may be filled more than once. The hon. member (Mr. Manion) has stated in a general way that in general practice prescriptions are filled more than once without anything in the shape of formal consent on the part of the attending physician. It is clearly intended under this amendment that the prescription should be filled more than once, and it would surely be wise for the section to state specifically how the authority to refill is to be given. Otherwise, we shall only be providing for litigation. The discussion so far has made it perfectly clear that no one seems to know exactly in what form consent is to be given to refill prescriptions. I think some provision should be made by which it would be possible to fill a prescription more than once without having the doctor's consent in writing, because in many cases it would be impossible to get it when it was required.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have now before me the Ontario Act as amended, and I find that as I suggested, that it is broader in its scope. It provides that:
(1)	No person or incorporated company shall sell by retail, furnish or dispose of alkaloid cocaine or its salts, or alpha or beta eucaine 'or their salts, or any admixture of cocaine or eucaine, or heroin, or codeine, or morphine or its salts, or any admixture thereof, or opium, including crude opium, powdered opium, or opium prepared or in course of preparation for smoking, except upon the written prescription of a legally qualified medical practitioner personally signed by him, which shall be retained -by the person who sells, furnishes or disposes of the same, and a record of the prescription shall be kept in a book which shall contain the name of the physician, the number of the prescription, the quantity sold, the name of the person for whom prescribed or supplied, and the date of the sale.
(2)	The prescription shall not be filled more than once and no copy thereof shall be taken by or given to any person by. the person who has the custody or control thereof.
The Ontario Act is, in its detailed statement as to "personally signed" and so on, even more sweeping than our legislation.
The Ontario Act specifically enumerates the drugs.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: These are the drugs enumerated in the schedule to this Bill.
The word "any" is what I object to.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have no objection to saying "any drug specified in this Act," though that is the effect of the Bill.
That would be better, to my mind.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am quite prepared to7 do that, but I think my hon. friend overlooks the serious character of these drugs; these drugs are looked upon, and in fact are so deleterious to health, if taken in excess, that the greatest precautions are thrown around their prescription and administration. They do not cure: they allay pain. They create conditions that will tend to a cure under certain definite conditions depending on the health of the individual to whom they are administered. They do not possess any curative properties in themselves. They are hypnotic in their influence. I am quite prepared to say "any drug covered by this Act."

Would it not be wise to make provision in the Bill that ordinary patent medicines containing a small proportion of these drugs shall be exempt under the Act? I understand that in the United States there is a law known as the Harrison Law, under which preparations and remedies which do not contain more than 2 grains of opium, or more than i grain morphine, or more than i grain heroin, or more than 1 grain codeine, or any salt or derivative of any of them, in a fluid ounce, are exempt. I think some such provision should be made in this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my hon. friend will read Friday's Hansard he will find that I have given notice of an amendment to cover that point. We will come to it on a later section.

I think the subject matter of this Bill is so technical that it would be better to refer it to a special committee where all parties concerned could have an opportunity of being heard. Any member of this House who is not a druggist or a manufacturing chemist or a member of the medical profession must find it difficult to follow the ideas that were in the minds of those who framed this Bill. It seems to me that it is designed particularly to prevent

druggists from selling their regular lines of patent medicines containing a small proportion of drugs of this kind. We all know that the medical profession is an admirable one, but the members of it are only human like the rest of us. I need only refer to what has happened in connection with the administration of the prohibition law in the province of Ontario during the last twelve months. Unlike Caesar's wife,
. the physicians are not above suspicion; and they are liable-
I must ask the hon. member'to substantiate his accusation.

The hon. gentleman
should read the press. One member of the profession is reported to have issued as many as 1,200 prescriptions in a month, and I am sure the minister will himself admit that this number of prescriptions, issued in so short a time, is at least sufficient to create suspicion.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend is a much better judge on that point that I.

I have certain letters
which have been written with regard to this legislation, and one communication from a druggist practising in the town of Chesley, Ontario, I should like very much to read to the committee, because it is pertinent to the subject under consideration. This letter reads:
Dear Sir,-Were the public at large to realize fully the effect of the provisions of the Opium and Drug Act now before the House, a storm of protest and disapproval would undoubtedly be raised for its immediate repeal.
Unquestionably no such radical enactment as this Act provides for would ever be conceived without the efforts of sinister and designing influences who stand to profit thereby. Personally I have only realized its significance during the last few days, and I am sure that a measure containing such arbitrary legislation will not knowingly receive your support in the House. In the past practically all the better known and reliable cough medicines have contained small quantities of sedataive drugs, certainly most valuable where their helpful use is indicated. Today practically every physician buys his cough mixtures in bulk (I know this to be a fact because I supply them), and these compounds contain just the same narcotic drugs, compounded in just the same manner as do the reliable so-called patent medicine lines. The difference is just this, the patient goes to the drug store and invests 25c. for his treatment instead of going to the medical man and paying $1.00 for a like article. This certainly would bring much grist to the medical man, but is it in the interests of the masses of the people? Certainly not.
Take another line of medicines which have and do serve a most valuable purpose, i.e., the wild strawberry compounds. I can well imagine the feelings of the citizen living in rural

sections who finds it expedient to have a hottle of the above on hand. An attack of dysentery would mean under the present provisions of the Act that the individual would have to drive to town to have his physician prescribe or administer a dose of an astringent medicine, and then back again in case the first dose was not effective. All effective dysentery remedies contain proper dosages of opium, and whose use in this connection cannot possibly be abused.
The amendments proposed to the Act are such as will overcome the above and similar injustices and still effectively protect the public from the indiscriminate use of narcotic drugs. These amendments provide for the quantity of said drugs to be contained in a given quantity of the medicine. I trust that you are giving careful consideration to this Act and will support proper amendments which will safeguard the public and prevent an injustice to both the public and the druggists, whose Joint interests are so vitally involved.
By whom is that letter written, and to whom is it addressed?

The letter I have just read is addressed to R. E. Truax, M.P., and it is signed by S. R. Davey, Phm. B. I do not know what these initials* stand for. I have another letter signed by some druggists of Renfrew, Ont. I shall not read the letter, but the druggists are: W. B. Clark, W. A. Cameron, D. J. Ritza, and Fraser and Smart.
I also have a similar communication, written on stationery of Henry K. Wampole and Company, and bearing the name of a prominent member of Parliament from the county of Lanark.
I think that a Bill of this kind, Mr. Chairman, could be much more effectively dealt with by a special committee, and I now therefore move that this Bill be referred to a special committee of the House in order that opportunity may be given to all parties interested to be heard and to give fud expression to their views upon the subject.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member's
motion is not in order. It is impossible for the comittee of the House to refer a Bill to a special committee. That motion must be made by the House itself.
I trust that at the proper time I shall have an opportunity of making this motion.

I have received several letters along the same lines as the letter which the hon. member (Mr. Pedlow) has read to the committee. A denudation of members met a large gathering of druggists here two or three weeks ago, and I believe that the objections that were urged by those druggists at the time were properly laid before the minister, and it is as a result of the representations that they then made that these amendments are now before the House. As
I understand these amendments, they cover all the ground asked for by the druggists. What the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) has just suggested is simply repeating what was urged'in hundreds of letters and telegrams sent to the House, that our Act should be amended to embody the provisions of the Harrison Act in operation in the United States. I must express my sympathy with the hon. member for Renfrew to this extent, that, due possibly to a lack of technical knowledge of matters of this kind, we are very apt to pass legislation and afterwards discover that we have made mistakes. And to some extent the amendments which we are asked to make today are due to the fact that the legislation we passed last year was not wisely considered nor fully understood. The tendency of the House is to assume too much an attitude of paternalism, which tends to make the people restless; and it is unfortunate that the House should pass legislation only to be repealed and re-enacted in some other form	the year	following.
I think it would be better to refer the consideration of these subjects to a committee which understands them rather than that we should arrive at conclusions in Com-.mittee of the Whole without a proper knowledge by the members of the subject undediscussion. But in view of the full representations that were made and in view of the fact that the minister has tried to meet these representations, possibly all the objections the druggists have had are fully covered by the amendments here.

This House has listened to many speeches from the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr Pedlow) but I doubt if it has ever listened to one quite so absurd and illogical as that with which he has just favoured us. He takes to task a learned profession which he seems to be very little conversant with and he says that very few members of the medical profession are trustworthy. Let me say to the my hon. friend that I am satisfied- that the medical profession can set up a cleaner record than his craft the retail clothiers, who have certainly not done anything to quiet the unrest which prevails throughout the country. He says that one member of the medical profession issued 1,200 prescriptions for liquor in a month. During the influenza epidemic I was making some fifty visits a day and I prescribed whiskey for every one of my patients. If you will figure that up you will see what it amounts to in a month. I do not know whether I prescribed 1,200 in a month or not but I pretty nearly

did anyway. I never knew a patient who took half a tumbler of whiskey, went to bed and stayed there, who did not get better of influenza. If the doctors had not prescribed whiskey, there are a great many people now roaming around who would be sleeping in the churchyard. If the whole medical profession appreciated the value of whiskey in certain cases, especially influenza, the results would be much more satisfactory. There is no comparison between the results obtained by those who treated influenza with whiskey and the results obtained by those temperance cranks who did not prescribe whiskey. Twelve hundred prescriptions a month during the epidemic were nothing out of the ordinary for a physician with a large practice to prescribe.
The prescribing of drugs such as this Bill deals with cannot be thrown wide open so that the person obtaining a prescription can have it repeated as many times as he wishes. In Winnipeg and other large centres we have many morphine and dope fiends and the only way in which we can hope to cure them is by cutting down the number of their prescriptions and reducing the quantity, and many have been cured in that way. If I were to write a prescription for a gramme of morphine and give to a person, and if that person could go to a druggist and have it filled as often as he wished, we might as well have no law whatever governing the sale of drugs. The small amount of two grains of morphine put in a cough medicine to be taken in eight doses is not going to do anybody any harm. People can get these patent medicines if they want them but when it comes to the prescription of morphine, cocaine, or any of the drugs that the schedule to this Bill contains, it is absolutely impossible to fling the door wide open. The hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) has spoken about farmers driving thirty-five or forty miles to town for medicine but you do not find these dope fiends out on the wide prairie. The people there live healthy lives and they have no need for drugs. It is only in the large centres of population that we find the dope fiends, and all they have to do is to go half a mile, or any short distance within the limits of the city, to get their prescription refilled. It is absolutely essential, if we hope to control the sale of drugs and help these people to get this habit out of their lives, to make it necessary that they must come for another prescription. It is not because the physician takes a mercenary view of this matter. I have only one dope fiend under my care. I 
do not know where she gets the money to buy the dope; she has never any to pay for the prescription and while I have given her six or seven doses, I am gradually bringing down the quantity. But, I have never got a penny for the prescription. ,1 think many other medical men have had the same experience. These poor people are generally extremely hard up, and they would be better without the drug. Unfortunately we have no institutions in Canada to which we can compel them to go and be cured. When they go into hospitals of their own free will the hospitals and the medical men are willing to treat them and they gradually reduce the quantity of the drug. The patients have nothing to do with administering the drug; it is given to them by the nurses and attendants and they finally are cured, and they can be cured if they set their minds to it and had sufficient determination. But it is absolutely hopeless to cure them if they are allowed to get a prescription refilled as many times as they wish. In some iAstances one prescription will serve a whole community because birds of a feather flock together, these people know each other, they congregate in districts, and one prescription may suffice to satisfy the whole lot if they can have it refilled constantly.

Reference has been made by the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) and also by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) to the representations made by the retail druggists when they waited on the minister some few weeks ago. The suggestion to refer the Bill to a special committee so that these representations might be considered further was made by the hon. member for South Renfrew. I was privileged to be present and to take part in the interview with the minister on the 7th April. I am sure that the amendment as suggested by the President of the Privy Council, and contained in Hansard of Friday, substantially covers the request made by that deputation relative to the terms of the Bill as originally drawn, with the exception of some matters of detail which will be dealt with when the sections are reached. There will consequently be no necessity to refer the Bill to a special committee for the purpose suggested by the hon. member for South Renfrew.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I may say for the information of my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) that before this deputation waited on the minister I

sent to the minister some communications received from the druggists and asked that they be given attention in connection with the Bill. I have understood from the minister that the particular matters referred to in these communications were those taken up by the deputation that waited on the Government and that the points to which special attention has been directed have been covered by the suggested amendments. If that be so, I do not see that any useful purpose would be served by referring the Bill to a special committee at this stage. If on the contrary the minister cannot assure us that the representations made by the druggists have been covered in a satisfactory way, there is something in the suggestion and it should receive consideration.

I am not quite sure that we all have in our' minds the fact that the prohibitions and penalties referred to in this proposed amendment are confined to the drugs set forth in the schedule. You will notice that subsection 4, wbich is being amended, provides that the Governor in Council may add to this schedule of drugs. Take the definition of the word "dTug" in subsection (a) of section 1:
"Drug" means and includes any substance (whether alone or in conjunction with any other substance) mentioned in the schedule to this Act or which may be added to such schedule under the authority of this Act.
Subsection 4 of section 1 gives authority by Order in Council to add to this schedule "any preparation named or described in such regulation," in these words:
Provided, however, that the Governor in Council may by regulation to be published in the Canada Gazette extend and apply the provisions of the said paragraphs (e) and (f) to any preparation named or described in such regulation.
If this is adopted the Governor in Council can declare anything to be an injurious preparation and add it to the drugs mentioned in the schedule. This proposed amendment would apply to the additions. I am not quite sure whether all the members of the committee have that in their minds. There are one or two other things I desire to point out. Subclauses (e) and
(f)	contain a prohibition against persons having drugs in their possession no matter how they obtain them; even if they have bought them from a druggist on a prescription from a doctor. For example the wording of paragraph (e) of subsection (2) is:
Any person who.-
(e) has in his possession or manufactures, sells, gives away or distributes any drug without first obtaining a license from the minister.
Although the person may have got a prescription from a doctor, gone to a druggist and obtained the drug, if he has the drug in his possession he may be prosecuted and fined a minimum penalty of $500. Something must be done to remedy that; it was never intended that such a condition should exist.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Might I suggest that we first dispose of the amendments we are now cosidering? I shall be very glad when we come to subsection (5A)-which is the one referred to-to deal with the point raised but I think we should first make some progress with the amendments now under review.

I do not like delaying
the committee but I am not at all satisfied with the section with which we * are now dealing. The minister surely can get around this provision in some way, at least to the extent that is permitted in the case of ordinary patent medicines. I do not think such a modification could be considered as going too far, particularly as regards the veterinary profession. We get some epidemics among our stock very similar to those which affect human beings -for example influenza-quite often, and if it is necessary to hunt up a veterinary surgeon it will at times be very hard to find one. In the West there are very few veterinary surgeons. Even in our larger centres there would not be more than a couple of them, and they have to cover a territory extending for forty, fifty, or sixty miles. It surely must be unnecessary to have such a restriction in this clause with respect to medicine required for live stock.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is the next section
which deals with the exceptions. The one I have moved-which is to repeal the old section 5 and substitute a new section 5, and which is set forth in Hansard of Friday-contains the prohibition against the sale without the prescription. It is the next section (5A) and the amendments I have proposed to this section which deal with the exceptions, that is the time, I submit, when we should deal with any modification or rather exception, if there is to be any, to the prohibition in this clause. Let us deal first with the general prohibition and then deal with the exceptions separately. The second amendment of which I gave notice Friday evening does exempt from the operation of this section,

prescriptions containing the limited amounts of these deleterious drugs which are mentioned in that subsection. In the case of medicines that do not contain more than' the limited amounts mentioned in the amendment a doctor's prescription is not required at all. That is expressly provided for. Medicines which contain these minimum amounts are exempted from this section entirely.
That refers to drugs; it does not make any exception in the case of physicians, veterinary surgeons, and dentists' prescriptions.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It exempts the sale of
these drugs entirely from this clause. No medical prescription at all is required for those preparations containing the limited quantities of these drugs mentioned in the new amendment. They are wholly withdrawn from the operation of this clause.

I can quite understand
going that far, but that does not enable a party getting a prescription from a veterinary surgeon to go and have the prescription filled again.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I cannot consent to
change that because of the serious consequences that might ensue from the distribution of these poinsonous and very deleterious drugs. Such a restriction has been found necessary in other countries. For example the United States is stricter than we are in some respects at least in connection with this law. They require registration by everybody who sells. This section has been the law for nine years and we are not now proposing anything new in this respect. I know it to be the law also in Ontario under provincial legislation, and I believe the same is in operation in a number of other provinces-a law which the provinces have enacted on their own initiative in order to protect the public from the noxious drugs.

The matter of the form in which the consent of the prescribing physician is to be signified is not dealt with in the section, and I submit to the minister that if it is the intention of the department that the consent of the prescribing physician should be in writing, the section should so state. The section is very particular to state that the prescription must be in writing, and that it must not be repeated without the consent of the prescribing physician, but it makes no statement as to the form in which that consent is to be signified. I urge upon the minis-

ter that the section in its present form will tend to cause misunderstanding and create litigation, and result in confusion in the courts if the matter comes up for adjudication.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would think that a fair interpretation of this section would involve that that consent be given in some written form because a record must be kept by the druggist, and he must be in a position to show his authority. It might be given over the phone, followed up by the necessary authority, but I do not think we should weaken it in that respect.
Very well, add the words " in writing."

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the committee desires to have the words " in writing " inserted I am quite willing, but I think that is what is required under the existing law.

I think the section should be left as it is for the reasons mentioned by my hon. friend from Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) in connection with veterinary work. The same reasons also apply to medical work. Very often a physician is in bed and in the night one of his patients requires to have repeated some medicine that he has been using. The physician may be two miles from the patient, even in a city, and both may be a mile or two from the druggist. It is too bad to insist that a patient must go a couple of miles to the doctor, then a mile or two to the druggist, and then back home, when the physician could telephone the druggist telling him to refill the prescription. I think the word " authority " covers that, and it is up to the druggist to see that the following day or at the earliest possible moment, he gets a prescription covering that authority. Such a change as that suggested would, I think, result in very great inconvenience and certainly would not be observed.
5 p.m. The minister tells us this requirement of the law has been in force since 19.11-I understood him to say that-but if so it certainly has not been observed. I have been practising all those years and I must confess I have never observed it; and I am sure that no other physician in Ontario has-I refer to the provision for written authority for the refilling of prescriptions. Orders for the refilling of prescriptions have repeatedly been sent over the telephone. I think, therefore* that the word " authority " is sufficient, without insistence upon the repeated written prescription.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.

On subsection 5, (former subsection 4)

Minister may issue licenses for import, export, etc., of any drug and may make regulations therefor:
I take it that "import" does not cover prohibited goods passing through Canada in bond en route to another country.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The section is broad enough to cover and is intended to cover drugs that pass through Canada. Apart from the practical considerations which might induce us to adopt such legislation from our own standpoint, one of the provisions of the International Opium Convention requires that the import and export of these drugs be strictly regulated. That is, you cannot export indiscriminately. Each country binds itself to carry out the provisions of this convention. They further bind themselves not to export to any country which prohibits import. This provision is to give us that control over both export and import which it is necessary to have in order to carry out the terms of the Treaty.

A consignment of silks arriving in Vancouver and destined for Newfoundland could hardly be regarded as an import into Canada. I have always understood that the word "import" to refer to goods brought into Canada for consumption in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The rule which has been adopted is to require even the drugs which come in in bond to come under the provisions of these regulations. During the past ten months requests have been received for license to import in bond very large quantities for storage in Canada, the ostensible purpose being to ship to Japan. The illicit trade is so profitable that the greatest care has to be taken. The intention of this Act is to cover the bringing into Canada of drugs for any purpose. It is intended to be broader than the ordinary case my hon. friend has referred to.

Well, if we are making new law, I am not so much concerned about it. But the case I had in mind is a case where goods went from New York through Canada to Newfoundland. A law was about to go into force in New York under which the shippers would not have been able to send the goods out of New York at all. The time was subsequently extended, but the shippers were not aware of that. They found that they could not export from Canada, the Canadian law evidently prohibiting such export. They consulted the British consul 105
in New York, and were informed that exportation could be made from Newfoundland, the law there not prohibiting it. Accordingly, the goods were sent to Newfoundland and thence to Japan. I do not want to get. any snap verdict from the minister, but I do not regard that as an importation into Canada. As a matter of law, the importation of goods into Canada is the importation of goods for Canadian use. If goods pass through Canada en route to another country, whether in a car or on a boat or in a flying machine, they can hardly be considered as importations into Canada. If the shipment of tea from China through Canada to Liverpool is not importation into Canada; if the shipment of a million dollars' worth of silks through Vancouver and across Canada to Liverpool is not importation into Canada-and nobody will contend that it is-I cannot understand how the passing of drugs through Canada en route to some other country is an importation into Canada. That is the point that I wish to bring to the minister's attention; I want him to think it over.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I should be glad to give further consideration to the point, but the question my hon. friend has raised has already arisen in the administration of the law, and the matter has been submitted to the Department of Justice. It is true that under the general 1-aw relating to shipments in bond, goods may be brought into Canada - in bond, passed through Canada and pass out again without being considered as imports under the provisions of our law. My hon. friend is quite correct in that general assumption as to the meaning of the law; but the Department of Justice is of the opinion that where we provide as we do in this Act that some specific class of goods shall not be imparted into Canada except under license and we make no exception for transmission of those goods in - bond through Canada, then a license is necessary. That is under the Act passed last year. In requiring a license we are not changing the law which .was passed last session. Of course, the object of requiring a license in a case of this kind is to prevent goods from being brought in ostensibly for the purpose of transhipment, which goods, once they get into Canada, .are removed from the oar, the look on the car being broken or through 'some other means, and disposed of in Canada or smuggled across the line, because it is very profitable to do that.

This .subclause 1 of clause 5A deals in its latter part with the amount



of the license fee to be charged, and it staJtes that the fee shall not exceed the sum of $25 for any license that may he granted under the Act. The question of the amount of that fee is one that will be affected by the further amendment which it is proposed to make under the notice contained in Friday's Hansard. Under the law a manufacturer who is manufacturing preparations containing less than the quantity of scheduled drugs permitted under the proposed amendment will, under the Act, be liable to pay a fee up to $25; but under the provisions of the exception contained in the further proposed amendment, .a retail druggist may manufacture his own remedies containing the 'permitted quantities of scheduled drugs, and as the Act now reads he would be liable to pay the same license fee as the manufacturer. Surely, a retail druggist who may manufacture a very limited number and quantity of his own remedies should not be liable to pay as large ia fee as a manufacturer who manufactures many lines and in very large quantities. The matter, of course, is, under the provisions of the clause as it reads now, within the discretion of the minister. All that the clause does is to limit the amount of the fee Ito $25. The suggestion, however, is that there should be one fee and that there would be no difference between the case of a manufacturer and that of a retail druggist. What is the intention of the department with reference to the license fee?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will look carefully at the clause, he will see that different forms of licenses are contemplated for different classes of dealers, and it provides for making regulations with respect to the issue, duration, terms and forms of the several licenses that may be issued hereunder and to the payment of fees for such licenses. I quite agree with my hon. friend that it would not be right to charge a druggist, who- is making up his own prescriptions, the same fee as you would charge a large wholesale manufacturer, and it is the intention in fixing the fees for the different classes, to have regard to the extent of the manufacture carried on by the different classes who are authorized under this clause to manufacture or deal in drugs. The fee for a druggist who would do that should be a very small one and I should think that $5 would be quite adequate to meet the situation. The abject of the provisions as to fees is not, as regards this Act, to get a revenue, but to pay the cost of administra-

tion. We want the Act to pay the cost of its administration and not to he a charge upon the public treasury, and that would he the factor which wuuld determine what the amount of the fee would be.
As regards the $5 fee to the local druggist, would it be the intention that he should pay a $5 fee for each variety of prescription that he makes up?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This does not deal with prescriptions in that sense; it is a license to manufacture, and it would be a license fee for a year for everything a druggist may manufacture.
He may manufacture a line of cough medicines and another line of something else.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He would not require 'Separate licenses under this legislation. The license would he a license to manufacture or to sell, and that license would he good for a year for whatever class of prescriptions he manufactures under the provisions of this particular legislation.

I -asked the minister a question in regard to subclause 1 of clause 5A, and he was good enough to tell me that there is a decision of the Department of Justice on a certain point. Might I ask the minister if, before this Bill passes, he will -give the committee the benefit of that opinion? When we are dealing with a Bill of this kind and are told that there is a decision of the Department of Justice, it is only fair, if the decision is not too long, that we should have an opportunity of reading what the Department of Justice says.	*
