The penalties imposed under this section are rather excessive. There seems to be a tendency, not only on the part of this Government but of other governments as well, to create crimes that do not exist under the Criminal Code, and to impose very heavy penalties either by way of imprisonment or by fine. Subclause (f) of this subsection, as amended, makes the offender guilty of a criminal offence, and provides that he shall be liable upon summary conviction to a fine not exceeding $1,000 and costs, and not less than $500 and costs, or to imprisonment for' a term not to exceed one year, or to both fine and imprisonment. If they make a contravention of these provisions a criminal offence, it seems to me that the Government should not deprive an accused person of any of the remedies which he would ordinarily have if convicted of any offence under the Code. Our methods of procedure under the Criminal Code are divided into three classes: Under indictment for criminal offence; under the section of the Code which provides for summary trial; and under section 15, I think, of the Code, providing for summary conviction. When a man is brought to trial under the summary conviction section of the Code, his rights are limited to the smallest degree. You may take a druggist who is summoned before a stipendiary magistrate or two justices of the peace who have equal (jurisdiction. If there is a conviction his right of appeal is cut off except where he may desire to appeal to the district court or county court judge. The result is that he has no trial before the district court or county court judge and if a conviction
is obtained any further right of appeal on behalf of the man is taken away. I believe that where a man is charged with anything in the nature of a crime, and this Act makes the contravention of its subsections a crime, the person so charged should have his full rights under the same procedure as that which applies where a man is charged with theft or burglary or any other crime under the general code. Another difficulty that arises in connection with this procedure is that under the Criminal Code, if a man is charged with a criminal offence and he is tried and appeals, there is no burden placed upon him so far as his appeal is concerned. He has the right to appeal to the supreme court of the province and, with the consent of the judge, to the Supreme Court of *Canada without his being required to deposit any security or to give bonds for costs. Take the first section here. A penalty is provided for any person who "imports into or exports from Canada any drug without first obtaining a license." Take a man who imports, through a' port of entry, say, in British Columbia, goods which are to be used perhaps in the province of Nova Scotia. The offence would be committed at the port of entry; the importation would take place in British Columbia. The accused is in the province of Nova (Scotia. He is brought before the magistrates and convicted. He desires to appeal. All the evidence in this case is in the province of British Columbia and the first thing that the magistrates would do under part 15 of the Code, under which they are compelled to proceed in this case, would be to say to the accused: "You have the right to appeal but one of the conditions precedent to your appeal is that you shall either deposit the amount of the costs or give a bond securing the costs in the appeal." What does that mean? Witnesses may have to be brought from British Columbia or the accused may have to go from Nova Scotia to British Columbia to stand his trial, and it involves great expense on his part. He might have to take witnesses from Nova Scotia. The justices of the pace might fix his costs at $500 or $1,000, as I have known them to do under the summary convictions sections. You make the appeal prohibitory in the case of that man, while as a matter of justice and of law he has perfectly good grounds for an appeal. One thing that this Government should frown down upon is the creation of a serious offence undeT any statute and then compelling a man to have his trial under the summary convictions sections of the Code, part 15. Having created

a serious offence, it is our duty to place at his disposal every right that a man charged *with a serious offence under the Criminal Code has and to compel him to go to his trial under the summary convictions sections of the Code, it seems to me, is to take away from him . rights which he should enjoy just the same is if he were charged with any other offence.

I mentioned previously that there should be a word or two added to clause (e) of section 2 because it makes it an offence for a man to have possession of any one of these drugs; it matters not how he came into possession of them. The point might be met by adding after the word,s "in his possession" the words "illegally obtained" or something to that effect. As the matter now stands a man might get a doctor's prescription, go to a drug store, buy a drug, the inspector might find it in his possession and he could be fined $500 by the magistrate for having it in his possession, no matter how he came by it.

No doubt my hon. friend is right. The intention was to cover the retailer or trader, but if you stick to the wording you find that a man who has in his possession a bottle containing some narcotic might be very severely punished even although he obtained it legally.
The point might be met by inserting after the words "in his possession" the words "without lawful authority."
Very good.
I therefore move to amend paragraph (e) of subsection 2 by inserting after the word "possession" the words "without lawful authority."

I appreciate the point raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Tweedie) but on the other hand if you are not going to permit these cases to be dealt with by summary procedure under the Code you are going to have delays in prosecution and a lack of harmony in procedure under different clauses of the Act.
I would submit it is wise to deal with cases under the section by summary procedure. That is the practice under the present law, that has been the law for the past nine years, and that is the reason for inserting in this section the word " criminal." I do not know that it changes the character of the offence at all; it was done as a matter of form, so that no argument could be raised as between offences. Under section 5 in the law as it stands where the offence is described as a criminal offence and under section 5a where it is simply referred to as an offence. Therefore for the sake of uniformity I proposed the amendment. It is, however, in the exercise of the

criminal jurisdiction of this Parliament that we are dealing with this particular matter-that is the basis upon which the original legislation stand's, as I am advised. Therefore I do not think we are adding to, or taking from,- the clause anything by using the word " criminal " I referred to. It is simply to avoid an argument being made that there is a distinction between offences under this clause 5a and under clause 5 that I have moved to insert the word " criminal " before offence.

I still maintain my
point. If small penalties were being imposed under this Bill-say $10 or $15-and if there was no option to the imposition of the term of imprisonment, summary conviction would be very good procedure; but here we are takng away the liberty of a man for a period of a year, and I think that is very unfair. The section might be worded so that the proceeding might be either under summary conviction or indictment and leave the election to the accused. If he wanted to get rid of the matter quickly and proceed by way of summary conviction all right. If he wanted to proceed under an indictment that he should have the right to say so. But to lay down the rule that a man is liable to the penitentiary for a year or to pay a fine of $1,000 depending upon the discretion of two justices of the peace, or a stipendary magistrate, i3, I think very unfair to the accused. A penalty of $500 is excessive and so is a year's imprisonment.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR (Antigonish and Guysborough):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish shortly to direct attention to the answers we have been receiving to certain questions on the Order Paper-answers which to some members of the House are not at all satisfactory. It is a well-established principle that Parliament is entitled to some information regarding the expenditure of money, but as appears from the answers that have been given to certain questions on the Order Paper this year, the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) are declining to give information that should be given. Merribers of the House are constantly being told that it is not in the public interest to answer certain questions that are placed on the Order Paper. Now, I want to lay down the principle that it is always in the public interest that the people should know how their money is being spent. I quite understand that there may be exceptions; that while negotiations are proceeding it may not be advisable to disclose all the facts. But after the business is completed; as regards, for example, the shipping industry, after the charter is signed and after the-money has been earned and the acoounts closed there can be no reason why Parliament should not have the information.
It is in regard chiefly to the management of the Government ships that. I make this complaint. The people of Canada have invested a very large sum of money in the shipping industry,-about $70,000,000. Instead of placing the title to these ships in the King, as would be the natural way to proceed, the Government have seen fit to organize a company called the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, and the title to the ships is placed in that company. We are told that that company is, in a sense, a private concern, and that members of the House have no right to know what it is doing. To my mind, that company is simply the Government. It is another name for the Government; the Government are responsible for its transactions and responsible to Parliament for all the expenditures that the company makes. The responsibility of the Government is not lessened in the slightest degree by the fact that the title to the ships stands in a company created by themselves.
These ships, as you know, Mr. Speaker, are under the control oif the Railway Department. On the Order Paper to-day I placed the following question:
1.	Did the Railway Department or the Canadian Government Merchant Marine (Limited) or any one on tpeir behalf purchase a cargo of coal at Halifax or elsewhere in Nova Scotia to load one of the ships of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine (Limited) for delivery abroad?
The answer I got was as follows:
The department has no returns in its records showing the information asked for. These are transactions which are carried on by the Cana-

dian Government Merchant Marine as an incorporated company.
Now, I submit that that was a proper question; that the- Canadian Government Merchant Marine is a creature of the Government, and that the Government should have inquired of the officers controlling that company with regard to this matter and should have answered the questions that I put. The other questions, with their answers, were as follows:	,
2.	If so, from what company or person was said coal purchased?
Answered by No. 1.
S.	What was the price paid?
Answered by No. 1.
4.	Was a commission paid to any broker or company or other person, and if so. how much?
Answered by No. 1.
5.	How many tons were purchased?
Answered by No. 1.
6.	Were tenders invited by public advertisement in the newspaper for the purchase of said coal?
Answered by No. 1.	.
7.	Who was the lowest tenderer?
Answered by No. 1.
Now. you can see that I got very little useful information in reply to my questions. Does this company own the Government, or does the Government own the company?- that is what I want to get at. The Government purchased the coal, I take it, with the money of the Canadian people, Yet the inference from the answers given to my questions is that Parliament is not entitled to any information in regard to the business of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine; that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine is here represented a close corporation under the control of the Minister of Railways; that it can do whatever it pleases with regard to the purchase of coal or anything else. The only information we can get about the management of these Government ships is that it is in the hands of a corporation under the name of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
This is not the first time this refusal has been indulged in. In the discussion of the Government's proposal to spend another $20,000,000 in the construction of tramp vessels, the Minister of Marine was pressed1 for a detailed business statement of the operation of the ships up to December 31, 1919. He did not give it to the House. He gave us a fragmentary statement showing certain things, but he did not give us a complete business statement similar to that which would be given by any joint stock company in regard to operations of this kind. He was pressed for this statement when he was putting the estimate through the House. He replied ;by saying that he had the statement on his

desk and that he was willing to place it on Hansard. Members on this side supposed that the statement would be placed on Hansard, and that they would see it on the following day, but when Hansard came out the following day the statement was not there. The leader of the Opposition (Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King) asked why the statement had not been produced as intimated by the minister. The minister replied that he could not put it on Hansard without the leave of the House. speechtext: I am sure that the hon. member does not want to make any statement which is not based on the facts. /

belonging to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine had made twenty-eight complete voyages before the end of the year. We are asking for the result of these voyages. That is the next explanation we get, and I want to take exception to that answer. I cannot understand how it would toe against the public interest for the people of this country to know the results of the operations of this branch of my hon. friend's department up to the end of the year. I can understand that, during the time negotiations are going on for charters for freight, it would not toe in the public interest to publish all the facts about the matter; but after a charter has been made; after a ship has made her trip, after the money is in the minister's pocket and the accounts are all settled, it surely must be in the public interest that the people should know what their vessels are doing. 1.	What was the total quantity of (a) Canadian coal and (b) American coal purchased for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine in Canada for the year ending December 31, 1919?
