These are all proper and pertinent questions asked by a supporter of the Government. What answer do you suppose he got?
Sir George Foster (Acting Prime Minister) : The Government has no returns in its records showing the information asked for. These are
transactions which are carried on by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine as an incorporated company.
There you are again! The Canadian Government Merchant Marine "as in incorporated company " is put up bet-wene the members of this House and the Government as a protection for these transactions. I do not say the transactions are wrong; I do 'not know anything about them. But this is a very proper and pertinent question, and it should have received a clear and definite answer. Instead of that we are told that the business is carried on by a joint stock company and practically that the Government do not know anything about it. >
I must confess, after a number of years of experience in this House, I have never before heard of an important subject like this being trifled with in this way by a minister. Each answer is inconsistent with the others. It reminds one of a story-in Comic Blackstone of an old woman who had borrowed her neighbour's pot and the pot was cracked and was returned to the owner in a damaged condition. She was sued for damages, and like my hon. friend, she decided to put up a defence and fight it out to the bitter end. The first count of her defence was that she never borrowed the pot; the second was that the pot was cracked when she borrowed it, and the third was that the pot was whole when she returned it. This is a similar case. One day we are told by the minister that he is quite willing to disclose the facts; he says: "I have the statements on my desk, and I will put them on Hansard." When the leader of the Opposition asks him the following day: "Why did you not do so?" "Oh," he says, "I could not do so without the unanimous consent of the House." And the unanimous consent of the House was never asked for by the minister. Then the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) says: "I want to know the facts about this matter," and what does the minister reply? He says: "It is not in the public interest to tell you anything about it." The next question is asked by a supporter of the Government, the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond: How are you purchasing the coal for these ships? Are you purchasing the coal by tender?" The answer is: "This is an incorporated company; we do not know anything about it; we have no information at all to give you." That is the way hon. members get information in regard to the management of this important business for which Parliament has voted the large sum of $70,000,000. I

should like to know why my hon. friends are resorting to all these excuses. Why do they not tell us frankly? This is a business transaction; we have invested a large amount of money in this venture, and we have a right to know all the facts about it. Apart from the railways themselves, I .suppose there is no other business venture that the Government have ever gone into that they have invested so much money in as this one. We all hope that the venture will be successful; but there is one thing that the people will not stand for, and that is to permit any irresponsible corporation to handle such a large sum of money without a strict accounting being given and Parliament being allowed to know all they are doing. All that we on this side of the House are asking for is a clear, business statement. Every incorporated company that is handling the money of its shareholders gives those shareholders at the end of the year a business statement. The minister has told us that he has on hand $1,400,000 odd to the good. That is all right; we are very glad to hear that. But the minister may have in his other pocket liabilities amounting to this sum. We do not know; we want to have, from the minister, or from some member of the company, a business statement, such as is given by any other company that owns vessels or a railway, that will show us just how much liability there is, how much the company has earned and how the business has got along up to the end of the year. My hon. friend has told us that twenty-eight completed voyages were made by these ships. His book-keeper will be able, without much trouble, to give us the freight earned on each voyage, the wages that were paid, the supplies that were bought, the insurance that was effected, and all the other expenses; then he can strike a balance, and we shall know what that ship earned on that voyage. It would not he very much trouble for the department to get out these statements, and it would certainly be very satisfactory to members of the House to have this information. It is no use for the minister to tell us that it is against the public interest to give out this information, or that this business is run by a joint stock company and the Government does not know what that joint stock company is doing. I do not see how it can be .shown that it is not in the public interest for the members of this House, who represent the people of this country, to know how the. people's 
money is feeing spent. Who are the guardians of the public interest? Is it the Government alone? Is not each one of us,- are not you, Mr. Speaker, and every member of this House a guardian of the public interest as well as the Government? Is it for the Government to sit back and say that because they have set up a joint stock company to do the business of shipping in this country, it is not in the public interest to tell the .members of this Parliament how that business is being conducted and what are its earnings? I submit that it is in the public interest for us to have this information, and I should very much like to hear the minister give us any good reason why he thinks it is not.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The question (that the hon. imember for An'tigonish and Guysborough ,(Mr. Sinclair) has raised is a very important o.ne. I have been in this House for many years, and I know something about the operation of the Intercolonial railway. I have seen questions on the Order Paper day after day with regard to the operations (of that road, no matter what Government iwas in power. Was it in the public interest that these questions were answered tat That time? Let me just give one or two [instances to show 'the results of answering just such questions as the hon. member has asked. I remember when I came into this House .some twenty-five or thirty years ago, the question of coal supplies for the operation of the Intercolonial was a very important one. Tenders wese called for by the Government from time to time. The coal supplied by the Dominion Iron and [Steel Company, and I think the Nova Scotia Steel Company, in the Province of Nova iScotia, was quoted at a certain price. The coal from New Brunswick was not worth half .as much as the cotal supplied by the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, and was purchased at a less price. But to-day for this inferior coal from New Brunswick, which is not worth half as much as the Dominion Iron and Steel Company coal, we have to pay, through the influence and pressure of members of the House of Commons, practically the same price as we pay for the higher grade coal supplied by these other companies. We have to pay the same price on account of the pressure brought to bear at that time. The same thing applies with regard to the prices of ties and other material. However, the Intercolonial railway was owned by the people of Canada, every dollar invested in it had been put up by The people of Canada,

and the read had no outside obligations. Now we have ether roads. We have the Canadian National Railway system. It is true that the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental are paid for by the people of Canada, and that there is not one dollar [DOT]against these roads, but we have also the Canadian Northern system, and we are [DOT]likely within a very short time to take over the Grand Trunk railway as well. Now the people have claims against these railways ,by way of bonds, and they have therefore a great interest in them. Is it right, or just, or in the interests of these railways,' that we should expose their operations from day to day? Is it right that we should (expose the operations of the merchant marine and of these railways to those who are jworking in opposition to the Government [DOT]system? Let me just cite a question that was on the Order Paper to-day and which was answered, just to show how much it is in the public interest that hon. members [DOT]should get this information. I do not believe this question originated with the hon. member. I believe it originated with some individual in the city of Ottawa who is here looking for a job, or else the answer was required for political purposes to destroy the cause of public ownership in this country. This was the question:
Mr. Chisholm: 1. What are the names of the captains now employed on board the ships of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine at present in commission and where were they born?
2. What are the names of the first officers of the said ships and where were they horn?
Obviously there may be some man in charge of one of the Government ships who was noit horn in Canada, and the hon. member wants this information in order that he may use it for political purposes or else to destroy the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
I want to tell the minister that the question did originate w,th me. I have my purpoise in asking it, and I want the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I accept the hon. gentleman's statement, but in my judgment the hon. gentleman wants this information in order that he may use it on the stump to destroy the Government Merchant Marine.
The hon. member is absolutely wrong. He does not know my mind. He has enough to do to know his own mind.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman will have his opportunity to reply.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I do not know the hon. gentleman's mind, but I have a right to draw my own conclusions. Here is another question:
Mr. Pardee: 1. With whom was the fire insurance on the Canadian National railways placed, and by whom?
2. What individuals or firms were asked to compete upon it?
S. In what companies was the insurance effected and at what rate?
There is no doubt in my mind that some person who wants to get this insurance and could not get it from the Canadian National Railways came to Ottawa and asked the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) to put that question on the Order Paper that he might use the information given for some political purpose. I might say that I have had- men coming here to Ottawa trying to use their influence to sell coal to the Canadian National Railway and to the Government Merchant Marine, but I have always taken the stand from the very first, and will continue to take it so long as I am in the position I now occupy, that they must deal with the management of these undertakings. A few days after these people have tried to get contracts from the management, if a contract is refused, you will see a question on the Order Paper in the name of some member of the Opposition asking the price that the Canadian National Railways is paying, for coal for instance, in different parts of Canada. I have seen this in the past and I know how it w'orks. If these people do not get a contract they will try and raise trouble in the particular locality from which they come. The Opposition has asked a question for the purpose of obtaining some information which they think will enable them _ to spread broadcast some sinister suggestion that the Government is paying more for coal in one part of the country than in another when they can avoid this inequality in prices. Every hon. member must know that the prices in different parts of the country, whether they be higher or lower than those obtainable in other places, are perfectly justified. This remark applies also to ties. In one part of the country you may pay more for ties than elsewhere owing to the greater cost of wood and of labour and hauling. But if hon. members can obtain an answer showing that the prices are higher in one particular part of the country than in another, of course they will seize upon this fact as ground for the charge that something wrong has been done. Now, the Canadian Merchant Marine is operating in opposition to the great Canadian Pacific

marine and other shipping interests throughout the world as well. Similarly, the Canadian National railways are operating in opposition to the Canadian Pacific. And if the Government are to be compelled to give answers to all these questions that are asked by those who are trying either to get contracts or to obtain some information that will give private interests an advantage against the Canadian National railways or the Canadian Merchant Marine, then I say that we might just as well put an end to public ownership at once. I think we should have in charge of the Canadian Merchant Marine and the Canadian National railways men in whom not only the Government but the members of this House and the people of the country can have the utmost confidence, feeling perfectly secure in the knowledge that they will manage these public enterprises with all the care, skill and diligence which they would devote to their personal property. As a precaution, therefore, we have established a system of audit which affords abundant protection. We have the company's own auditors who scrutinize every expenditure that is made; next, we have a set of auditors who are in no Way connected with the company and who carry on an independent and thorough audit; and in addition to that I have suggested another set of auditors who will be appointed. A man will be appointed by the Railway Department, another by the Auditor General's Department, and a third by the Finance Department, and these men will go over every account and contract and submit their own audit. The Canadian National Railways will then submit their own audit. The Canadian National Railways will then submit to Parliament through the Department of Railways an official report, not merely equal to but fuller than that which the Canadian Pacific Railway submits to its shareholders. The annual meeting of the Canadian National Railways takes place on May 10, when that report will be laid on the table of the House.
I leave it to hon. gentlemen in this House and the people of this country to suggest how in the world we can make the railway a success if we are to answer all these small questions that are put on the Order Paper for the purpose, as I conceive, first of making political capital and endeavouring to ruin public ownership, and secondly, in the interests of private individuals who are seeking, through the medium of members of Parliament, to get information that may be of benefit to them. I am firmly of the opinion that the railway can be made a
[Mr. J. D. Reid.l
success under public ownership if it is given a fair chance. I have taken the stand from the outset that so long as we have confidence in those whom we select to manage the railways, and so long as we are satisfied that their management is really and truly economical and in the public interest, they should be unhampered in their operations. But so long as I do not believe that it is in the public interest to answer questions which I know are put on the Order Paper, through any member of Parliament, by individuals who have been hanging around Ottawa for weeks trying to force contracts from the Canadian National Railways, I shall refuse to give such information, at least while I am Minister of Railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I explained a moment ago how the public interest is protected in this matter. We have the general manager and the directors and their officials, in whom we have every confidence. We have also a set of auditors appointed by those men. Then we have another set of auditors who are in no way connected with the railway, an outside firm of competent auditors appointed by the Government. Besides this the Auditor General's Department will audit every cent of expenditure and scrutinize every contract.
Do I understand the minister to say that this House will not have an ap-portunity to pass upon the conduct or to inquire into the purchases of this Board of Administration?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I do not think that the accounts should be submitted in the way in which the accounts have been in connection with the Intercolonial, and I say that for this reason: There is about $400,000,000 invested in the Canadian Northern railway by bondholders, whose property should be protected and not be allowed to be subject to political influence which may injure it. The same thing will apply to the Grand Trunk Railway Company.

I should like to state my question precisely, because either I did not quite catch the minister's answer or he failed to catch my question. Will the House

have any means of judging of the expenditures of the Board of Railway Administrators otherwise than by the report of these auditors?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This House will have the report of the Canadian National Railways on May 10. It will not give a detailed statement for every cent that has been expended similar to thut which has been given with reference to the Intercolonial.
Will it show where the coal is purchased and the price paid for it?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No, I cannot give any information of that kind.
Will the auditors give it?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I will give the information that is contained in the report of May 10, and that I will stand by. I cannot go into the details until we have had the annual report.
I understood the minister to say that the meeting of the Canadian National Railways was to be held on the 10th of May.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The 10th May.

The Canadian National
Railways?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Canadian Northern and the Canadian National; the report will be for the whole system.
A meeting of the shareholders?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The shareholders.
That is the whole people of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It means the annual meeting of the Canadian Northern and its subsidiaries and the whole Government system. There will be a report showing the operation of what is to be the whole -Canadian National system.
Who will be entitled to attend that meeting?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The shareholders.
The people of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The people of Canada ar^ represented by the Government and the Government will have their representatives present.
That will be the Minister of Railways himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It may be the Minister of Railways, it may be the Minister of Finance, or it may be the whole Government.
It might be the whole Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It will be the Government in this case. I want to emphasize the fact that these questions are not in the interest of this corporation, that they are not in the public interest, that they are not in the interest of the Canadian National railways and that they are not in the interest of the Canadian Merchant Marine. I have taken that position'; I believe it is right and fair; I believe the people of Canada will not stand to have questions of that kind answered which will have the effect of destroying public ownership in so far as the Merchant Marine and the Canadian National railways are concerned. Neither the Canadian Pacific nor any other corporation would give the information that is asked by some members of this House.
Would the Canadian Pacific not give that information to its shareholders?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No, they never have *ior has any other private corporation that ever existed. More than that, I do not believe there is a shareholder of any private corporation who would think it right, just or fair to ask some of the ridiculous questions that are asked by some hon. members on the other side of the House.

The statute under which the minister is operating this Canadian National railway states that the annual meeting shall be held on the second Thursday in April each year or on such date as the directors may from time to time determine. When did they determine to hold it on the 10th May, and for what reason?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: If I had the answer which I gave to the hon. gentleman to-day I would give the same answer to the question which he now asks. I do not know, because I am not operating the railway. The directors are the ones who might answer that question.
You had better bring them here.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I do not think it is through me that question should be answered. At all events, the meeting is being called in accordance with the charter. The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) is making statements and charges in connection with the men who are operating this railway that I do not believe any other hon. member would make. I think it is the most unfair and unjust criti-

cism that was ever offered in this House. The president and directors of the railway are all upright, honourable, honest men. Wherever they have lived, in Toronto or elsewhere, they are regarded as being men beyond reproach. They are doing their very best to operate this system and to make it a success, and I do not think it is very encouraging to have members of this House asking questions and criticising what they are doing. I do not think it is in the public interest, and I do hope that all hon. members on both sides of the House in future will not pursue a course of this kind. If they want information that is fair I am sure the board will be pleased to give it to them, but if questions are asked in order to make political capital or in the interest of some private individual I believe they are right in refusing it. I shall stand by them and try to make the operation of the Canadian National railways and the Canadian Merchant Marine a success.
Would the minister be good enough to give us the names of the Canadian Merchant Marine management?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: They'are the members of the board of directors who operate the Canadian National system. Mr. Hanna is president. There are also: Mr. A. J. Mitchell, the comptroller or financial man of the Canadian Northern; Mr. Bell, the deputy minister; Mr. Hobson, of Hamilton; Sir Hormisdas Laporte, of Montreal; Mr. E. R. Wood, of Toronto; Mr. Barnhill, of New Brunswick; Mr. Cantlie, Mr. Riley, and another whose name I cannot recall at the moment. These are all men beyond reproach and men in whom the public have full confidence. I feel that we can trust them. They do not believe that it is in the public interest that we should have all this little stuff answered for the purpose of making political capital or in the interest of those who are hounding them, coming to Ottawa and trying to use their influence with the department and with members. They do not believe it is in the public interest that this state of affairs should continue. I am the last one to withhold information that I believe to be in the public interest, but so long as I believe it is not in the public interest I must take the position which I do and abide by the consequences.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Am I right in understanding that as regards information respecting the merchant marine or the Canadian National railways, which members of this House believe to be 
in the public interest, no answer will be given unless the minister or the board of directors believe it is in the public interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Whenever a question is asked by any member in this House- whether on this side or the other side-it will be submitted to the Government and the Government will have to decide whether it is in the public interest or not. If it is a question that we can answer fairly, no matter whether it relates to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine or the Canadian Government railways, we will ask the Board of Management for the information and insist upon getting it, and will give it .to the public; but if the Government think it is not in the public interest that that information should be given, then I say we will not give it.
Mr. BEiLAND: It is agreed that if there is a deficit in the operation of the Canadian National railways this Parliament must be asked to vote the amount necessary to cover that deficit. I wish to ask if the expenditure on those railways can be the subject of an investigation by the Public Accounts Committee of this House?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: When the money necessary to cover a deficit is being voted by Parliament I am prepared to give information that I think should satisfy the members of this House or any other person who does not want to make political capital out of it. But I do not think it in the public interest that we should disclose what was paid for coal to one man in one part of Canada and the price paid to another man in some other part, simply that it may be used for political capital. In every legitimate case I will give information that I think will satisfy the House. If hon. gentlemen do not think sufficient protection as to expenditures is afforded by having an audit of the Canadian National railways by regularly appointed auditors-by an auditing firm having the highest standing in the country-and also by the auditing that is done by the Auditor Geperal's Department, the Finance Department, and the Department of Railways, it is up to them to say what further safeguard they want. If the system I have outlined is not satisfactory and the House authorizes further steps to be tatken then of course I will abide by its decision.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must remind the
House that on a motion to go into Supply each hon. member is limited to one speech. The hon. member for Antigonish and Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair) has spoken and the

Minister of Railways has replied; but for the last few moments the House has been proceeding in a very irregular way; the minister has been interrogated as though the House were in Committee of the Whole. I must therefore ask hon. gentlemen to observe the customary and well established procedure.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
The speeches which
are now being delivered would not have been made, Mr. Speaker, if the information asked for on this side had been given in the usual way in reply to questions put on the Order Paper. But that well estab-blished method of obtaining information from the Government has been discarded altogether. A reply which does not impart the slightest information is given to one question, and with respect to the twenty or thirty questions which follow we are told they have been answered by the answer to the first question. The answer to the first question gives you no information at all, and yet the succeeding questions are spoken of as having been answered by the first. I submit that is a new method of imparting information to this House which possibly has originated in the fertile brain of the Minister of' Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid).
The minister has enunciated another new idea to-night and that is that he will not place within the reach of any hon. member any material which would form the basis for a criticism of the Government. That is an absolutely brand-new idea on the part of the minister. Not only does this Government arrogate to itself the right to make the voters' lists, the right to create the electorate, the right to control the whole election machinery, but it is determined that no facts of any kind shall get into the possession of hon. gentlemen on the Opposition, the object being to render them dumb, to silence criticism. That brand-new idea is one that is worthy of the Minister of Railways. He tells us that no information is to be given about any undertaking in which the people's money is invested. Such an idea as that must be new even to the hardest-shelled Tory on the Government side-that the people of Canada who contribute to the consolidated revenue of the Dominion are to be told that the millions that are taken from their pockets and put into the public treasury shall be spent in any way the Government may think advisable, and that is the end of it, -nobody must rise in this House to ascertain what has become of the money. That
is another splendid principle of this Union Government. It may have been incubating 'for many years in the hearts and heads of hon. gentlemen who are supporting the Tory party, but they, never had the courage- if I can call it by that name-to come out into the open and avow that to be their principle. However we have it intimated now that that is the way things are going to be done in future. Whenever money is required the people will promptly hear about it, and we shall be permitted to vote it; but when it comes to disclosing what has become of the money strict silence is to be maintained. Well, things have been conducted in that way now for a couple of years, and last year we landed into a deficit of $47,000,000 by such a "secret service'' management of the public railways. That deficit represents $6 a head, if not mo're, for every man, woman and child in Canada, for one year's operations of the Canadian National railways. But when it comes to demanding details of that expenditure the doors are shut, the blinds pulled down, and nobody is allowed to hear a whisper of what is going on. I must ask the minister, how much worse must things become before he will condescend to tell the people what is going on? I hold in my hand a copy of the report which was published by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company on the 15th of March last. Their financial year closed on the last day of De-cember-but on the 15th of March this booklet was published-open, aboveboard, public-showing what the operations of the road had been for the year. The company also announce that they paid 10 per cent dividends to their stockholders and shareholders. Well, this is the kind of operation that suits me best; that is the kind of operation the people of Canada would prefer.
Mr. J. D. REID; Will the hon. member be satisfied with a report equal to, or better, than the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's report?

A report from the Government with respect to the Canadian National railways disclosing that an ample and efficient service has been given to the country, that every bill has been paid, that a ten per cent dividend has been declared and a lot of money placed in a rest account, and that everything is going full-swing, would certainly be satisfactory to me as one of the shareholders.

Yet the friends of hon. gentlemen opposite at one time declared

that the Canadian Pacific railway would not yield sufficient profits to pay for the axle grease.

I am thoroughly Scotch and we are sometimes accused of being stupid, and the hon. gentleman will excuse me for not being able to follow his meaning-I do not see where the point comes in.
Now, let me tell the Government and the Minister of Railways that the moment a suggestion comes to their minds that they have entered upon an enterprise about which they cannot tell the people, that is the clearest possible notice that they should not continue any further in that undertaking,-it is not their business. Because the people of Canada are the shareholders in this business and it is nothing but natural for every shareholder to know what has become of his money-what it is earning and what use is being made of it. You cannot hold shareholders in a company for any considerable length of time unless they are satisfied that the capital which they have invested has been properly expended. It will not do to tell them that it is in the interests of all concerned that the business of the company shall not be disclosed. In like manner, the Government have no right to conceal any information in regard to the operations of enterprises which they are carrying on. If they cannot give the information, they should not be in the business at all. The people have put their money in those enterprises, and they should know what is going on. The minister one day tells us that we own the Canadian Northern; that we own the Grand Trunk Pacific; that we own the-Intercolonial. 1 would like to ask the minister what is the difference, so far as the people are concerned, between the Transcontinental, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Northern and the Intercolonial? Are they not all owned by the people? Did we not pay our money for them all? If we are entitled to know what is going on in connection with the Intercolonial, are we not equally entitled to know what is going on in connection with the management of the other roads and of other Government enterprises? But the minister tells us that it is not in the best interest of the people that we should be given this information. Well, I have already said that if the Government find that they cannot tell the people about any business that they are carrying on, the sooner they get out of it the better, so that the people may manage their business in a more satisfactory w^y.
LMr. Davidson.]
The minister spoke about coal and the manner in which it was purchased. If the coal areas and the coal owners and the coal producers in Nova Scotia had been left alone in 1914 when the war broke out they would to-day be independent of any assistance of this or any other Government. At that time they were well established and were not a burden upon the Government. But what happened? The Government-I suppose quite properly so-took from them all the ships which had been carrying their product to Montreal and further up the river to points where they had established a good market. Then, their men went to the front; [DOT]the amount of coal produced was lessened; their markets went down and they lost their contracts. When the war was over they expected that the Government would give them some consideration. Their ships had been taken in the national interest; their men had thrown down their tools and gone to the front in the national interest. If there was loss to the shareholders or to the workmen engaged in the production of coal in Nova Scotia, it was because of service rendered not merely in the interests of Nova Scotia, but in the interests of Canada, of the Empire, of the world. All that we were asking was that some preference should be given to our own coal merchants so far as the supply of coal to national enterprises was concerned, and at a time when our coal merchants were trying again to get on their feet. But we are told to-night, as we have .always been told, that these producers must compete with those who have the coal right on the spot and who never sacrificed a dollar's worth of ships or gave up any men to the defence of the country at a crucial moment in the war, when ships and men were greatly needed.
As to telling the country what is being paid for coal on the Intercolonial or any of the other Government railways, I see no reason why that should not be done. The prices may differ in different zones; conditions in the far West may be different from those which prevail in Ontario and Quebec. But if the Government will ask for tenders for the coal and pay the lowest price, no fault can be found. The people of the country have a right to know what they are paying for their coal. They must know what the Government are paying for rails, for ties, for everything that goes into the operation of the Government railways. The same is true with regard to Government shipping operations. We must know where e'-ery dollar goes; we must be assured that every precaution is taken to see that a dollar

earns as much when handled by the Government as it would earn it handled by a private concern.
I again complain that the information which is given us dn answer to questions is not the full and complete information that we should get. It is the people who are putting the money into these enterprises; it is the people who want this information. We are the representatives of the people, and the Government are taking a wrong step when they say that it is not in the interests of the country that we should have -this information. If in the future the minister wants to avoid any discussion or any catechizing of this kind, he will give information that is quite properly asked for; be will see that the business which he is carrying on is conducted in a proper -manner and that reports are made whi-ch will give a fair and reasonable account -to the -Canadian people of what is becoming of -their money in the hands of the Government.
Hon. C, C. BALLANTYNE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries): -Mr. Speaker, I am rkther -surprised at the turn which this debate has taken, on the very important question whether our vast sy-sltem of railways, comprising 22,000 miles of line, and the Government Merchant Marine, comprising 63 ships, built and projected, are to -be managed -as heretofore, by the Department of Railways, so far as railways are concerned, and the Department of Marine, so far as the Government ships are concerned. If thes-e enterprises were being managed as -the Intercolonial -railway was so unfortunately managed under various governments from its very inception, I could well understand hon. members opposite asking for details as to the price of coal an-d the price of this, that or the other thing. I take no issue with hon. members when they ask for information which thi-s House has a right to receive from the Government concerning the Government railways and the Government Merchant Marine. But when hon. members get down to details of management and detailed information such as only the operating company can possess in regard to the railways or the Canadian Government Merchant Marine in reference to the ships, this Government adopted the only course-and I am satisfied that it meets with the general approval of hon. members of this House and of the country generally-and that is that the railways and the ships are to be free from 106
political influence. The only way in which that could be done was to adopt the policy that the Government put into force. The Government have given Mr. D. B. Hanna and his board of directors an absolutely free hand as to the management of our vast transcontinental system of railways and also as regards the Government ships. The Government could, of course, continue the same old policy that has prevailed in this country altogether too long; it could have ipade an attempt to manage this vast system of railways along the same political lines as those on which the Intercolonial railway has been managed to the sorrow of the country and with deficits each year. Our vast railway systems would then have been in the political arena; No government could have kept the railways free from political patronage under such conditions. I am sure hon. members will agree that the only chance of success for public ownership and operation of railways and steamships is to adopt and support the course that this Government has adopted, of endeavouring to manage those railways along the same sane, conservative business lines that any private corporation would adopt. The House has a perfect right to ask all about the capital expenditure as regards both railways and ships; it has a perfect right to know also about the profits.
I was a little bit surprised, to speak for a moment particularly regarding the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, to hear the hon. member for Antigonish and Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair) say to-night that the Minister of Marine had not given the members of the House the same information regarding the operation of the ships as a president or general manager of a large private corporation would give to the shareholders. Hon. members will give me credit for having at least some knowledge regarding business matters and the way in which annual meetings are generally presided over. I had the honour to give the members of this House as much detailed information regarding the Canadian Government Merchant Marine fleet as any president or general manager could possibly give the shareholders of any large private corporation. The pages of Hansard will show that when I was speaking on the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, I gave the gross profits and the net profits. I stated at that time that those net profits had been arrived at following the usual careful business course of providing for interest on the cost of the ships, depreciation,



insurance, overhead expenses, and all that makes up the difference between the gross and the net profits. The hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough said that I gave only fragmentary information, that I did not give any liabilities. I was careful to give to the House both sides of the balance sheet; I gave on the one side the assets, both fixed and current! I' gave, on the other side, the liabilities, and I showed that, for the first time in the history of any government of this country, nineteen ships that had been in operation for only a portion of the year, had made $1,460,000 net profit, and more than that, that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine had paid into the Consolidated Revenue Fund a cheque for $500,000. I offered also, with the unanimous consent of the House, to place on the pages of Hansard the open voyages, the closed voyages per ship, showing the profits on the outward voyages and also the profits on the inward voyages. This Government has nothing to conceal from the House; everything is as wide open and frank as it possibly can be. I am sorry that our able chairman did not put the motion^ to the members of the committee that night to ascertain whether this detailed information could be placed on the pages of Hansard or not. If the chairman had done so, I was quite prepared to hand over the detailed statement so that it could appear on the pages of Hansard. But as lion, members opposite seem to think that I was not desirous of doing so, I am ready to-morrow to hand that statement to the leader of the Opposition or to any other bon. member opposite. The Government are proud of the profits, both net and gross, inward and outward, that each one of these ships has made.
The real question before the House is which of the two policies should be adopted. If we are going to manage the railways and the ships by government departments on a purely political-patronage basis, then, of course, the Government will have the say as to who is to be an engineer or a conductor on either a passenger or a freight train; v e shall have all the political influence of the various members of Parliament as to where the coal and provisions are to be bought. I am sure the members of this House will at once come to the only conclusion that they can come to, namely, that there is no possible chance for the ultimate success of a government system of railways or a Government system of ships if they are going to be run along 
political patronage lines. As a member of the Government, I am, of course, heartily in support of the policy of the Government to free the railroads and the ships from political influence and patronage and to have those railroads and ships managed to the best of the ability of the men who are at the head of them with a free hand. I have never written a letter to nor asked a question of Mr. D. B. Hanna or any official of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine as to what route a ship will ply upon; I have not asked him how much he has paid for asparagus, or potatoes, or butter, or coal. The Government have something to do besides dipping into the petty details of management. Therefore, we say to Mr. Hanna and those who are managing the ships: All that we want you to do is tO' manage the ships to the very best of your ability; all that Parliament and the Government and the country are looking for is that at the end of the year, if that be at all possible, the figures shall be on the right side. But the management of the railways and of the ships cannot say that this Government or any member of it has interfered with them in the slightest degree.
It has been said to-night by hon. members that my colleague the Minister of Railways and the Government have a desire to withhold from members of this House information that they should have. Let me say at once on behalf of the Government that there is no such desire; that we are perfectly willing to give to Parliament all the information that Parliament ought to have and everything that the Government is aware of. But the Government will not, as the Minister of Railways has stated, inquire from the management of the railways or from the management of the steamship company where they buy their supplies, the names of their stewards, the names of their captains, the names of their engineers, nor where these officers were born, nor where the sugar or the coal was bought. This Government has something to do besides interfering with the able management of either the railroads or the ships. I observe my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. MoMaster) laughs at that, but I want to tell him-
A $47,000,000 deficit being claimed as an example of "able" management is somewhat amusing.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
While we all regret a deficit of $47,000,000 on the railways, it will be twice $47,000,000 if every hon. member of this House is allowed to dip in his oar and say: I want the coal for the railways bought

from So-and-So, the butter from somebody else, and so on. However, I am not going to deal with the railway problem to-night. I am simply discussing the 'broad principle whether our railroads and ships are to be run by political patronage or in a businesslike way, free from all political influence. I cannot see what fault the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough has to find with the Minister of Railways in regard to his question about the price of coal. The Minister of Railways does not know the price of the coal bought by the railways, nor is he familiar rvith the price paid by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. Suppose the Minister of Railways writes to Toronto and finds out the price of coal, what is to stop every member of this House asking for detailed prices on everything that the railways and the steamships buy? I am sure hon. members will agree that if we are to have a ghost of a chance to make public ownership a success in this country we must give the management of our railways and our ships a perfectly free hand.
Before taking my seat, in answer to the statement of my hon. friend from Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) that I did not place before this House such information as is placed before the shareholders of a company, I say that no. business man could give more detailed or more accurate information to a body of shareholders than it was my privilege to place before hon. members of this House a few days ago. I rvould be sorry indeed if the time of the members of this Government was to be taken up with writing to the men who manage our railways and our merchant marine to find out information on such matters as where their insurance is placed and whether they employ this man or that man. On the broad questions of capital expenditure, maintenance of way, deficits, earnings, and such like, every hon. member has a perfect right to seek information, and the Government Is always willing and ready to give it.

My hon. friend from Antigonish and Guysborough has brought a very proper and important matter before the House this evening, and in a very quiet way. We have, as a result, the Minister of Railways getting up and reading a lecture to hon. members on this side of the House on their rights and privileges and as to what questions they are entitled to ask of the Government. He went on to charge hon. members on this side with playing politics, 1061 , ,
with having questions put into their mouths by gentlemen outside this Chamber so that they might make political capital of the information they receive in answeT to those questions. Before dealing with the remarks of the Minister of Railways I wish to correct an error in the mind of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne), and to prevent a false impression from going out to the country. That hon. gentleman stated that the Intercolonial railway was unfortunately mismanaged in the past, irrespective of whatever political party was in power.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says "Hear,, hear." Let us look into this matter for a moment and see if my hon. friend can consistently say "Hear, hear." When I first knew anything about politics a gentleman, Mr. David Pottinger, was manager of the Intercolonial railway, and 1 challenge the Minister of Marine or anybody else to say anything against that man as manager of the Intercolonial during the many years he was in charge. After that, Mr. Brady was general manager of the Intercolonial, with general offices at Moncton. If he mismanaged the railway why *has he been placed in the responsible position of superintendent of the Canadian National railways from Fort William to Sydney and Halifax? Mr. C. M. Hayes wras Mr. Brady's successor as manager of the Intercolonial; and if be mismanaged the Intercolonial, I would ask my hon. friend why, in heaven's name, he was appointed vice-president of the Canadian National Railways, controlling 22,000 miles of railway. My hon. friend's mouth is closed when he attempts to argue that these gentlemen did not properly manage the Intercolonial.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I made no reference whatever to personnel in my remarks about the management of the Intercolonial railway. My remarks were confined entirely to the effects of political influence on the operation of the road, which I say has been a sad blot on public ownership eveT since the Intercolonial was started.

When my hon. friend said that the Intercolonial ivas unfortunately mismanaged, the conclusion was that the general manager of the road must have been the man who was to blame for the mismanagement. He did not say that these people were derelict in their duty, but that is the only conclusion you could draw. When the Minister of Marine rises in his

place in this Chamber and charges that Mr. Pottinger, Mr. Brady and Mr. Hayes did not properly manage the Intercolonial, I "take sharp issue with him. but if true they should not have been retained in the service and given greater responsibilities.
The Minister of Marine then went on to talk about patronage. My hon. friend from Antigonish and Guysborough had not said a word about patronage; he was not asking for the flesh pots of patronage; not at all; he simply brought to the attention of "the House that proper and reasonable questions had been placed on the Order Paper by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House to which they were entitled to an answer, and to which they would receive answer if hon. gentlemen opposite were not afraid to give the facts to the public. The only conclusion that we can come to is that the Minister of Bailways, who has charge of the Canadian National railways, and is therefore able to give the facts to this House and the country, is afraid to do so. The Minister of Marine very courteously said that hon. gentlemen have a perfect right to ask questions. Undoubtedly we have, but hon. gentlemen opposite claim that there is no obligation on them to reply. They maintain it is their privilege to reply or not as they see fit. That, I suppose, is their right, but I for one do not propose to accept such an attitude without protesting. Hon. gentlemen opposite control the purse strings of this country; they are the guardians of the people's money; they take the people's money to the extent of a billion of dollars and place it in defunct railways, and then say: We will not answer your questions concerning operation of said railways. We were told that there was a deficit on the Canadian National railways of $47,000,000 and the Minister of Bailways says we have no right to dip into this little matter. Is $47,000,000 that has been lost in operating these railways, in a way known only to the Government themselves, a little matter?
My hon. friend also took occasion to find some fault with the chairman of the committee because he did not put the motion the other evening as to whether the facts should he put on Hansard and go out to the people of this country. My hon. friend did not make the motion, or I am sure the chairman of the committee would have put the question and the facts would have gone on Hansard. I have no intention of insinuating that the hon. gentleman is not prepared to give that information. He says he is prepared to give it, and I hope he will have an opportunity of placing it on
[Mr. Copp.J
Hansard. It does not do to say: I will give the leader of the Opposition a copy of it, it is the people of this country who want to know the facts. The Minister of Bail-ways says that there is to be a meeting of the management of the Canadian National railways on the 10th of May. Who will be present at that meeting? The ten directors of the railway, I suppose. Whoi will represent the people? The Minister of Bailways will go there to represent 8,000,000 stockholders. The people of this country own the railway, and my hon. friend who goes there to represent 8,000,000 stockholders, informs us that he will come back to Parliament in his capacity as representative of the whole people of Canada on that directorate and arrogate to himselt the position of censor in the submission of information to this House. He says: "I am going to give the people of this country what information I like in regard to the operation of this system, and I will censor that information." Sir, the people of this Dominion have just as much right to inquire into the operations of these railways as any stockholder in any business concern in the country 'has to ask for all the information he desires in connection with the conduct of that business. At a general or annual meeting of any company in this country any stockholder can obtain all the information he asks for in regard to the operations of the directors, and he is at perfect liberty to criticize every ,aot of theirs. And if the shareholders in a business concern enjoy this right, how much more is it the right of the people of Canada, who are the owners of this railway, to ask for and to be given every bit of information they desire in connection with the workings of the railway. .1 want to correct a statement made by the -minister lest a wrong impression may go abroad. I take issue with him, and I say that he does not know the facts in regard to the purchase of or use of co-al when he makes the statement -to this House and through the House to the country that the coal purchased in the province of New Brunswick is not worth half as much as the co-al purchased in No-v-a Scotia. I know I shall have the support of -hon. gentlemen from the province of New Brunswick when I say that -the coal that comes from that part of Canada is known throughout the length and breadth of this country as one of the best steam coals produced in the country, and when my hon. friend says that if the mine-owners of New Brunswick found out what was being paid for coal in Nova

Scotia, the coal in New Bruniswick would cost the same as ithe coal from Nova Scotia, let me tell him that those who operate the companies in New Brunswick have a perfect right to get as much for their coal as the Government is paying for coal elsewhere.
As a member of this House I desire to associate myself entirely with the statement of the hon. member for Arutigonish and Guysborough in- regard to the rights of hon. members of this House. And standing here as ia representative of a large proportion of the people of Canada who are stockholders in the Canadian National railways and the Canadian Merchant Marine, and who provide the .money for the operation of these utilities, I claim the right to all the information which tbo.se people desire to obtain. For my part, I protest strongly and emphatically against the minister's assumption of the right to censor the information which he may give to this House, and I object to. his saying that he will lay on the Table what he likes. The minister talks about the auditors' reports. The people of Canada have a right to know wha/t the auditors have to say in regard to the operation of the railways, and *they ought to have the details of those operations if they desire. The people want to know rwhat they are paying for coal and rails and sleepers; they want to know what the operation pi a public utility costs. Let me say to my hon. friend, who charges us on this side of the House with playing a political game and who talks about patronage, that so far as the coal owners in Nova Scotia wishing to sell coal to the Government, it may not be worse than to have private merchants selling coal to the railways without any information as to what prices are being paid. When .my hon. friend talks /about "playing polities," surely he cannot deny that if in the operation of the railways the game of politics has ever been played it has been played to the limit while he has been Minister of Railways, and by himself.

I would not have intervened in this discussion had my genial friend, the Minister of Railways, not referred to a certain most innocent question which I put upon the Order Paper. He got so really serious over that question, as only he can get when occasion demands, as to think that the information asked for would ruin the National railways and the merchant marine of Canada. The idea of asking what the insurance was upon the National railways, how
much was the premium, and whether or not tenders had been called for, was to the mind of the minister a most heinous offence. , If the question I asked, as well as that of the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie), so perturbed the minister, it is apparent that, in the mind of the minister, any question even as to where a man was born would ' simply disintegrate the whole system of: railways. Let me say to the hon. minister that the question which I innocently put on the Order Paper did not emanate from any one who had been hanging around this building. No one hanging around the building was good- enough to come to me and say, "Do, please, ask this question." Let me tell the minister that the question was conceived in my own mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That surprises me.

Possibly, but- surprising
things happen in this House, and the hon. gentleman has been a member of Parliament long enough to realize tha-t fact. I say in all seriousness that the question I asked was a perfectly fit and proper one. Here you have a government administering two public utilities, the merchant marine and the railways; and you .will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that in all things it is only fair that people should take their choice when they pay their money. But in this case the people of Canada do not take their choice when they pay their money. According to the doctrine of the minister they are bound to pay their money for something of which they know absolutely nothing, because he refuses to give the particulars asked for. Is it to be said for one moment that the people of Canada, who are to put up deficits, as they have done already, ior public ownership, are to be told that while they are bound to pay their money they must expect no information in regard to the details of the operation of the utilities in respect of which they pay that money, and that as regards the question as to whether or not tenders have been called for they must remain in the dark? In effect, they are told by the minister; So far as information is concerned, we will give what we like and give it when we like, and the stockholders must be satisfied with this. The hon. gentleman takes refuge behind the fact that he will have auditors, more auditors, and super-auditors again. I do not care a button about the auditors so far as this phase of the question is concerned. What I want to know, and what the people want to know, is whether or not large payments are being properly

made, and whether supplies are being obtained at the best prices going. The minister has laid down a doctrine, and I do not know whether his colleagues are absolutely standing by it.
I did notice in the speech of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballan-tyne) that he was rather edging away and getting on the other side of the road. I am quite satisfied that he was not prepared to go down the road absolutely with the Minister of Railways when that hon. gentleman said:	" I will give such information to
this House as I deem best to give; no more shall I give and no farther shall I go." The Minister of Marine was surprised at the turn the debate took. There are more people and more members than the Minister of Marine and Fisheries who object to the doctrine that the people of Canada, the stockholders of two wonderful, great, huge national undertakings are to be told that " I, the Minister of Railways will give such information as I think well; I will withhold such information as I think proper and the people of Canada will be entitled to the remnant." That is a marvellous doctrine. It is so marvellous that I noticed coming into the House in double quick time after this policy had been laid down in the most perfervid way by the Minister of Railways, that master of political strategy, my smiling friend, the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder). He came in at once, he came down the steps gently and gingerly and seated himself beside the Minister of Railways. I fancy the following conversation took place:	" Don't
you think you have gone rather too far?" "No," says the Minister of Railways and Canals, " that is the way to treat 'em." " Oh, no," says the Minister of Immigration and Colonization in that suave way he has, " don't you think it would be better not to say it so loud, but to keep it under the hat a little? We may do it all the same, but don't give the thing away." "No," says the Minister of Railways and canals, " none of that for me, I am used to the good old Tory way-hit 'em on the head and knock 'em down. We are not for the people, the people are for us."
And so on with the little colloquy. Then the Minister of Immigration and Colonization says:	" Although for Union Government you have gone pretty far and you have committed us pretty deeply, still, for the rest of the evening, be just as quiet as you can." And the Minister of Railways has been quiet ever since. I know that took place; I could feel it in my bones the

moment the minister entered; I know it cannot be denied.
I do not in. the least -agree with that doctrine of the Minister of Railway -and Canals. The hon. gentleman talks about certain particulars and he -says that certain joint stock companies do not give those particulars. That is one thing; but when to-day you are managing a company with 8,000,000 stockholders composed of the people of Canada, you have a right to let them know -mything that they ought to- know in connection with the enterprise and to say to these people: "We will give you a full statement, our receipts, our expenses, our tenders, our bids, what we buy and what we have paid for the things we buy, and we will lay every card upon the table". They should do this so that the people may know if they are being treated justly and may feel assured that there is absolutely nothing to be kept back from this great mass of stockholders for whom I speak.

speakeroldname: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
