Once you put him in control we are right back again to the old system of departmental management, the old patronage system. If the minister cannot control, if he has nothing to say as to the management -and that is the only way it can be run- how are you going to put him on his defence day by day for the conduct of the company? In a word, you cannot. You cannot put the company on its defence in this House day by day as to individual acts and management, unless you have somebody in this House who is competent to answer for the company, and if he is competent to answer then he must have something to say as to the management and daily operations of this great system. Furthermore if the directors must, through the mouth of the Department of Railways, be called upon from week to week and from day to day to expose to the whole country each individual act of railway operation-thousands every day, in fact thousands every hour-if it is compelled, I say, to expose these matters to the whole country and to its great competitor or competitors in this country, then would anybody suggest for a moment that it could meet those competitors successfully? Does its competitor have to do that? Is any shareholders of the Canadian Pacific at liberty to frame an inquiry and demand an answer from day to day from the Board of Directors or from the general manager, as toe "Why did you do so-and-so- in such a case? Why you let such a tender to such a man and not to some one else? Why did you dismiss John Smith? Why you paid so much for butter, and so much for eggs? Why did you do one thing instead of doing another?" Certainly they are not. They are not compelled to disclose to the Canadian National Railway management the individual facts as to the management of their road and the conduct of its operation. If that is the case, how are you going to fasten on the Canadian National system the disadvantage under which its competitor does not labour? So it must *be clear that the plan cannot be worked. Once you follow that principle, you have done away with corporate management altogether, and you expose the management, whatever it may 'be, to conditions under which it cannot succeed.
Now what is there, that in justice and fairness to the system, and in full compliance with the undoubted requirements of the people as stockholders of the road, can 
be done? The Minister of Railways has said that as respects questions that may be asked from time to time the Government will have to take the responsibility of saying whether those questions are such inquiries into the operation of the road as make them for the time being the concern of the operating board and consequently, not in the public interest to answer in this House-the Government must take the responsibility of saying whether such questions are in that class and can be answered or not. The minister has also very clearly said that there will be presented to this House as representatives of the stockholders of the system, an annual report in complete and full detail similar to-and in detail better-than the annual report of the Canadian Pacific. That report will come to us audited by the auditors of the road, audited by the auditors appointed by the Government, and the minister suggests tonight a third board of auditors on which the department of the Auditor General of Canada will be represented, to consist as iwell of two others appointed by the Department of Railways and the Department of Finance respectively. In such form and with such assurances and credentials, the report of the system for the year preceding will come to this House,-every act and every expenditure vouched for and exposed to the gaze of every hon. member of this House. When that report comes, there is no reason that I can think of why everything disclosed by it should not be sub-10 p.m. ject to investigation either on the part of the Public Accounts Committee or on the part of a special committee that may be appointed by the House for the purpose. If that is done then undoubtedly nothing is denied the representatives of the people of Canada with respect to our system of railways that is given the representatives of the shareholders of any other company in respect of their properties. Nothing is denied the shareholders of the Canadian National Railways that the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific have; and indeed greater facilities will be given for the purposes of investigation, because no such facility as exists in connection with the Committee of Parliament can possibly belong to any committee of shareholders looking into the management of a private system. /
I have sought to lay before the House what seemed to me to be the line that could be followed to meet on the one hand the requirements of the system as a great business enterprise, to meet on the one hand

the essential safeguards that corporation [DOT]directors must have if they are to have any chance whatever of making their system succeed; and to meet on the other hand the undoubtedly justifiable demands of the representatives of the people to be informed fairly and fully in due course of all that concerns the taxpayers of Canada. By this method all that is secured without interfering with the management from day to day, and without entailing vast expense land untold labours upon the clerical staff, the directors and all concerned, as well as without fastening on the road those shackles that would involve its disablement, if not indeed actual disaster.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am under the disadvantage of not having heard the first stages of the debate. I came into the House just in time to hear that remarkable declaration of policy on the part of the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) which has been briefly and succinctly described by the member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee). The minister proposes, in respect to information which is requested by Parliament, to give to the House whatever he thinks proper; whatever he and his colleagues think should not be communicated they will not give to the House, no matter how much money may be involved in the transaction. It is a new doctrine; it is a startling doctrine. In some respects it is not quite startling to me, because the events of a year ago have prepared me for it.
A good many years ago, when men like John A. Macdonald, Alexander Mackenzie, Edward Blake and Richard Cartwright were in Parliament, there was placed on the statute book of Canada an Act which was held to be one of tremendous importance. The purpose of that Act, commonly known as the Audit Act, was to demand on behalf of the people of Canada an accounting for every dollar that was spent of the people's money. There was no question as to the necessity of the Act; there was no question as to its propriety. For decades that Act remained on the statute book and was carried out in all its fulness. Every minister and every official who expended a dollar of the people's money had to render an account in detail. That account had to pass through the hands of the Auditor General and had to be set forth in the Auditor General's report, and the minister or official had to appear if necessary before the Pub-lie Accounts Committee and stand crossexamination upon it. That is the law of Canada regarding everything-except these particular transactions in respect to the railways.
I cannot say that I am surprised at the doctrine laid down by my hon. friend tonight, because when the Canadian National Railway Bill was before the House a year dgo I ventured to make what I thought was a very modest request. I thought that they had omitted something from the Bill-you know, they do omit some things from the Bills and we on this side occasionally have to remind them. I thought they had forgotten to put in a provision that these expenditures should come under the Audit Act, so I reminded them of it and ventured to move an amendment which would have the effect of correcting the omission. But they said: No, we will have nothing to do with the Audit Act.
Now, there was a deficit last year of $47,000,000 in the operation of the Canadian National railways. Whether that was necessary or not I shall not stop to discuss. We are not now discussing the question of the management of the road; we are discussing the question of giving an account to the people for public money that has been spent. Hon. gentlemen opposite say: We admit that there has been a loss of $47,000,000, but you will be good enough to ask no questions about it, because it is none of your business. That is not too strong a statement on my part; it is absolutely within the four corners of what has happened. It is a startling statement, to men who have been accustomed to the methods of carrying on public business which have prevailed in the past.
Well, what is the reason given for this extraordinary decision? The ministers tell us that as respects these railways-and I suppose it will apply also to the Department of Marine-if you treat expenditures in connection with the railways as you treat other expenditures, why that brings them under political management. The Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meighen) said that these things could not be managed under a department of government. The argument is that if they are managed under a department of government the management becomes political and partisan, and patronage enters into it. That is the argument-is the statement of hon. members opposite, not mine. Well, if that is true, what follows? If everything that is managed under a department of government-I	am quoting the

Minister of the Interior-is political and partisan and carries with it patronage, then all the rest of the business of Canada as managed by departments of the Government comes under that condemnation.
I open the Auditor General's report, and just where I happen to open it I find the details of expenditures of the Department of Agriculture. Page after page is filled with details showing every item of expenditure-some items amounting to only two or three dollars; some involving large amounts. But they are all set forth in detail; they all go to the Auditor General; they are all subject to examination by the Public Accounts Committee. But we are told that we must not do the same with the items of railway expenditure, because if you do that -you make the management of the railways political. Well, if the submission of the railway accounts to the Auditor General and to the Public Accounts Committee makes them political, then clearly all these other expenditures are political; they are all being managed politically, according to the argument of my hon. friend.
I turn over a few pages, just at random, and I come to the (Customs Department. Here are many pages setting forth in detail the expenditures of that Department. But we are told: You must not ask the railway people to do -that, because that would make the railway operations political. Does the submission of detailed accounts of expenditures of the Customs Department to the Auditor General and to the Public Accounts Committee make the administration of the Customs Department political? That is the inference to toe draw from the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite.
It is the business of an Opposition sometimes to be critical, and I think that sometimes they ought to offer constructive suggestions. In the few remarks that I shall make I want to try to toe constructive. I want to help the Minister of Fnance (Sir Henry Drayton) who, I am sure, is having some anxious moments about the manner in which he shall obtain the (wherewithal to meet his coming Budget. I want to show him how he can save a little money. If it is possible and proper to get along without the intervention of any department in connection with the management of the Government railways; if it possible to get along without the Public Accounts Committee, why in the world do we need the departments for managing other things? The Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) has set forth in the Auditor General's

report many pages of details of expenditures made in connection with his Department. They are political, according to the argument of my hon. friends, because they are being managed toy a department. Why do we have the large staff which is under the Minister of Immigration, with all the attending expense? Why not turn the department over to this Toronto board and have -them manage it? Excellent men, the members of this board are; I am not for an instant questioning their ability of their good intentions. But if they are capable of managing this vast business, and if there is no need for the intervention of a department in that connection, (why not go down the list of departments and turn the whole thing over to them? You are wasting money; you are keeping a lot of men at work rendering detailed accounts of transactions which must be political, according to the contention of -hon. gentlemen opposite. All the departments are .squandering -time and money, they say, in the carrying on of work which could better be done by this railway board in Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman not recognize the difference between a service conducted by a department which is not a purely -business enterprise and not competing with other business enterprises, and such a system as the Canadian National railways, which must so compete?

If the system of public ownership of the Canadian National railways can only be conducted by concealing all the detailed facts from the people, then that is the best evidence that the system is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Nobody suggests that.

Vast sums of money
are spent in connection (with the administration of postal services. Go across -the street and you will find an army of men engaged in preparing details of expenditures to go before the Public Accounts Committee. What are you wasting time on that for? If hon. gentlemen's arguments are logical; if it is necessary to conceal from the public all the details of the vast expenditure in connection with railways, then it is well to conceal the details of the small transactions, comparatively speaking, carried out in connection with other departments. From time immemorial the foundation of the carrying on of Canadian public business has been the principle that for every dollar of public money that is spent an account shall be given, and it is provided in the law

that an account shall be rendered to the Auditor General, and submitted if called for to the Public Accounts Committee. If the Government cannot conduct the business of the Government railway in that way; if that business must be conducted with secrecy; if the facts have to be kept from the public, that is the best possible evidence that the system is wrong and should not be continued.

I should like to say a few words on a matter of national importance to the country and also a matter of international notice. A message has been received to-night that the Winnipeg " Falcons " have won the world's championship at the Olympic Hockey Match by a score of thirteen to one.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to enter into a discussion on the railway question to-night, and it is not my intention now to make any extended remarks. I simply want to put the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne) and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) right. They spoke of what an awful mess the political management of the Intercolonial railway was; how bad it was. In the report of the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton)' the Drayton-Acworth report, he states:
Whatever question there may be as to the propriety of endeavouring to earn interest on capital, it will hardly be questioned that the line ought to be so managed as at least to earn operating expenses, including therein a proper allowance for taxes. And even ignoring the early history of the undertaking, and considering merely the years from 1888-1916, during which the greatest advance has taken place In Canada, and the traffic of Canadian railways has shown the greatest increase, the Intercolonial has paid no taxes and still not earned operating expenses. During this period the total operating deficits reported amounted to $11,188,885.50. The total operating surpluses amounted to $1,651,239.73. In addition, however, there was, in the years 1912-16, an amount of $3,046,406.86 charged to working expenses and devoted to renewals, which, under the accounting methods in force before that date, would have been credited to surplus. Adding together these two latter figures, and deducting them from the deficit, we find that in the twenty-eight years from 1889-1916 there was an accumulated deficit on operation of $6,491,232.91.
How many years?

Twenty-eight years. The
Minister of Railways told the House that for this year the deficit on the Intercolonial was something over $4,000,000, or an amount equal to the deficits on the Intercolonial
for a period of eighteen years previously. The result under political management, which the Minister of the Interior holds up as something to be got away from, is as I have stated; but the minister prefers the system of my hon. friend (Mr. Reid) who appoints his friends to run this railway by a secret method, in the dark, where the light cannot get in. I am glad to hear the Minister of Railways say that he is going to give us a real statement.
When?

Before his Estimates pass. -I am taking that for granted. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) tells us that that statement will contain all things that it is proper for us to know. I will tell the Minister of the Interior that we shall be the judges of what we believe it is proper for us to know, and when we are on the Estimates, we shall take care of that phase of the matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up the time of the House, but I think it is important that the country should clearly understand the amazing doctrine that the Government has put forward this evening as regards public ownership, especially as the Government prides itself somewhat on having gone in for public ownership on a scale that no other government in the history of this country has attempted or even thought of. Unless I am completely mistaken, the significance of all that has been said by the Minister of Railways, the Minister of Marine and the Minister of the Interior, has been to the effect that with the extension of government ownership, there is to be, not an increase of publicity, but a diminution of publicity in regard to matters pertaining to operations.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I would ask
any of the hon. gentlemen to whom I have referred if that is not what was said.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, the very opposite.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Then, I shall have to leave the country to read the debate for itself: I have stated what I understood all the ministers to say. Take the remarks of the Minister of the Interior. He said that when we were dealing with enterprises of limited scope, it was all very well to have a minister answerable to Parliament who would give detailed information in

regard to the business that was being carried on-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend is
making a very poor inference from my remarks, if that is the way he took down what I said.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Again, I must say to the House that if any hon. member will take the trouble to look at Hansard to-morrow, I think he 'will find that the expression the Minister of the Interior used was "enterprises of limited scope," and in that connection he referred particularly to the Intercolonial railway; he said that it was all right as regards enterprises of limited scope for a minister to come down and give to Parliament a detailed account, but when we got beyond these "enterprises of limited scope," in other words when we got into these vast undertakings in which this Government has landed the country, then we were to have something different; we were to have corporate management as private business enterprises were conducted.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I said that it was all right to be answerable in those cases which are of limited scope in respect to purchases or matters of operation from day to day, but I never suggested-in fact I said the very contrary-that there was any detail that should not ultimately come down or be ascertainable by members of this House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister has an unfortunate manner of stating his views in a way that conveys one impression, and then of taking exception to the impression that his remarks convey.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is precisely what I said.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The point I
wish to make clear is this. As I have understood all the ministers who spoke this evening, their remarks have been to the effect that inasmuch as these enterprises are so large, we can expect less in the way of detailed information; that there must be more and more of secrecy in the management of these great undertakings.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has said this evening. Parliament heretofore has had the right to take account of the public expenditure of the different departments in detail. His remarks were called forth simply because

the impression which he, along with other members on this side, received, was that the Government did not propose to bring down in detail in future in regard to these enterprises the particulars that were given heretofore in regard to other departments of the Government. Here is something which the people of this country should clearly understand, namely, that as regards government ownership, as regards the management of government-owned enterprises, the people are to expect less and less by way of information, and their representatives in this House are to have less and less in the way of right to inquire of the ministry particulars or details in regard to these concerns owned by the people of the country. So long as that is understood the people will the better be able to judge of the wisdom of the new policies. It is important to know-and I think the debate has helped to bring out the fact-that as regards the future, the people of Canada are to have less in the way of information and their representatives in Parliament less in the way of privilege or right to inquire respecting the conduct of businesses which are supposed to be owned by the people. The Minister of the Interior said-and his remark was very significant-that while the Government would bring down a report somewhat in the nature of the report made by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, Parliament or any committee of Parliament would have a right to investigate everything disclosed by that report. I think I have reported my hon. friend correctly in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But what about
the things that are not disclosed in that report? That is just exactly what we want to get at through the questions we are asking.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If they have to dio with the company, the hon. gentleman will have a right to information as to those also. Is the hon. member satisfied?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The point to which I wish to direct the attention of the House is that it should be a matter of principle that there is nothing connected with the properties that the people of Canada own that the people's representatives in this Parliament should not have a right to inquire into, not at one particular time, but at all times. That is a principle which the people of this country will expect to see respected in this Parliament. If

Government ownership is to mean that there is to be less and less in the way of publicity, a good many who have been advocating Government ownership will think twice before they continue their advocacy. I ask the ministry what is there that can be done, if it is done in an honest and straightforward way, that will suffer from publicity? What is there to be feared from publicity?
Mr. RIOHiARDISON:	Nothing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The more extensive a business becomes the greater is the need of publicity.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The vaster an organization the greater the need of publicity. I say that the ministry is heading .in the wrong direction when they seek to stifle the giving of information. Their aim should 'be to encourage wider and wider publicity in regard to public affairs.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. GALDER (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
I had not the
slightest intention of taking part in this debate, but the statements made by two or three hon. gentlemen opposite are such that as a member of the Government I find it necessary to state what my position is in regard to this matter.
In the first place let me say that the imaginary conversation which took place between myself and the 'Minister of Railways did not take place at all. As a matter of fact, while 'I was sitting here on the minister's left I did not discuss with him at all the matter that is now under discussion by the House.
'Some hon. MEMBERS:	Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen may question my word, but I desire to assure them that I had some other matters to discuss with the Minister of Railways.
I thoroughly agree with the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) that so far as the 'business management of the Canadian National Railway system is concerned, every opportunity and every facility should be provided to this House to examine into every transaction. Everything that the management do may be brought under review, but there is a proper time when that should be done. The leader of the Opposition referred to criticising the conduct of different departments. Oh yes, but when is the time for that. When are the public accounts submitted to the House; when do those public accounts go to the Public Accounts Committee of this House?
-not until after the fiscal year is closed, and then all the work of these departments comes under review. I am rather inclined to think that there are some hon. gentlemen opposite who are trying to create a condition, and to bring about a state of affairs in this country that will not be favourable towards the cause of public ownership. They wish to have all the officials of the Canadian National Railways come here and expose all the details of their business to the Public Accounts Committee from day to day for a period of say six months. Does any hon. gentleman think that such procedure would be for the benefit of public ownership in this country? I say it would not. I say that the business for the year should first be completed and closed by those who are responsible for the conduct of that business, and then when it is completed it will come before this House in full detail and every opportunity will be afforded to hon. members on 'both sides of this House to examine every item pertaining to the conduct of that business. If the men whom we have placed in responsible positions in the management of that business are not carrying out their duties, then the responsibility will rest upon this House and the Government of this country. But that is not what hon. gentlemen opposite want.
Mr. '0 A HIRE:	Speak for yourself.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: I am speaking for the Opposition. They ask that from day to day while the business is being carried on, they should have the privilege, not merely of asking questions, but of bringing these men here and putting them on the stand and obtaining information from them before the year's business is concluded. The Government takes the opposite view. We take the stand that that would not be good business, that it would not be in the interests of the National railways or the cause of public ownership in this country. We take the ground that the men who have been made responsible for the conduct of these railways should he permitted to close their year's business, just as is the case with any other corporation. And when they have closed their year's business, they will prepare their statement in detail, and bring it down to this House. That statement will be placed on the Table and referred to a committee of this House where hon. gentlemen may scrutinize and inquire into every dollar's worth of expenditure that has been made. That is all we ask; nothing more, and nothing less.
The question that gave rise to this discussion referred to matters that were closed in 1919. The Government refused to answer a question in regard to business that had closed on December 31, 1919.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
I understand that the annual meeting of the company will be held very shortly, and that the annual report will be submitted at that meeting. The annual report will then be submitted to this House, and before the House prorogues it will have opportunity of doing just what hon. gentlemen opposite have asked. There is a time for everything, and that time will come. Hon. gentlemen will have the fullest opportunity to satisfy their wishes with regard to every expenditure that has been made in connection with the Canadian National1 railways during the past year-
The point I desire to make is briefly this: There is no desire and no intention on the part of the Government to burk inquiry; none whatever. That report will be laid on the Table, and this House will have the fullest opportunity to inquire into every dollar's worth of expenditure that has been made by the Canadian National railways during the past year. What more could hon. gentlemen ask? Instead of that, it is asked that day by day, while the expenditures are going on, a hundred questions with regard to the conduct of the business of the National railways should he answered by the Government. We take the view that that is not good business, that it is not in the interests of the Canadian National railways. That does not mean that we are trying to burk inquiry, that we do not wish to let the light of day in on what is taking place in connection with the, Canadian National railways. It amply means that there will be a time when the fullest opportunity will be presented to Parliament to inquire into every detail of the work of the Canadian National railway system.

While I listened to the remarks delivered by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid), the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), and the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder), I was reminded of the comparisons that we used to see in the grammar books-autocratic, less autocratic, least autocratic. The Minister of Railways, laying aside his usual geniality for the moment, assumed this position: We, the Government, and I, the Minister of Railways and Canals, and the Minister of Public

Works, will decide what information to give the House. If I do not think it wise to give the House certain information, I will not give it that information. That was softened down a good deal by the remarks of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen).
The Minister of Marine.

No, not the Minister of Marine; I shall deal With marine matters afterwards. I do not wish to mix Land and water at the present time. I am referring to the remarks of the Minister of the Interior, and incidentally I may congratulate that hon. gentleman on bi.s speech to-night. I was pleased to observe that he did not say an unkind or ungenerous thing about the Opposition in the whole course of his remarks. He was somewhat Less autocratic than the Minister of Railways. Then we had the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) who rose and said, "Perish the thought of secrecy"-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: Hear, hear.

-"Perish the thought of keeping anything back at the proper time and place; you shall not only receive what the Minister of Railways may wish to- give you, but I can .assure you that everything will he thrown open to the light of day; until then, however, in order that the management may not be hampered, a certain amount of reserve must be maintained." That, I think, is a proper characterization of the speeches we have heard from the other side to-night. Now, let us, in considering this matter, get down to the real facts. We have two companies, one to manage the railways, and one to manage ships. In fact, if I mistake not, I saw in the Canada Gazette the other day that every single ship constituted a separate company. So. that we may have sixty-three different companies to manage the Canadian merchant marine. What are the real facts? These companies are merely species or kinds of machinery. The people of Canada are the real owners of these organizations, and unless we have departed from the principles of British Con&tit u ti on a 1 i sm, the executive committee of this House, the Cabinet, is responsible to (this House and to the people for the conduct of these organizations; and the people, I take it, have the right to inquire into everything in connection with them. What is the information that is sought? The Minister of Marine said we must not give our attention to these little

details, such a.s the asparagus and the sugar which are bought for the ships. I suppose his captains are so successful that they are now given asparagus ; but we must not bother with the asparagus and the sugar and the coal. Petty details of that sort we must leave to the management. The Minister of Immigration said: We will give you all the information which is given in regard to, other departments of the Government. He shakes his head, but that is what I understood him to say. The difference between the position he takes in regard to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and the position in regard to the Department of Railways is this, that we have the right, in connection with all the other departments, to ask questions from day to day if we like about these other departments, and the Government is bound to answer them. But in regard to the railways a different principle has been asserted. And if the doctrine of the Government is sound in respect of these two great spending departments, that they can withhold information, then we have departed from the principles of the British constitution, and that is what makes this debate of such paramount importance. If the position assumed toy this Government is persisted in, that they have the right at their own sweet will to withhold, even for a time-, information as regards any great spending department, them we have departed from the principles of British constitutionalism, because one of the prime principles of British contsitutional practice is that there shall be in the House members of the Government who from their places- in the House must from time to time, and when the House asks it, give information concerning the departments of which they are in control. The Minister of the Interior said: "If you take that view, then there must be a minister in the House prepared to answer for the Department of Railways." I say, certainly there must be in the House a minister prepared to answer for the National railways, and the fact that the Government is attempting to get away from this primary obligation by creating a company is a tendency which this House should put a stop to immediately; because I consider, and I believe the people .will consider, thait it will constitute a very dangerous precedent. There must be an adherence to British practice. After all, we have been taught in this country to regard British responsible constitutional government as the highest development so far known in the art of self-government, and
one of the great principles of that system is that 'there must be a minister of the Grown ;n the House responsible to the representatives of the people. Have we not prided ourselves in the past on the fact that whereas the President of the United States, by the constitution of that great country, surrounded 'himself by advisers who had no seats either in- the House of Representatives or in the Senate, our system was such that the Prime Minister of this country had to select advisers who had seats in one or other of the Houses of Parliament, in order that those men might come in direct contact with the representatives of the people, and be prepared to answer their just questions. Now, what is the argument made by the defenders df this new system on the- other side of the House? As I understand it, it is this: The new administration of these great depart-mentis carry on business which is not primarily the business of the Government, and they must be allowed to conduct that business in a way which wall enable them to meet the competition of privately owned .companies. Hon. gentlemen opposite say: We must be put on an equality in this regard with the privately owned companies, and if you insist on knowing everything that goes on, then we shall be placed at a disadvantage. Is there anything very sound in that argument? I do>
not think there is. I do. not believe that the great competitor of the Canadian National railways, the Canadian Pacific railway, has ,to learn, through questions asked in this House, what the Canadian Government .railways are paying for coal, or ties, or rails. I believe that without doubt the Canadian Pacific railway have a sufficient number of branches and sufficient sources of information all over the country to be able to get that information without having recourse to questions asked by members in this House.
, Mr. CASGRAIN: They are better organized than the Canadian National railways.
. Mr. CALDER: Will the hon. member (allow me ia question that goes to the crux .of the situation? Who. buys the coal, and who is responsible in that matter? It is pot the Minister of Railways. The Minister of Railways does not decide upon these contracts; it is the management of the system that does that. The hon. gentleman, I am sure, can distinguish between the exercise of authority by the Minister .of Railways and by the management of the company.

I am opposed to the
system because I think it is absolutely unconstitutional. It is absolutely dangerous that, a minister, when asked a question about a great spending department, of which he is nominally the head, or is regarded by the people of the country as the head, should refuse to give the information which that question calls for. When I say that the minister is at the head of his department the ton. the Minister of Colonization and Immigration shakes his head. All I have to say is that under our constitutional practice he should be the head. If there is a deficit we hold him responsible. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has been as proud as a peacock about the profits he said his boats had made. He takes it as a cause of justifiable pride. I wish for the sake of my country that the Minister of Railways would show the same kind of pride. This Government is being blamed for the deficits on the government-owned railway. If you are going to have responsible government you cannot slough off your responsibility on phantom companies which have no real existence.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: In the $47,000,000 deficit there is included some $15,000,000 for the Grand Trunk Pacific which is still a privately owned corporation and which loss was caused by the Opposition building that railway.

The minister says that this is a privately owned company. He is the receiver of that privately owned company and as the receiver he is responsible for the way it is carried on. You cannot have your cake and eat it. If you want to have government ownership of railways the Government must be responsible.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
As I understand it, the
hon. gentleman advocates that the Government' itself, through the minister, should undertake the complete operation of the National system.

I never said anything of the sort. What I do say is that if you are going to have government ownership you cannot get away from the fact that the Government is ultimately responsible. How you shall arrange to conduct the details of your business is something that I am not considering to-night but we all want the Government railways to succeed because if the Government railways do not make a better showing in the future than they have in the past it will be a sorry financial outlook for Canada. Whatever scheme you inaugurate or carry out, whether it be a gen-

eral manager having a large share of ultimate responsibility to the minister, whether it be the phantom companies which you have created of which the managers and directors are your creatures, you will be regarded as finally responsible and you must be regarded as responsible to Parliament and the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: Wooild the hon. gentleman, under the scheme that he advocates, approve of the idea that the Minister of Railways should ultimately decide as to what coal should be bought and at what price?

Yes. If we are going to keep up our constitutional practice, in the long run, he must decide.
Mr. J. D. REID Then he will have to run the whole show.

I will be generous if
you want to cathecise me?
Mr. MEIGHEN That is. a pretty generous admission to make.

The point I want to
make is that under our system of responsible government the minister ultimately has to be responsible. It is quite true that he might leave to a general manager, as the minister would leave to an experienced and faithful deputy, the decision in a great number of points, but in this House he must speak, and be prepared to answer questions for the railway administration. If you have not got that, you have not got responsible government. Of course you may have government ownership but you have not government control. If you carry out your system to the logical conclusion you hand over the railways, which do not belong to you but which belong to the people of the country, to an irresponsible board. Either the board is responsible or it is irresponsible. If it is responsible, it has to be responsible to some one. It is responsible to -the Minister of Railways and Canals in the case of railways and to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in the case of ships.
That has been one argument and I think I have disposed of it. The next argument is that if you maintain responsible government you maintain the old system of patronage, graft and political pull. That does not follow. The Minister of Justice conducts an important department. He has no phantom company to shove off his responsibility upon. Is it to be supposed that the Minister of Justice, in making his appointments of judges, is merely influenced by partisan considerations. I do not think

anybody pretends that. I can not admire a fugitive and cloistered virtue, and the Government will not be able to get any credit in the country if they endeavour to place themselves in such a position as to make it impossible to exercise patronage. To resist temptation is virtue, but sometimes it is virtuous to flee from temptation. But I return rather to politics and leave the field of theology. Let me sum up by saying that if you are going to maintain the old traditions of responsible government you have to be responsible for what your board! of directors do and in regard to- any company you may form you should be prepared-aye, you should be glad-to answer every question that is put to you. For instance, is it of interest to the people of Canada to know where the coal is bought for the railway, whether the coal was bought by tender or otherwise and whether the lowest market price was paid? Surely that is of prime importance to the people. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries prided himself somewhat upon the statement which he had given to the House and which he said was as full and complete a statement as he would have given as president of some large company to its shareholders. The people of this country, or their representatives in this House, are in a very different position from shareholders. The shareholder in the ordinary company has inherited, or has more likely, bought, his shares. If he is not satisfied with the management he sells out, sometimes at a loss and sometimes at a gain. But the people of Canada cannot sell out their shares in these phantom companies which have been created. They have to reap the benefit in the case of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who says there has been a benefit and they have to suffer a loss in the case of the Minister of Railways who says there has been, as no doubt there has been, a serious loss. The people of Canada have to bear the loss or to take advantage of the gain. Therefore they are in a different position from ordinary shareholders and being in a different position-being shareholders, so to speak, by constraint; being forced to be shareholders- they have infinitely more right to information than the ordinary shareholder has.

I did not intend to take part in this debate but it has consumed so much time that I thought I would be justified in giving utterance to a few words. Last year when the Canadian National .Railway system was before the House different views were expressed by hon. gentlemen on both 107
sides as to what the future would be of this new organization that would have the management of the Government railroads. We on this side entertained grave apprehensions as to the results which would follow. Some people expressed the fear that in doing as we did we abrogated constitutional rights, that we abolished the inalienable right-as it might be said-of the people's representatives to investigate the affairs of a big public department and ascertain how the people's money was being expended.
Sir, to-night we have had a very sad situation revealed. The exact conditions with respect to the birth of this "child" of last year has been revealed. This offspring of the Government, the Canadian National railways, has been brought into the world, and what do we find? That we have created a body but that it is a body without a soul. We cannot find exactly who is responsible for this "child" and when we ask for information we are told that the facts must bfe kept secret or otherwise it would mean the ruin of the whole organization and it would be useless for the Government to longer continue administering these railways. I have one question to ask the Minister of Railways. He states that later on we shall be furnished with a detailed statement as to the operation of the different railways and then we shall ascertain exactly what we want to know. Well, Sir, I submit that these details are available at the present moment and for this reason: On the 30th of last March the Minister of Railways asked to submit -a statement to the House and he used these words, "I desire to place before the House a statement dealing with the operation of the Canadian National railways for the calendar year 1919." Further on in his speech we find this item:

Mr. SPEAKERThe minister would not be in order in answering-the hon. member; he has exhausted his right to speak. If the minister were speaking, he might, with his consent, be interrogated, hut not since he has concluded his speech and resumed his seat.

Like several other hon. gentlemen who have spoken I had not thought of taking any part in this debate. But I have followed the discussion very closely and I am of the opinion that the method being followed by the Government in the administration of these railways is in the right direction. On the other hand if the course which has been advocated to-night by hon. gentlemen here opposite were followed it would indeed be unfortunate for public ownership in Canada. The first, test it would appear to me that should be applied to the proposition of hon. gentlemen opposite is this: we have in the Canadian Pacific a very large company which has been splendidly managed and conducted. If the suggestion were to be made to the directors of that company that all the various items of expenditure connected with the carrying on of that great enterprise should be brought before the House of Commons and discussed in detail, I am sure the Board of Directors would be the first to say that they would not be ahle to successfully carry on the undertaking.
The constitutional question has been raised in connection with this matter and it has been emphasized by the hon. member foT Brome (Mr. McMaster). I am no authority on constitutional practice, but it seems to me that the method which has been adopted in the administraion of these railways is not new in Canada; exactly the

same principle is applied to public utilities in municipalities from one end of the Dominion to the other. The same argument which the hon. gentleman (Mr. McMaster) advances might be advanced in connection with the expenditures of a municipal council. In the case of municipalities in days gone by, it was always the practice for the expenditure of public money to be voted by the council. But as municipalities have gone into the operation of public utilities of various kinds they have found that in the carrying on of these utilities the practice referred to was not feasible or businesslike. Therefore a different form of government was worked out and in its working out by our municipalities the same principles are involved as in this scheme of government operation of railways. In the province of Ontario we find a great public utility to-day known as the Hydro-Electric system. That system is not operated as the Intercolonial railway used to be operated; it is conducted on lines very similar to those now followed in the management of the Canadian National railways. The Ontario Legislature votes money for capital expenditures, or for an extension of the Hydro-Electric system, but it has no control over the way in which that money is expended. It is true that expenditures are voted by the Legislature for a certain specific purpose, but in the administration of the Hydro-Electric system the expenditure of that money is left entirely in the hands of the Commission. At the end of the year that Commission submits a report to the Legislature and members then have an opportunity of looking into the various items of expenditure. However I submit that it would not be possible to carry on the Hydro-Electric system in that province as a department of Government and have every item of expenditure voted as is proposed by hon. gentlemen opposite. I am convinced that to adopt any other method in the administration of our national system of railways would be a move in the wrong direction. Only along these lines can we get proper business administration, free from political control; only by pursuing this policy can we hope to make a success of public ownership in this country.

Mr. Speaker, although the evening is far advanced I cannot let this debate conclude

without protesting against the manner in which the Government have met the remarks made by the hon. member for An-tigonish and Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair). The hon. member complains that the Government have not given members of the House the information that they have asked for. The Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid), instead of sticking to the point and answering the hon. member, wandered about in all directions in an effort to draw a red herring across the trail.
It was amusing, Mr. Speaker, to see four ministers of the Grown come to the rescue of fhe Government and endeavour to answer what the member for Antigonish and Guysborough had said. It is unusual to see so many ministers get up one after the other and endeavour to apologize for their actions. The Minister of Immigration (Mr. C'alder), the last minister who spoke, told us that at the end of the year members of the House would be given detailed information concerning the operation of the Canadian National railways. Now, that was rather a strange statement, in view of what happened a few days ago. I regret that under the rules of the House I am precluded from quoting Hansard, but I assume that I will be allowed to mention the date on which the Minister of Railways made his statement. On March 30, the Minister of Railways deliberately stated that one year having passed, he was in a position to give to the House an account of his stewardship, and of the stewardship of Mr. D. B. Hanna and the other directors of the Canadian National railways. He went on to say that he was prepared to do that. Now, let us see what kind of statement he did give to the House and the country. Was it the kind of statement that the Minister of Immigration says we are going to get? Was it the kind of statement that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company would give to their shareholders? Was it the kind of statement that the Canada Steamship Lines would give to their shareholders?-or that any $20,000 corporation in this country would give to its shareholders? No; if you read Hansard you will find that although the operations of the railways showed a deficit of $47,000,000, the minister put it all down in a statement which occupies three lines of Hansard. That is the kind of statement the people of this country and the members of this House get with regard to the National railways.
The Minister of Immigration told us also that we would have some kind of statement with regard to the Canadian Merchant 107)
Marine when the year was up. Well, we have on Hansard-and by a strange coincidence it was given on the very same day that the Minister of Railways (made his statement-a statement made by the Minister of Marine (Hon. Mr. Ballantyne) on the occasion of his asking the House to vote $20,000,000 to complete his shipbuilding programme. The Minister of Marine gave us a statement of the operations of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. I am almost inclined to advise hon. gentlemen to go down town and obtain from a dentist a pair of forceps with which to pull the information out of the Minister of Marine. He told us to-night that he gave us all the necessary information gladly and willingly. But what happened on that occasion when we tried to get the information? First he told me that he had $1,500,000 in the bank or in the vault in cash and Victory bonds. When I nailed him down and made him put the statement on Hansard-it will be found in Hansard of March 30-he submitted a statement comprising five lines for the assets and two lines for the liabilities. In that statement, instead of having $1,500,000 to his credit in cash and in Victory bonds, he is shown as having $400,000 in cash and $504,000 in Victory bonds, a slight discrepancy of almost $600,000. That is the kind of statement that the Minister of Marine gives to this House.

No; I say that the Minister of Marine made the deliberate statement to me on the floor of the House that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine had $1,500,000 in cash and in Victory bonds, but when I nailed him down in the evening and made him read the figures-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid we are getting rather 'far away from the original motion and the original discussion. So far, indeed, away have we got from it that, instead of considering the question whether a specific question, this question or that, should he answered, iwe have got rather into a consideration whether or not it is possible to carry on public ownership in this country under business principles. I had not intended for one moment to intervene in this debate, but I am prompted to rise in view of some statements that have been made by hon. gentlemen opposite. Operation of railways by Governments has, pretty nearly everywhere outside of Prussia, been condemned because it has not Worked as economically and efficiently as has private operation, although on the other hand, there have been great compensating advantages. The idea has been and the idea of the Government, as I understand it, is to see whether those compensating advantages which public ownership gives as against private operation can he retained under a direct and intimate business administration. The suggestion is that that is impossible; that it is entirely unconstitutional that we should carry on this particular phase of public business except, forsooth, by a responsible minister who must appear in his place in the House and always be posted as to the details of that tremendously diversified administration. Let us stop for a minute and see what that means. It certainly means one thing, and that is that everything that is being said against Government operation in any direction holds good as regards railway administration. I am not saying anything about patronage. Patronage has practically ceased to exist; hut the hon. member for Brome (Mr. MoMaster) wants us, having got rid of it, to put ourselves into a position where we shall be able to claim some credit for

resisting temptation by reason of that temptation not being removed ifrom us. But apart from any question of patronage, apart [DOT]from any question of party politics, the generally accepted idea is that men work better for an immediate reward which is open to them in private business, than they will work for a government, and that you will get better results from a private company than from a 'Government department, no matter how well it is run. I have always had the idea that the functions of Parliament ought to be divided, that there was such ,a thing as administrative as well as legislative functions. I thought that what England had found wise and safe to do in connection with the Admiralty could well be tried in Canada, to see if it were not possible under a similar system to run efficiently and honestly the people's railways for the people.
Mr. iMoMiASTER: Is not the administration of the Admiralty directly under the responsibility of the First Lord, with a seat in the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not that immediate knowledge of the situation which would enable me to answer the hon. gentleman with absolute accuracy, but my strong recollection is that in England all Navy and Admiralty matters are absolutely removed from the floor of Parliament.
Mr. MoMASTER:	Oh, no. The First
Lord of the Admiralty, like the Minister of War, brings in his Estimates and they are discussed on the floor of Parliament.
iSir HENRY DRAYTON: I am not speaking of Estimates or votes but of the details of administration, of the class of work done by the Navy. I do not think you will find such questions as, where the Navy buys its coal, discussed in the British House of Commons.
Mr. IMdMAlSTER: Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is there any
real reason why this experiment should not be tried in Canada? ilt is said that people won't work for governments. I have found a lot of men around Ottawa who are willing to work hard for governments.
Mr. M'cKENZIE: They are willing to get their cheques.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A large number of them earn their cheques pretty well, and are perhaps just as much entitled to those cheques as the workers of any private company are entitled to theirs. This is how the theory of the thing appeals to me: We

are expected to have absolutely successful operation of railways by private companies. The suggestion is that a man working for a private company, as compared with a man working for the Government, is working for personal advantage, for gain. That may be true of ordinary business, but it is not true of railways. In so far as the executive and the officials and the men are concerned, outside of a few they have no more financial interest as a rule in the success of the railway than have the workers on the Canadian National railways. On the other hand, the workers on the Canadian National railways have some interest in their railway because it is their own. I think it would be a great pity if this experiment, for it is an experiment, and a great experiment, were not given a fair chance, and it will not be given a fair chance if from time to time at the mere whim of an hon. member or somebody else, perhaps suggested by a paragraph in 'a newspaper that is absolutely dedicated to the destruction of public ownership, questions are put on the Order Paper and have to be answered dealing with such matters as: What are the names of the employees, their nationality, their religion,-everything but their railroad experience. The question of railroad experience, again, would seem to me to be a matter for the management. With very great deference I would suggest that this very necessary experiment, this attempt to get rid of difficulties most gravely pressing upon us, be given a fair opportunity. There is absolutely nothing to hide so far as the business of this company is concerned. The House will be given the fullest opportunity to examine the report when it is brought down. Have committees or anything else you like. These committees will be a great deal more than the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific will get, but make thorough inquiry then, if you will, so long as the detailed business from day to day is not of necessity more or less interrupted. There is a great deal of difficulty in getting traffic, and in making traffic connections; there is more difficulty in keeping them unless business is looked after promptly and properly. Make absolutely no mistake about this, that if the management of the Canadian National railways, no matter how able, is to be pilloried from day to day, is to be subjected to any charge thrown out to-day that may be shown to be absolutely false in two days' time, it will have no chance of making the railways a success; there would be great danger that they would be too busy answering question to look after their work.

I would like to add one further suggestion: I think any hon. gentleman is absolutely within his rights in asking a question in connection with a matter as to which he is prepared to make a charge against the management. In other words, the management, simply because it is through a company, should not be protected against wrong. They should be open to atttack; they should be open to proper proceedings being taken against them in a proper case, but they should not be open to widespread general fishing expeditions which can do nothing except to condemn the project to failure before it is fairly started.
;Mr. VIEW:	I have the very greatest
sympathy for the ministers who have spoken after the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid). If these gentlemen ever damn anything, they must surely damn ministerial solidarity, which compels them to exert all their mental alertness to defend the astounding statements of the Minister of Railways. They came one after the other, ' but put on the soft pedal, and did not repeat his statements with the audacity, if I may be allowed the expression, shown by the Minister of Railways himself. The Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) thought that the matter was so simple that it should not have involved the House in such a protracted debate; but who caused all this debate, if not the Minister of Railways, in saying he would not divulge to this House the information it was seeking? The ministers who spoke after him (Mr. J. D. Reid), notwithstanding ministerial solidarity, took care to say that they would not go so far as he, and they declared that the information asked for would be forthcoming, but with this reservation, that, it *would be given in due time. Their attitude was just a defence of the Minister of Railways, allowing him a safe retreat from the difficult position in which he had placed himself. The ministers assured us that we would get the information because we were entitled to it, but we would get it a little later on.
After the House rises.

Yes, after the House rises, next year or the year after, or after the next election, when we shall be in power and have an opportunity of digging up the records. As the Minister of Finance has said, there is a question of principle involved, a fundamental principle which is one of the cardinal points of British responsible government. But the Minister of Railways, who is not very scrupulous as
regards principles, generally leans on the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) when it comes to questions of constitutionality or the legal interpretation of points which confront him. To-night, however, he was too far away from his mentor, who would probably have pulled him down by his skirts. When he had made his astounding statement, however, there was only one thing left to do, and that was to explain it as best they could, and it was a hard job. The arguments that have been put forward to-night by the ministers are really not a fair reflection of their talent, and one who must have regretted very much the situation in which he was placed by the Minister of Railways was the Minister of Marine. That hon. gentleman came here and told us that he was ready to place the information on record, that he had nothing to be ashamed of. The administration of the ships of the Government had shown a surplus-
On paper.
: I take it for granted-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not want the remarks of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) to pass unchallenged by myself as Minister of Marine and as a member of the Government. Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the profits I gave to the House were only profits on paper?
Am I allowed to answer, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If the hon.
member desires to answer, I am sure the House will accord him the privilege of doing so.

I said that the statement given by the Minister of Marine was on paper, and I proved in my remarks tonight, that the Minister of Marine had said he had a certain sum in cash and Victory bond at the bank, while his own statement contradicted that. Until I see a regular business statement which I can go over I have not much faith in the minister's statement on paper.

I had not the opportunity to go into the figures, but I will take it for granted that the statement made by the Minister of Marine is correct, and that he has a surplus, and therefore has nothing to hide. But it was his misfortune to-night to have to stand by the statement of the Minister of Railways, that this information

would not be forthcoming in all cases. He said: "Surely you do not expect the Minister of Railways, in regard to the administration of the roads, to give to the House more than a big corporation would give to its shareholders." I grant that, and as the member for Oape Breton North and Victoria (Mr, McKenzie) said, we would be satisfied with such a statement as that of the Canadian Pacific Railway. So long as the shareholders of a big corporation receive from their managers and their board of directors a statement showing an honest, progressive, and successful administration' and reasonable returns on their investments, the majority of them will be satisfied and will seek no further information. But what would one think if the board of management of a private concern should inform its shareholders that it had a deficit of over $47,000,000, to meet which they proposed to assess all the shareholders? Would not the shareholders of such a company call upon their directors for a strict account of their stewardship?
I differentiate very clearly the position of the Minister of Railways from that of the Minister of Marine. The Minister of Marine tells us that he has a surplus to show and, as he states to night, the information is available. But his colleague, the Minister of Railways, not only has deficits to show, but, to aggravate this already serious situation, he announces his determination to withhold any information which hon. members, perfectly within their rights, ask on behalf of the people. He says that the people of the country will pay this deficit and that he will exercise the right to give just what information he sees fit, and if any hon. member asks a question whether on the Order Paper or by any other means, he alone will judge as to the propriety of giving or withholding the desired information. I say, iSir, that the propounding of such a theory in this House of Commons is subversive of all the cardinal principles of British constitutional government.
There is much to be said in answer to the statements which have come from the hon. gentleman and his colleagues. The Minister of Finance takes this attitude: "Do you think that a minister will always be prepared to answer on the spur of the moment all the questions that are put to him?" Well, Sir, I say that when questions are put on the Order Paper in the ordinary course under the rules of the House, and when the minister can take sufficient time to acquaint himself with the matters con-

cerned, hon. members have a right to expect complete information dn regard to any question which they put to the ministry. A minister can take five, six or seven days if he likes, in order that he may obtain the facts required, tout he is obliged to answer the questions that are asked him if he desires to observe the ordinary rules of procedure and to conform to those principles that underlie our government and the political institutions which we cherish.
It has been said that to call the Minister of Railways to account for all the expenditures of the National railways, is to introduce partisan politics and political patronage into the administration of the railway. Nothing is further from the truth, for if we are called upon to pay $47,000,000 to cover the deficit with which we are faced, it seems only fair and reasonable that we should obtain from the (minister who is in charge of the department full information as to how this deficit came about. And how can we know from the minister, or from any responsible parties, if not the minister, just what the details are, if not through questions placed on the Order Paper? The Minister of 'Immigration and Colonization, who is always very adroit dn extricating himself from difficulties1, has put up a straw man for the mere pleasure of knocking him down. He said: "Just imagine the officials of the Tailway standing here for six months and coming with bulky documents to give explanations and information on every possible point, stopping the management of the Canadian National railways during all that time, and costing the country vast sums of money." Well, Sir, there is really nothing in this bit of humour. I think that if an hon. member on this side puts on the Order Paper a question asking the Minister of Railways how many tons of coal were bought last year for the Canadian National railways, at what price, from whom the coal was bought, and how it was distributed, he could very well give that information without disturbing the managers or interrupting their operations. And when he comes here and tells us that the country is faced with $47,000,000 of a deficit, I think that it must strike him that some explanation will be called for by the country, and that above everything else the members of this House have a right to know how the moneys of the people have been expended, and to get such information as may enable them to ascertain just where the leakage has been. But how can we find out unless we put on the Order Paper such questions as those to

which answers have been denied us? I think the Minister of the Interior said that the auditors would Tender a full statement concerning the railways, and he scouted the possibility of this House questioning the accuracy of their report. But, Sir, while the auditors' report will contain the information that such and such an expenditure was incurred, that so much money was spent on coal, it will not give the facts in regard to which hon. gentlemen have put questions. We have been asked: Do you think that the Minister of Railways is going to introduce partisan politics into the management of the railways? And again: Do you think that he should interfere? Well, that was one of the jokes of the Minister of the Interior, and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) in reply told him that he thought it was the duty of the minister to have the final say in every question arising in the management of the railways. This opinion of the hon. member for Brome the Minister of the Interior characterized as a very generous admission, which he claimed to be a justification of the Government's policy. I say, Sir, that the Minister of Railways ought to have the final say because he is the person who is responsible to this House; and if he discovers that among the managers of the railway system there are some who do things which, in his opinion, sane judgment cannot approve, then I decalre that it is his duty to dismiss such officials.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: Would that principle apply to the appointment of all officials?
Not directly; but I say this

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: Pardon me. If the hon. gentleman takes the position that the Minister of Railways should have the final say with regard to the purchase of all material and all supplies, and he responsible to Parliament directly as the Minister of Railways-

I said "not directly."
iMr. CALDER: -why should he not be responsible for the appointment of all officials and employees of the railway as well?

The hon. .gentleman is trying to evade the point. He endeavours to put into my mouth the statement that the minister should acquaint himself with every minute detail of management. That I have not said. I say the minister should have the final say when he finds, either as a re. suit of personal investigation or through information from other sources, that there
has been culpable mismanagement, because he is responsible to this House and to the people. And if he finds that his managers have appointed any man who in his opinion is obviously unfit for the position he holds, he should exercise his undoubted prerogative of dismissing such an official. Will the minister contend that it is the duty of the Minister of Railways to suffer an appointment when such is to his- personal knowledge entirely bad, and should refrain from intervention?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: Not at all.

Then the minister admits
that if the Minister of Railways finds something wrong in the management of these railways he is obliged to intervene and he has the final say. That is the principle that the hon. member for Brome presented a minute ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: If I were the Minister of Railways and I found that condition I would remove the management.
And have the final say.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: I would remove the management if the management was not conducting the business property.
And not the appointee5

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: Not the appointee.

The minister states that if
he were the Minister of Railways and he found that the Board of Management of the Canadian National railways had made an improper appointment and that the wrong person had been appointed he would not change the appointee but he would change the Board of Directors. That is not the proper thing to do. The manager or owner of any big business would not do that. He would remove the Board of Managers if he thought they were wrong in all things, but the man who was wrongly appointed would be removed first, and the management would not he removed if that was the only fault. This does not mean that the minister should enmesh himself in details and have his finger in every question of management. These are the only principles that we have advocated and there is nothing in them that is subversive of sound principles of good management in the affairs of the Canadian National railway. We say that the House having been called upon to vote $47,000,000 to cover a deficit in the operation of these railways

we have a right to get some information with respect to it. From whom is the House to get that information if not from the Minister responsible for the Department under which the National railways dome? The colleagues of the Minister of Railways have said that this information will be forthcoming. That it will be forthcoming in documents and can even be submitted to the Public Accounts Committee. But the Minister of Railways said exactly the opposite. He said that he would not give the desired information and that he would not permit his Board of Directors, or his Board of Management, to appear before the Public Accounts Committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I did not say anything of the kind.
Surely.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I did not.
The minister now states that he did not say anything of the kind. The House will accept that as an example of the "retreat" of which I spoke a few minutes ago.
A shunting operation.

It exemplifies the situation in which the minister finds himself that he cannot now adhere to what he said a few minutes ago. I will not protract the discussion longer than to say that to find ourselves, in discussing matters of such magnitude, in which the gravest interests of the country are At stake, confronted by a minister of the Crown making such an astounding statement amounts to action subversive of all the principles of sound and responsible government.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On the motion of Hon. Arthur iMeighen (Minister of the Interior), Bill No. 68, to amend the Soldier Settlement Act, 1919, was read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

Before we take up the
