first clause would the minister explain the principal changes proposed, and the reasons therefor?	.

That, of course, can
only be done in committee by unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I gave a general outline of the Bill on its introduction, but I can give it again. The first clause is intended to confine the responsibilities of the Soldier Settlement Board as respects women to members of the Canadian Expeditionary Forces, to make it clear that women nurses with the British Army for example, were not intended to be included. The second section gives the Chairman the rights in respect of transportation which the rank of deputy head of a department involves. The remaining sections are designed to enable the board to give special advantages to settlers who take up unimproved land, as distinguished from settlers
who go at once upon improved land. The Bill somewhat restricts the advantages of the latter class and extends the advantages of the former class, particularly as regards advances for stock and equipment. That is done with a view to encouraging new cultivation, rather than the continued cultivation of land already improved, ll purpose to move in committee a further amendment to enable the board, in the case of advances for equipment and stock to insist upon the inclusion in the security, of other stock or equipment owned by the settler. We find very considerable difficulty in the administration of the loans for stock and equipment for the reason that the identity of the article is hard to follow, and settlers sometimes take advantage of that fact to ascribe to the stock owned by the board- because sold by the board and not paid for by the settler-all the losses that occur, though as a matter of fact the losses by death may be in their own herds. Indeed, it is more difficult to administer loans made for equipment and stock than any other *class of loan. The dangers surrounding the investment are much greater, and the securities which surround the advance must be strengthened accordingly. I did not intend on this occasion to make any remarks at all on the general work of the board for the year, as I purposed to do that immediately upon the introduction of the Estimates for soldier settlement. I think that would he a more appropriate occasion.
On section 1-"settler" to mean male member only of certain military forces:

May I ask why the
privileges that are accorded to Canadian imen who have served with the British Army are not extended also to Canadian women who have served as nurses in British hospitals? This Bill, I understand, excludes women from the privileges given to the men. 'That, I think, is an injustice. A similar injustice is done in connection with the regulations of other departments of the Government. I have in mind the *case of a girl from the county of Kamour-aska who served as a nurse in a British hospital for two years, but who was refused the gratuity that was given to nurses with the Canadian forces and also to Canadian soldiers who had served in the British Army. What is the reason for this distinction?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot speak specifically for the Militia Department, but it would occur to me that it would be hard to justify placing in exactly the same position

the person who served in our army and the person who served in the British army. If they were to be in the same position as respects one matter, they should be in the same position as respects all, and that would involve the payment of the scale of ipay and allowances that the Canadian army carries. These people chose of their own accord to go into the British army instead of ours, and they cannot expect the advantages of both. If they take the advantages of one, they must take the disadvantages with it. They cannot have the advantages of the course they took and the advantages of taking a different course. As regards this Bill, the purpose of the whole settlement programme, primarily, at least, is to secure settlement, and we did not feel we would be justified in including Canadian nurses because there might conceivably be *cases where a nurse would be so circumstanced, having a son, possibly, or a husband who was not a soldier, that she could become a settler in a position to perform farm duties. We have had some such cases, but we did not want all the nurses who are in the British army to get the idea that they can come under this plan if they merely come to Canada. We want to make it clear that so far as women settlers are concerned we accept only women who were in the Canadian Expeditionary Forces.

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a certain class of soldiers in regard to whom I have received a good deal of correspondence, and that is the members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force who did not go overseas.
I quite appreciate the fact that in some cases they may not be justified in claiming any of the benefits of this Act, but unquestionably there are a large number of C.E.F. men who were unable to get overseas who would make excellent settlers. In fact, comparatively speaking, the great majority of them would make first rate settlers, and I have always felt that this privilege of the Soldiers' Land Settlement Act should be extended to those members of the C.E.F. who were compelled to remain in Canada. I should like the minister to make a clear statement as to the official decision of the Government in regard to this class of soldiers. The only argument that I have heard advanced against their inclusion under the Act has been the apprehended danger of extending this movement to limits that might financially embarrass the Government, but I must say frankly that I do not anticipate

any such difficulty. As the Government are in a position to obtain a greater amount of information than any private member can get, it may be possible that the minister can give the committee some explanation that may be satisfactory. And I am reminded that these advances being based on the principle of a loan, the risk which the Government would-be running in extending the scope of the land settlement scheme to the men I have mentioned would be very slight. As I have already stated, I feel keenly that this class of the C.E.F. should be afforded the privilege of the Soldiers' Land [Settlement Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As I stated a moment ago, the first object of the whole land settlement policy is settlement; and the second object is to give exceptional advantages for settlement to those who are particularly the creditors of the State in respect of the war. Now, in order to satisfy both requirements, the second at least must be fairly complied with. In deciding to whom we owe the most we must draw the line somewhere, and undoubtedly we have not drawn it in any narrow or niggardly spirit. The definition of the word "settler" in the Act to-day is extremely wide, and as a consequence the offices of the Soldiers' Settlement Board throughout Canada have been serenaded almost night and day for over a year. The mass of applicants is so great that it has indeed taxed the capacity of the organization to absorb them. It must be understood that the denial of the privilege of the Soldiers' Settlement Act is not in the way of penalty. If it were a penalty we would have to ascertain those who were to blame and those who were not among the number that did not go overseas. But that is not the criterion. All other good citizens of Canada who could not possibly enlist may be entirely free from censure, but they are not included in the Soldiers' Settlement Act. We simply draw a rough line and say that those who went from Canada shall be included. We may deny some very deserving men who remained in Canada, but we -have taken a bold step, and until we have cared for a great body of deserving applicants from among the overseas men, I do not think it would be wise to extend the boundaries of the scheme and open the door to others. It will undoubtedly be a charge on the people of this country for some time in taking care of the financial responsibilities to which we are already bound. The commitments of

the board last year amounted to something over $58,000,000, and while we trust the commitments for the next year will be somewhat less, they will be still very high. It is true the moneys are given by way of loan, but the loss on interest is very considerable. The cost of administration necessarily is anything at all but small, and besides that there are certain remissions of interest which count for a very great deal; and in the whole programme there is an element of danger which must be followed by a proportion of loss that is certainly inevitable. In the circumstances, therefore, I would strongly recommend that there should be no extension of the privileges of the Act for some time at all events.
Mr.W.F.MACLEAN: May I call the attention of the committee to a case that came before me yesterday of a returned soldier who served throughout the war? This man is a mechanic and is building his own house in my constituency, and he feared an event that seemed imminent in Ontario, but one that was postponed by the legislature of that province, and that is the extension of the moratorium. He thought that under the moratorium he would have to pay all his mortgage by the first of July, as the Bill first provided, and he wrote to me to ascertain whether it would not be possible for the Dominion Government to widen the application of the Soldiers' Settlement Act so as to provide loans for those returned men who are building homes of their own. I quite realize, as the minister has pointed out, that the commitments under the Act have been very high, but I feel it incumbent upon me to bring this man's case to the attention of the Government, because there are many other men similarly circumstanced throughout the country who are in dire need of assistance. Will the man who served overseas and who is not competent nor desirous to be a farmer be afforded some means of re-establishing himself in some walk of life other than farming?

I desire to express some views along the lines of the remarks which have been addressed to the committee by the hon. member for North Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) with reference to the Canadian soldiers who enlisted in Canada and who did not get overseas. I understand that the overseas men are divided into two classes: those who were disabled a,nd are in receipt of pension, and those who are entitled to the benefits of the Soldiers' iSettlement Act; that is to say, they
may take a grant of land, receive a loan for livestock, etc. But the Canadian soldier who did not get overseas is not in receipt of pension nor entitled to consideration at all. I know some Canadian soldiers who unfortunately did not go overseas, and one I have in mind at me present moment enlisted early in the war. He relinquished a good position, and got as far as Valcartier where he sustained a broken leg. He will be lame as long as he lives. He is too much of a man to ask for a pension, and is not entitled to the benefits of the Soldiers' Settlement Act. I think the minister would be well advised to take this matter into careful consideration. I find no fault with the minister, but I think them is need for further investigation. The soldiers who enlisted in Canada but did not get overseas are not receiving any benefits under the Soldiers' Settlement Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Referring first to the
remarks of the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), there is no doubt a very large class of just such men as he describes,, a class I know it would be the desire of the Go\ernment to assist by loans were such a course possible or practicable. The committee on Civil Re-establishment last year very carefully considered that class of cases and the finding of the committee was that as' we had already provided needed assistance to the provinces by loans for the purpose of house building, that should constitute a measure and method of assistance for the meantime any way.

Supposing the
soldier has a house built- with a mortgage on it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think that
this country is in a position as yet to undertake loans for the purpose of paying off all the debts of those who may have debts upon their properties. There is of course a lot to be said in favour of that position, but it lacks this that can be said for the soldiers settlement assistance that the soldiers settlement assistance looks to the cultivation of land and production and therefore an increase in the wealth of the country. That has been the primary object to be attained. Assistance along the other line has one object and one object only namely, settlement, giving the soldier some money and getting him better fixed. That is not only all right but most commendable, but the other class of expenditure can he defended on the double ground that you can advance for soldiers settlement.

The country can afford to do more when settlement and the cultivation of land results than it can afford to do when these do not result.
Coming to the remarks of the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Reid), I realize the merits of the single case that he brings to attention, namely, that of a man who being disabled in Canada could not proceed overseas and cannot get the assistance of the board for the reason that he, first of all, does not get a pension and the reason that he does not get a pension in that individual case is because his pride prevents him from applying for it. If it were possible to make an Act so detailed as to cover such isolated, rare, and peculiar cases as that I would be very glad to do so. I cannot understand why such a man would not apply for a pension because if I understood the case and the circumstances aright he would be entitled to a pension and being entitled to a pension he comes under the Soldiers' Settlement Act. I do not know how we can amend the Act to cover such very special and extraordinary cases. If we were to say: "We will take care of all who are in Canada " that would include the great mass of men who were taken under the Military Service Act, hundreds- yes, thousands-of whom never got away from their own farms. It would mean that when the hand of the State was placed upon them they were admitted to the full advantages of this Act involving very great costs and commitments to the country. I do not think that could be justified. There is nothing at all in the way of special recognition that that vast class of cases deserves and I do not think for the sake of some who did not leave Canada and who may perhaps have special desserts, we would be justified at all, under present financial conditions, in undertaking to extend the commitments of this Act to the whole body o,f those who in a great many cases, never even left their farms.

Having regard to the
number of applications for settlement under this Act, what about the available, suitable, land?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The available Dominion land within anything like an economical distance from railways is very small. We have had since the first Act went into operation 6,500 soldier grant entries on Dominion lands. That shows that only about one-quarter of those who have come in under the general benefits of the Act have gone on Dominion lands which they get free. All the rest have bought lands or have

asked for assistance in paying off the encumbrances on land they had. Of course there is any amount of land; you might say there are unlimited quantities open to purchase, but of free lands under the Dominion Lands Act the areas that are worth while taking up are for the most part exhausted.

I take it from what the minister says that roughly about 24,000 soldiers have been placed upon land of one kind or another. Would the minister mind stating how many applications have not yet been dealt with, or how many placements have not actually been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The total number of applications received up to the 31st March was 50,423. The total of those who had passed as qualified was 36,830. There have been 1,556 undergoing training.

I think the Act is just a little bit too rigid. If it were more elastic I believe a great majority of the soldiers would be satisfied. I had not in my mind at all what is in the minister's mind, that the benefits under the Soldiers' Settlement Act should be extended to every soldier whom the State put its hand upon because hundreds of men never left the farms although they were in the enlisted forces. The benefits of the housing scheme do not extend to the soldiers in every province. The Government of the province in which the soldier lives may or may not take advantage of the scheme. We have two Provincial Governments that have not taken *advantage of the offer and therefore the soldiers in those provinces are not getting the benefit of that money.

Referring to the Act of
1919, I see that the word " settler " has practically four definitions. The word " settler ":
means a person who at any time during the war has been therein engaged on active service in a military force,-
I suppose those words " active service " would protect the minister from those who have remained on the farm while the war was going on because I do not presume they were on active service unless they donned khaki.
(1)	of Canada .	.	. and has served out
of Canada.
And who is entitled to a pension. That is one of the classes that is not excepted.
(2)	of His Majesty or of any of His Majesty's
allies .	.	. and, being ordinarily resident in
Canada when he enlisted in or otherwise be-

came a member of such force, has served thereafter out of Canada, In a theatre of actual war.
Paragraph (3) applies to the resident of another dominion who has served in the army. Now my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) has ju^t stated that there was a discrimination in this case as against .the women. The word "settler" in paragraph (1) includes women who served in the forces of Canada, or were in active service out of Canada, and who are entitled to a pension on account of being wounded. Paragraph (2) applies to the case of a man ordinarily a resident of Canada. Why not leave the second class oult of the amendment and make this privilege apply to residents of Canada who. have joined His Majesty's army or the army of any of the Allies, and saw active .service? Because paragraph (2) includes Canadians, or if not Canadians, people who. resided in Canada and intended to. become Canadians but left the .country for .the purpose of joining either His Majesty's army or the army of one of the Allies. The class referred to'-in paragraph (3) is different. Paragraph (3) applies to a person who has been on active service in the forces of Hi.s Majesty or of any British Dominion or colony, and has served out of the country wherein he enlisted or otherwise became a member of such force in a theatre of actual war. I do not see that a woman who was an ordinary resident of Canada and enlisted for fwhat is considered active service and went out of Canada to do that service either in the armies of His Majesty or in the army of any Ally .should be deprived of the privilege referred to. I do not know whether my hon. friend catches the distinction I desire to make. If my hon. friend wants to make a discrimination against the women-I suppose it is only in favour of nurses in this case-why discriminate against a woman who. was residing in Canada and left this country for the purpose of doing actual .service? Furthermore the widow of the mian who died on the battlefield should foe entitled to. take .advantage of the provisions of ,the Settlement Act. Again, I do not see why a Canadian, or a person who. intended to become a Canadian, and who left our shores to go on .active service abroad should not be entitled to the same advantages as are accorded to the other classes referred to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Of course the Act does include belligerents in any of the Allied forces, inclusive of the forces of the United Kingdom. Whatever Parliament might do were the whole legislation to be recast at
the present time might be doubtful, but the point is this: The' soldiers overseas in the British army particularly, and in the French army, were informed of the contents of 'the original Adt .and many of them prepared to come <to Canada and have been coming under that Act. Now we have a board at work in England sifting the applicants who desire to come in ordeT that none may cross the ocean who are not Sudh as should foe admitted under the provisions of the Act-such ais can qualify and are practically certain to succeed as settlers. That being the ca.se it would never do now to restrict that class, much less to remove it altogether-it would be looked upon .as a breach of faith.
A.s regards this clause which seeks only to define the class (of (women iwho can come in, it is not of great consequence because we know, and must frankly say, that the number of women who by themselves can qualify as settlers and undertake farm work and .show to. a qualifying board that they can go out on the farm and do the iwork and make a living is very small indeed. We admit nurfees and say to them "If you (served in our forces and oan qualify we will let you go out info, this northern country and see if you can succeed;" but we do not want to have any such invitation held out to nurses in the British army, no matter where they come from. In the first .place the number who might possibly ever succeed in entering the gate would be very sm-all, if any at all.
Have you had any applications?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes we have had one or two. We want to make it clear that in so far ats women are concerned we are prepared to take care of those of our forces ; but we do not want the women of other forces to feel that they have a right to come here and make application for these special advantages, because the fact of the matter i.s they cannot succeed even if they get out on farms in Canada.
The minister is not meeting the exact point that I made. I am not asking him to open the doors wide to all the women who. served in the Allied armies.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
means simply to. Canadians?

Those who were residents of Canada .at the time they enlisted and went on service in the Allied armies overseas. The number is so restricted there is not such .a danger of an invasion of our

vacant lands 'by womanhood. But even if the numbers were greater their claims should be recognized and the advantages given here should not be refused to them. Now paragraph (2) defines a "settler" as being:
A person who at any time during the war has heen therein engaged on active service in a military forces-of His Majesty or of any of His Majesty's allies-and being ordinarily resident in Canada when he enlisted in or otherwise became a member of such force, has served thereafter out of Canada, in a theatre of actual war.
Some of these persons, as I have already said, would not be Canadians but the fact of their having been resident in Canada would indicate that they had intended becoming Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think the matter is of enough importance to prolong the discussion. Provided the hon. member would simply agree to omit from the clause in the present Bill the figure "2" and the word "and" his views would be met. Then if they are really Canadians and went over and served in the British army-if there are any of those who can qualify-I . have no objection to giving them -a chance but I do not know of any. We have had no such applicants so far.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Meighen moves to amend clause 1 by substituting the word "class" for the word "classes" and striking out the words "2 and." Shall the aonend-pient carry?
Amendment agreed to and section as amended agreed to.

If I understand aright the purpose of the Act passed last year in regard to the settlement of soldiers was to enable those who were anxious to settle on |the land and become farmers to do o. It seems to me there are other men who served in the British foroes-either on ,Canadian patrol boats or in the British fleet-during the war who are also entitled to such consideration from ithe Government. It seems to me that the privilege granted under this Bill should also be extended to1 our fishermen who were on naval .service and who would like to purchase .boats or gear to conduct the fishing business, because the fishing industry is just as important for the production of food *as is farming. I would therefore like to ask ithe minister if he is willing to extend a privilege similar to that granted under [DOT]this Bill to those men who>
wish to prosecute the fishing business,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That matter has been urged on my attention by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who has supplied me with memoranda. I thought it w/as a fit question for .adjudication by the special committee *which is now sitting on the subject of Soldiers' Re-establishment. Therefore the chairman of that committee has been placed in possession of the file and will have the matter reviewed by his committee.
Mr. J. H. -SINCLAIR: Will there be an opportunity later on to deal with it by legislation? I would like to impress on the minister the importance of the matter mentioned by my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff). Large numbers of men in the Maritime Provinces were engaged in the fishing industry at the time they enlisted, many of them being seventeen to eighteen years of age, who had been accustomed to work in their father's boats or to assist somebody else. They came back grown-up men and anxious to go into business for themselves, but they did not have the necessary capital. It is much less expensive to set up a fisherman in business than it is to establish a man on the land, a large sum comparatively being required to equip a farmer, and it is a long time before he can produce anything to recoup the outlay. It is different with a fisherman. A boat and nets would cost perhaps not more than $2,000 in all, he could commence operations at once, and with moderately good luck he would very soon be able to begin paying back the money advanced to him. So long as his boat is insured, it and the nets would form a very good security, in fact, a better security than an abandoned farm in certain parts of the country. I think it would be well worth while for my hon. friend to give this matter his earnest attention, and I hope if the committee report favourably he will introduce legislation at the present session to give effect to the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Duff).

I know, Mr. Chairman, there are difficulties in adapting the details of such a measure as this to the needs of . various classes of the community, and I sympathize with the minister in that respect. I have not any particular scheme to suggest in regard to helping the fishermen, but I do want to join my hon. friends from Lunenburg and Antigonish (Mr. Duff and Mr. Sinclair) in asking that something should be done for these fishermen, who are a very large and important class of the community. I know cases of young men re-

turned from overseas who have found it very difficult to resume their pre-war work, being without the means to provide themselves with the necessary outfit, although but a moderate sum would set them up in business as fishermen. I do not dwell upon the matter further; it is sufficient for me to state that I trust it will be taken up again and that the minister will be able to give it his cordial support.

Is the Government giving any assistance to fishermen on the coast?
1 understand instructions were sent out to some officials of the Department of Marine and Fisheries to go among the fishermen and ascertain what they would like to get by way of assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know of any
assistance being given to those fishermen.
I would rather presume that the
4 p.m. activity the hon. member refers to resulted from the efforts of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. When he pressed the matter upon me I asked him to have an investigation conducted and a practical report made as to what forms of assistance might be given to certain classes of men, what the security would be like, what the payments should be, and so on, and it is very likely that the minister's inquiries led to some such action as the hon. member (Mr. Chisholm) has in mind. I do not know that I look forward with pleasurable anticipation to the possibility of that added responsibility being placed upon the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Board; because the board is an agricultural board, the chairman being particularly an agricultural man, I do not think that he has any more practical knowledge of the fishing business than has the minister who is in charge of the work. Still I would not think there is anything so technical about it that it would require special knowledge on the part of the chairman of the committee, although we might require a technical man who had had actual experience and special educational advantages in fishing to take charge of the work. The matter, as I say, is before the Civil Re-establishment Committee. It all depends on when their report is presented whether its recommendations, if accepted, can be put into effect this session. I merely stated my general attitude towards the matter. I would rather like to see assistance given, for I think this is a class of assistance that perhaps comes closest in point of desirability and practicability to what we are giving now. But I know it will mean a great deal more in commitment 108
than the hon. member has in mind. I do not think I should say any thing that may influence the judgment of the committee one way or the other. I need only add that the report of the committee will be very promptly and seriously considered by the Government, and if that report is favourable, and is brought down in time, there is no reason why action should not be taken on it this session.
Mr. D. D. McKENZlE: As I have some fishermen-soldiers in my riding it might be construed as indifference on my part if I did not join my hon. friends who have very properly urged on the minister the desirability of giving some assistance to these men, and I can only say that I heartily concur in their suggestions and confirm what has been said regarding the excellent security which the equipment would afford for the advance made and the ability of the fishermen to begin repaying the loan at an early date. There is one of the things that I would like to bring to the notice of the minister, particularly in view of the fact that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballan-tyne) is taking an interest in this particular matter. Last year I brought to the notice of the Government that it would be a pity to dispose of the boats that were acquired by the Government during the war unless they could be sold at good prices, and it seems to me that they could be utilized with splendid results by these fishermen who understand how to handle such boats. If such craft are still in the hands of the Government, I think a company could be formed on the Atlantic coast to take charge of them and hire them, if not sell them outright, under reasonable terms to the fishermen, and so give them an opportunity to produce more of that food which is so necessary in this country.

I referred a few minutes ago to the fact that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has been making inquiries of these fishermen as to what assistance they would like. I would like to impress upon the minister the desirability of having something done this year, if possible, because the impression was made upon the fishermen that something would be forthcoming. They gathered together and made their presentation to the Superintendent of Fisheries, and they decided upon the amount of money that they would like to get and the security which they were prepared to give. I do not think the impression of the fishermen was that this was only a sort of investigation; I think they



understood something practical would 'be done, and they will be very much disappointed if it is not done. I thought the minister would be incorporating this in legislation before the House this session. I quite understand that the matter is now before the committee of which I am a member, and I hope the committee will be able to present its report in time for some legislation to be passed this session.

I heartily approve in the main the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Chisholm). The Albemi constituency which I have the honour to represent is made up very largely of fishing territory, and I regret that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) is not here to give some encouragement to members like myself who represent fishing districts. If anything is to be done, it must be done quickly if we expect the fishermen to take advantage of loans this year. Fishing boats cannot be built in a month or in two or even three months, and in British Columbia the fishing season is now in operation. As regards the very large fishing territory comprised in my constituency, there is very little suitable land available for the settlement of returned men, and my opinion, based on considerable experience, is that loans to fishermen would be safer than loans upon the land. I am speaking, not of loans to any one Who does not know anything about fishing, but of loans to actual fishermen who understand how to 'take care of their boats and nets, and I hope something will be done for the actual fishermen, as is being done for the returned man who goes on the land.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must point out to the committee that rule 13, clause 5, says:
Speeches in Committee of the Whole must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
I did not want to interrupt an hon. member who desired to put a single question to the minister concerning fishermen, but I must rule that a series of questions on that subject is entirely out of order, and I would respectfully request the committee to return to the subject-matter of the clause before the committee.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 2-chairman of board to have free or reduced transportation:
Does that apply only to the chairman?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I will ask the Acting
Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) to allow me to get out of order for a second or two in order to make a suggestion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Even the hon. the Acting Prime Minister could not give that permission.
Then I will ask the consent of the House to give me permission for a minute, just to make a suggestion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the hon. member (Mr. Bureau)the unanimous consent of the committee?
Go ahead.

It is very difficut to follow a clause like this unless the original section is reprinted). Perhaps on the ground of economy, the right hand -sheets of the Bill are blank; and as every hon. member has not 'time to read the Act as passed last year and has had time to forget what was enacted, I think the original section should have been reprinted.

A still better suggestion would be to repeal the entire clause and reenact it in the amended form. The general practice of making amendments by striking out a few words and inserting a few others is very apt to be embarrassing.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-calculation of cost of land and improvements:

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will read the original clause.
Section 17 reads:
1.	The board shall calculate in each case of sale the price at which any land may he sold under the provisions of this Act.
2.	In calculating the cost to the board of any land acquired by purchase, the board shall take into consideration not only the cost of the land, but also the cost of improvements, if any, effected by the board.
That would mean the cost of improvements already effected. The purpose of the amendment is to enable the board to take into account improvements to be effected. That is to say, in determining at what price the board can sell land to a soldier, they can take into account improvements to be effected on that land and sell at that price, thus lending him the money with which to make the improvements instead of waiting and having later on to make a further loan.

Is the object of the clause to allow the board to calculate the cost of

lands even although they are not acquired by purchase? The section says:
In calculating the cost to the board of any land acquired by purchase.
The words "acquired by purchase" qualify the land. The minister is striking out those words, so that the board may make the calculation in regard to any land whether belonging to the Government or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is true, if the board sells land that we did not buy, for example, Hudson Bay land and what we call Douk-hobor land, lands of special value that are beyond the ordinary class of homestead lands and we do not feel that we would be justified in giving them away as homesteads. We sell those, thereby creating a fund which we use for certain purposes, for insurance against loss, for money in order to assist disabled men. That is what the board has in mind.
Under the old section as it stands, the board, in calculating the cost of all lands purchased, before they were resold to the soldier took into consideration the improvements effected?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
The words "or to be effected" are to he added. Is that not in the way of a loan to the soldiers in addition to the cost of the land?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Besides the cost of the land and improvements already effected, the board can add the cost of the improvements to be effected in determining what they will sell the land at. In that way they make to the buyer a loan sufficient to enable him not only to take the land, but to make those specific improvements.

If the land is not purchased, it belongs to the Government. It is sold to the soldier who intends to make certain improvements. He is going to charge himself for his labour and improvements if the cost of those improvements is to be added to the cost of the land. He is to be his own victim; that is, he is to work against himself, if you are to charge him for improvements he is going to make. I do not think it is fair for the board to charge him with them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is not charged.
If you charge the improvements in the price of the land, he pays for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I may not have stated the position quite accurately. The clause will read:
The cost of the improvements, if any, effected, or to be effected, by the board.
These must be improvements to be effected by the hoard, not improvements to be effected by the purchaser from the board.

It means that the board, before disposing of the land, can effect certain improvements, build, for instance, and have a certain acreage broken, and then they can wait to dispose of the land until somebody applies for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the purpose of the board is to utilize the purchaser o.f that land, to fix what the land is worth, and then pay him to make the improvements. In that way the man is improving what is to be his own land. Under the statute the improvements are made by the board, and then the board sells to that man at the price not only of the land itself but of the improvements already made to it, and to be made by the board through the instrumentality of the purchaser.

I am not sure I understand that perfectly.' The last man either buys or does not buy that land. If the title remains in the board the man leases the land, and I do not see how the board can put a value on the land unless the man buys it. If he becomes the purchaser the board has a mortgage on the land, and the transfer is absolute. The owner of the land then improves it, thereby giving more value to the security held by the Government, and he is to be made to pay a higher price for having made these improvements, unless he is to be treated as an ordinary labourer and paid so much per day for these improvements he makes on his own land. I cannot understand the dual role he is playing, first as the purchaser working on his own property, and secondly as a man hired by the Government to work on government property. If it is his own property I do not see why he should be paid for improving it, and if it is not his property I do not see why he should pay the Government for the improvements he himself has made.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The board sells a soldier a certain quantity of land, say 160 acres, upon which there have been some improvements already made-a house has been built, let us say, worth $400 or $500.

That is different. You
said improvements had been already made.
108i

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am taking a case
that will cover both. The farm costs, say, $2,000 with the improvements. The sale then is for $2,500, but the board arranges with that man after the purchase goes through to do improvements in the way of breaking say, amounting to $400 more. He will be paid for doing that by the board, because he cannot do it unless he is paid. The board then sells him the land for $2,900, but as he goes on and 'makes those improvements the board pays him for them. In other words, the board sells the land for $2,900 and undertakes to make those improvements, using the settler himself for that purpose. In that way the man pays exactly what the land costs, and he has it improved.
'He is reimbursed for the $400 worth of improvements he makes?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is reimbursed, and he pays that amount back in the purchase price.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-prescribed forms:

Section 32 of the Soldier Settlement Act, 1919, reads as follows:
All agreements of sale or otherwise, all instruments evidencing liens or charges, and all other documents authorized or required by this Act, shall be made in such form and according to such forms and shall contain such provisions as by way of regulation made the board shall provide.
The amendment proposes to strike out the words "by way of regulation made." That will mean that instead of all these documents and instruments being uniform by regulation each case may be treated differently by the board, for these instruments are simply to be in such form as the board shall provide. I do not know what reasons there are for this change. If there are advantages to be gained by striking out these words "by way of regulation made" perhaps the minister would explain what they are. It seems to me we are giving the board discretion to make a special instrument in any case they see fit.
Mr. MEIGtHEN: The purpose is simply to provide that the board shall not require to have regulations setting out each form. If it were merely a regulation of the board it would be all right, but a regulation means a regulation approved by the Governor in Council, and we do not want to have to go through that procedure every time that a new form is put out by the board. We have to use so many forms that it would be too tedious and cumbersome.

We want the board to be empowered to provide such forms as it may see fit. Certainly the board is bound to have them uniform, or endless entanglements would ensue. I wish to move that this clause be struck out and that the following be substituted therefor:
Section thirty-two of the said Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
(1)	Every settler obtaining- advances from the board for any of the purposes of the Act may he required to furnish security on any property owned or held by him.
(2)	All agreements of sale or otherwise, all Instruments evidencing liens or charges, and all other documents authorized or required 'by this Act, shall he made in such form and according to such forms and shall contain in such provisions as the board shall provide and every such document shall have effect as if the form thereof were statutory, and were provided by and as part of this Act.

Is the purport of this amendment that it will be within the discretion of the board to require any man making application for a loan to give a mortgage on other property than that which he acquires from the board., but that this need not invariably be required?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I hardly think that is fair. There ought to be some general rule laid down. I think it is too wide as it stands. I think it would 'be better to say that if in the judgment of the board the land sold is not sufficient to guarantee the advances made, and the man is possessed of other property further security may be required. I do not say that the board would improperly use their discretionary powers, but we have seen that done, and I think it would be well to put some limit on those powers.
Mr. MEIiGHEN: I have no objection to embodying that principle as one of the board will be bound to follow, because that is really the principle they ought to follow. They should be governed by the value of the securities that they otherwise have. As I said before, the purpose of this Bill .is to provide that in the case of advances for stock and equipment, security may be taken on other stock held by the settler, because if not, it is too often the case that he lets the stock on which the Government has the lien hustle out in the cold while he takes good care of the stock that he regards more as his own private property. I do not know what the hon. member would suggest, but it might perhaps read like this: "May be required if the board considers the security otherwise insufficient."

I suppose we should consider the proposed amendment in conjunction with subsection (b) of section 18, under which all these advances are already made a first charge on any land purchased by the settler through the board and on the settler's own land if he has any.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, so far as the land is concerned. As I said before, the purpose of this amendment is to enable the board to get the other chattels as security for advances in respect of the stock and equipment. The section the hon. member refers to gives us no help in that regard.
What is the meaning of "otherwise"?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps I may read the clause as amended, and the hon. gentleman will appreciate its significance:
Every settler obtaining advances from the board for any of the purposes of the Act may be required, if the board considers the security otherwise insufficient, to furnish security on any property owned or held by him.

The minister mentioned a circumstance that ought to be provided against if possible. It seems that some men have two sets of cattle, one on which the Government has a lien, and the other which the settlers regard as exclusively their own property, and of which they take better care than the other. The minister says that sometimes the farmer neglects the Government stock, devoting more care to his own. It is not so much the value of the property as the cruelty to the animals that appeals to me. I do not think that the Government should have such a class of stepchildren treated in this manner.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Undoubtedly we should avoid any inequality in the treatment of the stock owned by settlers by any means in our power, and this is the best means I can suggest, namely, to make it an equal loss for the farmer to neglect any of the stock.

The board cannot take any really effective measures to remedy this condition of things. All they consider is the value of the stock, and if they have a sufficient value they are not likely to take any further facts into consideration. If they advance $1,000 and get sufficient security they will not consider anything else.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is the method
adopted, to secure the same end, by large stock loan companies operating in the
Western United States. Experience has shown them that this is the only precaution they can take.

If the inclusion of the whole stock in the bill of sale, or whatever form of security the board takes, prevents any partiality in dealing with the stock I would be in favour of putting it all in.
I am sure the minister would be always ready to release, on reasonable terms, any stock that a man might want to sell.
M'r. MEIGHEN: We can release stock, and the supervisors who pass from farm to farm looking after the settlers are vested with authority to exercise that power. So far as I am aware there has been no complaint as to their discretion, and there is therefore no reason why we should not take all the security there is.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Subamendment agreed to.
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section five-powers of board.

Section fifty-nine, which
this section in the present Bill amends, is of considerable length, and the subclauses which are now added to section fifty-nine are almost as long. Section fifty-nine refers to sections sixteen and eighteen, and section five of this Bill also refers to those two sections, and I think we are entitled to some explanation from the minister. Every hon. member has not a copy of the statutes, and it is very difficult for us to know just what we are amending. Hon. members do not know what is contained in subclauses (a), (b) and (c) of section fifty-nine, and the minister should state their purport. If the minister would give a few explanations in regard to this matter it would assist us to understand it and if we are not satisfied we can put questions to him. I would first ask him to explain subsection (dl in regard to unimproved lands.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Subsection (d) empowers the board to vary the terms of payment provided by section 16 so that the first annual instalment shall be repayable not later than two years from the date of the sale and shall consist of the accrued interest only. Section 16 as it stands provides for interest at the end of the first year. This enables the board, in the case of a settler on unimproved land, to ask for no payment for two years and at the end of the second year to ask for the payment of the accrued interest only. The settler

gets no remission; he only gets a longer time by one year. It is necessary in the case of unimproved land because he cannot get a crop the first year unless under speoially favourable circumstances he may get a crop of flax.

If a man is paying an instalment of tflie capital yearly does this give power to the board to say that the capital which is paid yearly shall not be paid as part of the instalment 'but that the instalment shall consist only of accrued interest during two years?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
.No, he makes his first payment on the accrued interest date, but he commences to pay the capital only after the second payment.
. Mr. BUREAU: The second payment, I suppose, will be at the end of two years.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: At the end of three years. He pays nothing at the end of the first year. He has to under section 16, tout this enables the board to vary that and to defer the payment for two years. He pays the accrued interest after two years and thereafter be commences to pay the capital.
Then, what is the explanation of paragraph (e)?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This applies to the terms of payment on the sales of stock and equipment to be used on unimproved land.
What is the object of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is to enable the board not to ask for anything in the way of repayment for three years instead of two years. He gets a remission of interest for the first three years by the Act as it stands, but he does not have to make 'a payment for three years under this Bill, whereas under section 18 he would have to make it at the end of two. It is another advantage to the man settled on unimproved land.

It is to the disadvantage of the Government. The stock is perishable in that it is imore liable to disappear than the buildings and the farm itself. On the constant security you give him two years while on the lesser security of live stock, which is liable to disappear over night in a storm and which must be classified as perishable, you give him three years. Why not reverse that and on the safer and greater security give him an extension of time and on the lesser security you give him a shorter time?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is what we do because the advance to the settler for the stock has all to 'be paid back in six years, whereas his land has not to be paid for until the expiration of twenty-five years. It is true we do not start so soon to collect from him interest on the stock; we start a year later, but we collect it all almost twenty years sooner. The hon. member must remember also that for our stock and equipment advance we have the land as security as well, so that it does not make a great deal of difference because if there is an equity in the land we have that security for the stock advance just the same as we have it for the land advance. The reason we are asking him to have all his stock paid up in six years is because in all likelihood there would not be very much of the stock left then.
Half of the stock would be gone in three years, assuming, as the minister says, that all the stock would be gone in six years, and yet we give him three years to make his first payment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It does not go, as a matter of fact, the same .in the first three as in the last three. It is in the last year that most of it would go. It should all be there practically intact in three years and it would not all be gone in six years, but normally there would be a substantial impairment of the security in six years; so that we may say, "You must have it all paid back in that time."
There is subsection (g). What is the object of giving the board power to determine what is the status of a farm?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Paragraph (f) means that the board shall have power not to grant to the purchaser of improved land the two years remission of interest on stock and equipment. There is no reason why a man getting improved land should not start almost at once to pay for his stock and equipment as well as his land. As to paragraph
(g)	providing that the board shall have power to determine the character of land and what constitutes unimproved or improved land on a farm, somebody has to determine what is improved and what is unimproved land. If you do not put this clause in the court will have to determine. You simply say that the board shall have the power to determine whether it is improved or not.
Whether the land is a farm or not a farm?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. It may be that three acres in British Columbia would be sufficient to constitute a piece of land an Improved farm; whereas in Saskatchewan it might require fifty acres. It depending on the circumstances in every case, the only way to deal with it is to enable the board to determine whether it is improved or unimproved land.
What would the difference be if they found that it was not a farm as against finding that it was a farm?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The difference would be that if it was found not to be a farm they would not have anything to do with it. I do not see the value of the words "or a farm."
I do not know how the board can determine how it is a farm or not. I do not think a farm is determined by its area. They generally call farms, of small areas but which give big returns, ranches.
I do not see the value of these words, but they do no harm.

I did not have time to
read section 61 of the Act as it stands. May I ask the minister if there have been any cases where agents, working under the board, have been trying to work both for the purchaser and for the board at the same time, and trying to collect a salary from the board and also a commission from the intended settler?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Our experience has
been such that we consider the section very necessary. I could not say that we could bring home this offence to any person at the moment
I do not want the names of any persons, I simply wish to know what is the object of the section.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: -but we have had reason to suspect that certain men who are not now in the service of the board, and who have considerable speaking ability, are of the class of those sought to be legislated against by this section.

Who deeidel upon that
ability, the board or the minister?
; Section agreed to.
On section 7-regulations as to loans and advances:

What is the difference
between this clause and the old section?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The purpose of this
is to enable the board to have payments that come due on different advances mature at the same time. The intention is to have them all mature on the 1st of October, I think, in the West, and at different dates in other parts. The board desires to have the power to make due dates, on advances that are made at different periods of the year, the very same.

Under paragraph (c) of section 63 of the existing Act the board can make regulations prescribing:
The security to he given for loans or advances, the conditions subject to which loans or advances shall be made, and the manner and dates in and at which such loans or advances shall be repaid.
Now it is proposed to add to this paragraph the following:
Including dates at which amortized or other payments shall be consolidated or commence.
Paragraph (c) is pretty broad already. Has any concrete case come before the department of the board which they are not able to settle except by the enactment of this amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The board has power
to set the manner and dates at which such loans or advances shall be repaid. But that must be read in connection with other clauses of the Act which limit them to a year or two from date, depending on the character of the advance. Now they want power to limit for a year and six months, and for that purpose to consolidate the loans and have them all mature at the same date each year. That is the explanation. If I were operating this matter myself I think I would have gone ahead and assumed that I had the power
I should say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: -but the board's solicitor advises them that the power is not very clear.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 8-marks or brands to denote the board's ownership of property:

We ought to have a
sample before us of the " lazy S " referred to here. What is the " lazy S?" Supposing there are already marks or brands which may not be in the " lazy S " but in quite a " live S " and the broad arrow referred to here may come through the " live S." There must be -registration in some province. I know nothing about these brands, I have never been a rancher, but in order to avoid

confusion it might be well to say that this mark chosen by the board shall not be used by any other rancher or any other organized company. The mark may only be used for cattle; but when it comes to agricultural implements somebody else may adopt a similar mark.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The "lazy S" is our
undisputed property. We have made search and found that no one else has this particular brand. The branding of our animals is one of the real difficulties of the board. There are only certain men who can brand successfully and they are not very often settlers under the Soldiers' Settlement Act. At the same time making provision to have experts for branding on hand all the time is a very expensive business.

This does not apply
merely to animals, it applies to all property.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We want to be able to use this brand on anything. We do not want to have to go through the formality the same as a private individual has to, of registering our brand and making that registration at all the offices throughout the West. This enables us to avoid that difficulty.

With regard to
this provision which makes it unnecessary to register brands in each province, is there not some possible danger of a similar brand being registered quite innocently? Therefore would there be any objection to having this brand registered in all the provinces ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If we register the '
brand we become subject to provincial regulations and we do not want to be so subject. We are not so subject with respect to registration of our ownership of anything, and we should not be in this regard. I do not think there is any danger of any other person taking this brand because the operations of the board are so widespread that this brand would be the most familiar in the Whole country. Should any one be foolish enough to adopt this brand then the Act declares " It is no good to you, you cannot use it even after you have registered it." So the contingency which the hon. gentleman fears is, I think impossible.

It is not impossible although it may be improbable. I certainly see no harm in the registration of the^ brand. If we were to declare that the registration should not be subject to any 
of the other provisions of the provincial Acts I think the difficulty which the minister fears would be overcome. It is a simple matter to provide that it shall not be subject to any other provisions except the registration. Would the minister have any objection to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We do not compel him to register; he can still register if he sees fit.

If the minister does
not want to be embarrassed by the laws of the provinces he ought at least to follow the laws of the Federal Government. I do not know anything about cattle brands, but the procedure ought to be the same as for the marking of logs. I happen to know more about log marks than I do about ranching or cattle. No one can get a log mark unless he comes to Ottawa and registers it, and before he can have a certificate entitling him to the privilege of using that mark he must make a search in the department to see if a similar log mark has not been already registered. Then if at any time he wants to purchase a mark already registered he must get a transfer from the owner before a certificate is issued to him for its use. The same procedure could apply to a cattle brand.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think so. Certainly if there is a Dominion law that requires us to register a log brand or a cattle brand we would have to comply with it. But T think my hon. friend refers to some regulation prescribed by the Department of Trade and Commerce.

By the Department of
Agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But it is made especialy for the purpose of protecting the lumber industry as an industry. It does not cover cattle, because the branding of stock is entirely a matter of provincial law.
It is the. same with logging operations, they are purely a matter of provincial jurisdiction.

The only
three provinces where branding is used at all are Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and it would be unwise to conflict with the brands in those provinces already registered, for it might cause endless trouble. Has the minister consulted the provincial authorities in regard to this pai-ticular brand?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have done so, and we feel we have a monopoly of the brand described in this Bill.

iMr. WILSON (Saskatoon):	In addition
to the branding, provision should be made for the transferring of the property. There should be a way of marking to indicate that the property has been disposed of. That is a common practice in ranching; when a certain brand is registered its mark of cancellation is also registered; that is, a certain figure is placed under the brand to denote that the stock has been transferred from the original owner. I think it would have been well for the minister to have consulted the registers of brands ol the three prairie provinces and ascertained that he was not duplicating a brand already registered, and in that way appropriating some other man's property.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The method the hon.
member refers to is the prevailing method, but it would not do for the Government to adopt it, because it would admit of fraud so easily as against 'the board. All a man would have to do would be to place that cancellation mark on the property and thereby he woud be relieved, so far as the public were concerned, from all the restrictions and obligations under this section. Instead of that, as soon as a man has paid for the property, or as soon as he sells it by permission, we give him a certificate under a certain authorized signature. He can pass that certificate on to another purchaser, and in that way the Government is much better protected.

In registering a brand
under our provincial laws it is always stated where the brand is to be placed, whether on the left or right side, the shoulder, the flank, and so on. The reason for that it that you may know where to look for the brand. I would suggest that that' practice be followed here.

The board wants to reserve that, because it is just possible that a brand is already used at the spot they would describe, and they want to be able in that event to put it somewhere else. Also, it is pretty hard to describe where to put the brand on an implement.

There is plenty oE room
for three or four brands to be placed on the shoulder or flank, or on the right or left sides. I think we should be specific.

In connection with that
idea I may say that people engaged in the leather industry are asking those who take out registration for brands to consider carefully where they are applied, because the worth of the hide is frequently very much depreciated because o,f the branding. I
received a letter only last week complaining of that particular feature of the Bill and I think it would be a good idea for the minister to give the matter his carefuJ consideration, so that the hides of these branded animals shall not be depreciated in value.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is for that very reason chiefly that the Board has adopted the practice of looking after the branding itself by competent men.

I undertsand that the
marking on the property which is given as security operates as a mortgage-more than that, that it practically operates as a bill of sale in favour otf the Government, and that the release or transfer is made by a document given by the owner or individual whose cattle or property is branded. There ought to be same way by which the public may know exactly whether or not the property is free. 'Suppose I make application under this Act, I have a lot of cattle branded that way, and I sell them to my friend from Bonaventure; an agent of the Government passes iby, he sees those cattle and he takes them. It is true the minister will answer:	"They will be released. All you have to do is to show us the document of transfer." But why should my purchaser be put to that trouble? There should be a registration of the
5 p.m. bill of sale or the chattel mortgage, so that when the property is finally released the public can ascertain that all incumbrances have been discharged and that the vendor is selling cattle that he is really entitled to sell.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We gain the same result in a much simpler way,-and it is simplicity we are after. A man has this property, it is ours whether branded or not, but as an additonal warning to the public or as an evidence of our ownership, we brand it. That man wants to sell some of that property. If our supervisor approves of the sale, he gives the man a certificate describing the animals and authorizing their sale, and that certificate or a copy of it passes to the purchaser. Therefore, it is far easier for people if they have to deal with that man than if they had to chase to the county court office every time they were negotiating for the purpose of an animal that was branded as the property of the Settlement Board.

The matter is so simple that it becomes rather complicated. A man has to trot up to the board if he wants to sell a steer or a cow or a plough or anything else and get a certificate showing that

he has a right to sell it, and he has to attach this evidence of the release of the mortgage to the chattel that is being disposed of. That is multiplying the difficulties.

I did not hear all the conversation between the minister and the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Wilson), but I thought that hon. member raised a point which should have received more consideration than it did. I am not very well posted on branding laws in the West, but I understand that a "vent" brand is put on below or somewhere else in connection with the original brand. It seems to me that when the interest of the Government ceases in this property, some simple mark should be provided with which the animal can be branded or some provision should be made whereby the owner can obliterate the brand so that the public would know that the Soldier Settlement Board had no further interest. Do I understand from the minister that in every case they will provide for that by issuing to the soldier a certificate showing that the interest of the Settlement Board has ceased tc exist. That seems to be rather an awkward way of handling the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The certificate is that the chattel is authorized to be sold. The other way should afford no safety to us, because all the fraudulent settler would have to do would be to attach the extra mark and our evidence of ownership would vanish.
That would be rather a serious crime.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would not be any more serious than to dispose of the cattle anyway; the fraudulent settler would not be taking any extra risk.

The minister
might say that he could forge the certificate. There are ways of getting over everything.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He would be guilty of theft anyway.

Supposing there are two animals so similar that it is almost impossible to tell them apart, especially in the winter time when they are running out, what would happen? Supposing a man has a certificate for an animal and his neighbour has an animal exactly similar in appearance, but does not have a certificate for it. A dispute might arise as to who has a claim in case of loss.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The certificate would designate the name of the settler who would 
have authority to sell such and such an animal, and that certificate would not be any good at all to another settler that had an animal like it.

But supposing the two animals are similar in appearance and branded the same-they stray away; one of them gets lost completely or killed, and only one is left. They are so similar that only by a brand can you distinguish your uiimai.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That difficulty, of course, may arise, and similar difficulties arise in everyday life, over and over again, but you cannot help that. You would lose the whole value of your brand provided that all a settler had to do was to attach some extra mark and thus obliterate the effect of the original mark. The man who is honestly in possession of the stock is very likely to be able to prove his property.
Do you place the brand wherever you like on the animal?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
M r. MAHARG [DOT] Then, you are making a very serious mistake. During the winter season, when the animals are running out, if is impossible to tell what a brand is withou: clipping the hair, and if you do not know where the brand is located, how are you going to tell?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The purpose of the board is to place that brand on one shoulder for Saskatchewan, on the other shoulder for Alberta, and on some other part, but always following the same practice, for British Columbia and Manitoba. That is the practice the board will follow so that there will be no difficulty in locating a brand.

Not if you follow that practice, but I understood the minister to say that he could place the brand anywhere he liked, and an illustration was given of o case -where there might be a brand where t1 e board wished to place theirs.
Is it the intention of the board to allow the individual farmer to put on a distinctive brand of his own? Otherwise, how is he going to tell his cattle from the cattle of Tom Jones?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is permitted.
Has the board taken steps to find out from the different provinces if those brands are not in use in any of the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Is there any provision made for branding the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This clause applies to the increase also.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 66-insurance of property in favour of board by settler when indebted to' board.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps it would be better to add after the word "board" in the twelfth line, the words "as the interest of the board may apply.'' Then the insurance can only be utilized to the extent of the board's interest.
He would have to assign the policy in that case too.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but only to the extent of the board's interest.
Is it in the contemplation of the board that there should 'be life insurance on live stock? My experience in the WeSt has been that the rates on insurance of that kind are prohibitive.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is not intended.
What other property is meant by "other" in line 8 where it says "upon property, real, personal, or other?"
