speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not see how there can be any other property than real or personal.
I thought it might refer to something peculiar to this Act.

Subsection (2) provides that:
It shall be lawful for the board to pay such rates, taxes or assessments.
And so on. Would that be wide enough to make the board safe in paying, say, the .annual premiums? Nothing is said about those.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That follows further on.

Subsection (2) provides that all these moneys that are expended by the board become part of the purchase price of the property, and they are therefore secured by the mortgage. The wording is that these expenditures "shall be added to the purchase price of such property, or shall become a part of the principal." What is the difference? Why not simply say "shall be added to the purchase price of the property and shall be secured by a mortgage or lien in favour of the board? ' What is the difference whether it is part of the principal or part of the purchase price?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are two methods. In some cases the settler is in a position of a purchaser on agreement, and in that case these expenditures would be added to ,the purchase price; in the other case he is a mortgagor to the board, and in that case these moneys would be added to the principal of the mortgage. In reply to my hon. friend (Mr. Thomson) subsection (2) provides that in case of default to insure, we oan insure, but not that in case of default to pay the premiums, we can pay them. I think the subsection should be amended accordingly.
The minister makes a difference between the purchaser and the mortgagor. If I buy a piece of land and give a mortgage, I am the purchaser and mortgagor. What is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In that case you are the mortgagor. Where the board sells the land to the settler on agreement the settler is not a mortgagor. He is a purchaser, a vendee.
A conditional sale.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is a distinctly western method of sale.
A strange method.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The best in the world in eases of thi-s kind-far better than a mortgage, because we are not put to the trouble of foreclosure proceedings at all. I beg to move that after the word "aforesaid" in the nineteenth line, the following words be added "or to pay any premium of insurance upon such property" and that after the word "aforesaid" in the twenty-first line the words "or to pay such premium as aforesaid" be added.
Does that imply the right to pay the premium?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the settler insures his property but fails ito pay the premiums, as the section stood, we were not empowered to pay the premiums.
You already have the right to insure.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but this deals with paying the premium after the property is insured.

But subsection (2) provides that:
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this Act, if the settler fails or neglects to pay any lawful rates, taxes or assessments, or to keep such property insured.
The board may insure the property. So if the settler fails to pay the premium, the board will have the right to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I think that covers it. I will withdraw the amendment.
Amendment withdrawn,

I think 'there should be some kind of connecting clause between section 65 and subsection (2) of section 66. Subsection (2) makes provision for extra expenditure. Suppose an individual has used up his one hundred per cent credit with the board, and his inventory shows that on his farm he has isix cows and three ,brood mares. Suppose that these stock breed four calves and three colts. Section 65 provides that the officers of the board piay brand these animals, but where is the board's authority for the expenditure necessary for a visit from some one who is authorized to brand?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He iwould not make a special trip. We have a system of supervisors who periodically visit certain districts. As time advances, the number of those whom they visit is reduced. The supervisors do not bother to visit the men who have shown that they are able to stand on their own feet, and that saves expense. Where branding was necessary, it would 
simply have to wait till the occasion of the next visit. In the case of a naan who is getting on all right, we would not likely brand at all, but would leave him to do that, because it would be to his own advantage as well as ours. It is the man who is struggling and trying to get on his feet that our supervisors regularly visit, and they would take care of the branding on one of their visits.
At what date is he Obliged to notify the board of these increases in his stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He is not required to notify the board at all. The supervisors will find it out on the occasion of their regular visits.
Section as amended agreed to.
Bill as amended reported, and amendments concurred in.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House again in committee on Bill No. 20 to amend the Opium and Drug Act -Hon. N. W. Rowell-Mr. Boivin the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: The minister is making a classification by this amendment?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
The section as it stood provided that the fee should not exceed the sum of twenty-five dollars for any license. It was discretionary.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is still a matter of discretion as to what sums shall be charged, but the maximum is fixed for the different classes. The retail druggist does not require a license unless he himself wishes to manufacture; but we cannot charge him more than five dollars.
That is the maximum.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Subsection as amended agreed to.
On subsection two-penalty for importing or exporting drugs without license.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My recollection is that we had passed subclauses (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e), and were discussing subclause (f).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Subsection two of section 5A was discussed in its entirety, and some slight amendments had been made. The words "without lawful authority" were added after the word "possession" in the first line of paragraph (e); the words, "a criminal" were substituted for the word, "an" in line 36; and the word "two," was substituted for the word "five," in line 38, all on page two of the Bill. The amendments were carried but the subsection as amended was allowed to stand.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I move an amendment to paragraph (f), which I think will make the meaning clearer. Under subsection one of this section the minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council, may make regulations in regard to the record to be kept, and it seems to me quite sufficient that in subclause (f) the entry which is required in "a proper book kept for such purposes, of the quantities of such drugs," etc., should be succinctly referred to by the words, "keep the record." I therefore move:
That paragraph (f) of subclause 2, of section 5A, be amended by striking out the words " enter in a proper book kept for such purpose the
quantities of such drugs received, manufactured, Imported, exported, sold or distributed by him and any other particulars " in the twenty-eighth to the thirty-first lines, and that the following words be substituted therefor: " Keep the record," and by striking out the word " book " in the thirty-third line thereof and substituting therefor the word " record."
The section as amended will therefore read:
Manufactures, imports, exports, sells or distributes any drug, and refuses or neglects to keep the record required by any regulations made by the said minister, or neglects or refuses to produce such record for inspection, etc.
This makes the meaning clearer, and brings the clause into harmony with the previous subsection.

I was not here yesterday during the latter part of the discussion. I, see that the last part of the clause provides that any person convicted of a violation of these provisions shall be guilty of an offence, and liable upon summary conviction to a fine not exceeding $1,000 and costs, and not less than $500 and costs, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or to both fine and imprisonment.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That was reduced to $200.

I did not know it was.
I think perhaps it might be reduced still further.
Do I rightly understand that this subclause imposing the penalty is not finally adopted?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The amendments have been adopted but the subsection is not yet carried.
The minister speaks of regulations to be made by the minister. I do not see anything in the Act itself as to how the regulations were made.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In 5 (a), first subsection, the words are inserted "with the approval of the Governor in Council the minister shall have power" and so on.
In the original Act, not this?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In this; this was amended yesterday.
Section 13 of the original Act of 1911 gives full power to the Governor in Council-

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: To make regulations.
Yes.

The definition contained in
paragraph 1 declares what a drug shall mean according to this section and it says that it includes not only the drugs mentioned in the schedule to this Act but all those that may be added to this schedule under the authority of this Act. I understand this authority to add to the schedule in the Act is contained in the original section 13.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The original section 14.
So that the Governor in Council will have power to add to the schedule to the Act a certain number of other drugs if from time to time he thinks it advisable.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend evidently has not section 14 of the original Act before him. The power to add other drugs ie confined to other drugs of this character. It is power to add from time to time any alkaloids, derivatives, or preparations of the drugs named in the schedule. Chemists are constantly at work and they are either discovering or producing new alkaloids or getting new derivatives and therefore they succeed in producing some drug which will have the same narcotic or deleterious effect. The power is given to the Governor in Council to add this to the list and it then would become subject to the provisions of the Act.

We have been introducing legislation at this and the last session considerably restricting ordinary trade in Canada. We have just passed the Food and Drug Act and we are now passing another Act which is restricting general trade to a considerable extent and submitting it not only to the regulations contained in the Act but also to other regulations under the powers given by the Act to the Governor in Council. The penalty imposed by the Act is extremely drastic. You say that:
Any person who .	.	.
(a)	imports into or exports from Canada any drug without first obtaining a license therefor from the minister;
(b)	imports into or exports from Canada any
drug at any port or place in Canada which has not been named by the said minister as a port or place into or from which any drug may be imported or exported;	.
(c)	exports any raw opium or prepared opium or any drug which is not packed and marked in such manner as may he prescribed by the minister-
Even the fact that the drugs have not been packed as prescribed by the minister will be an offence under this Act.
(d)	without first obtaining a license therefor from the said minister, imports into or exports from Canada, or manufactures in Canada, any prepared opium, that is to say, any product of

raw opium obtained by any series of special operations.
And so on-becomes liable under this Act. The offences that may be committed, and which are created by this Act, are so numerous that trade in general may on some occasions, though acting in good faith, be caught by some provision of the Act and will be punished by a fine that may not be less than $200 for the first offence and the magistrate may make it as high as $500. I think this punishment is too drastic and that the penalty should be lower. I would suggest that the maximum for the first offence should not be over $100 and that there should be no minimum so that the magistrate who is hearing the case may take into account the special circumstances under which the offence is committed and may exercise some discretion in view of the circumstances in special cases. I would make a distinction between the first and second offences, and I would therefore move that the penalty for the first offence be reduced to a maximum of $100 without any minimum leaving the penalty for any subsequent offense as it is provided in the Act.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Probably my hon. friend is not aware of the character of the infractions of this law with which we have to deal. .There is no real trouble with the honest wholesaler, importer or druggist, but we are confronted with the gravest possible difficulty by those who deliberately go into this business for the enormous profits that may be made out of it. The one complaint we have had so far in reference to the existing law has been the inadequacy of the penalty. We have had that complaint from the authorities at Vancouver and Victoria. In the six months ending the 31st December there were 384 convictions in Vancouver alone for the violation of this law. They ask that the penalty should be increased. The men pay the penalty easily because their profits are so great. I confess that I had no idea until I came to investigate the matter what th'e ordinary prices for morphine were. Bought in the usual way the price will be about $10 per ounce. They can buy it in that way and retail it illicitly at about $120 per ounce. Opium they will get at $10 a pound and retail it illicitly at $100 a pound. They bring it into the country in the most deceptive ways. My hon. friend refers to importing-we have had in the past month a man who declared that he had some of these drugs and was prepared to pay the duty thinking by that means no doubt to escape detection. When his baggage and property came to be inspected it was found

that he was bringing in some sugared fruits, the most lucious peaches, which when examined were found to contain morphine. It was found that he had in each single peach more than $100 worth of morphine. He had $10,000 or $12,000 worth of these prohibited drugs which he had not declared and out of which, if he could have got them into Canada or smuggled them into the United States, he would have made $50,000 or $60,-
000.	You must therefore have the penalties drastic to reach these men. The Harrison Act in the United States makes the maximum penalty $2,000. We have not imposed nearly so drastic a penalty as the Harrison Act provides for, although we were urged to adopt a similar penalty. While I appreciate what my hon. friend has mentioned I do ask the House to give the Government and the department the legislation necessary to reach and punish those who are deliberately seeking for gain to debauch the people of this country or to make illicit gains by smuggling into the United1 States. There are reports from some centres that the me of cocaine and opium is on the increase, particularly among young people. In others, I am glad to say, the report is that it is decreasing; but the department desires the support of the House in enacting effective legislation to enable it to cope with the evil as it existe to-day.
'Mr. VIEN: Surely the minister does not think that a judge or a magistrate will not, in rendering judgment, in every case, take into consideration all the elements that the minister has explained. All the circumstances of the case will be put before him, and the lawyer representing the Government will certainly point out the necessity of imposing a drastic sentence. But what I desire is to protect a man who violated the Act because he did not comply with all the regulations -made- regulations that the 'Governor in Council may vary from time to time without due notification to all concerned. Technically speaking the insertion in the Canada Gazette of an Order in Council amending the regulations may be such a publication as will render any one guilty of a contravention - of the regulations liable to a fine; but as a matter of common sense such publication will not come to the knowledge of all these traders, and therefore it some cases hardship may be occasioned by the application of the law in its present form. I would therefore ask that a certain discretionary power be given to the magistrate. Of course in every case where there is a clear
and outrageous violation of the law, the magistrate will certainly apply the maximum fine; but where it is a first offence I would like the maximum fine not to exceed $100. With respect to subsequent violations by the same party the law may be left as it is.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
One further word in
answer to my hon. friend. These provisions are all binding upon us by the terms of the International Convention. It is recognized that in order to control this trade the strictest penalties must be enforced. Take the case of Japan,, another country which is seeking to control this trade. Japan gives no option of a fine the penalty for violation of the law in that country is imprisonment. If abuses had arisen, or if innocent people had been prosecuted, 1 could understand the force of my hon. friend's argument. But no complaint has so far arisen of people being prosecuted unfairly under this Act, and the effort of the department is to get at the deliberate vio-laters of the law. My hon. friend says that the magistrate might take the facts into consideration. It is true that he might do so, but on the other hand he might not; and the department feels it is important that any man who deliberately violates this law should be subjected to substantial penalties. I think that in reducing the penalty from $500 to $200 we have gone far enough in the direction of leniency.
In the case of information being laid against a druggist and the imposition of a fine does the informer get any part of that fine?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Under the original Act
of 1911 it is in the discretion of the court to award the informer one-half of the fine.

That is where the danger lies in such a provision. It offers to some irresponsible person the opportunity of making almost a living by laying traps against responsible druggists and getting them to commit a violation of the law.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The informer cannot get any portion of the fine unless the magistrate so directs and no case has come up in the past nine years in which this provision has been abused, neither have any complaints come to the department, I should think, therefore, that if the law had worked satisfactorily for nine years we might trust it for a few years longer.

In order to show how even
a man acting in good faith may be surprised in the matter of the application of
I am not doing so.
Yes, my hon. friend is pleading for the trader who might be unaware of the illegality or unlawfulness of the transaction.
I am pleading for those trading in good .faith, not for the illicit traders.

I venture to affirm once more, Mr. Chairman, that there is not a single trader in opium, cocaine or morphine in Canada or elsewhere who is not fully aware of the regulations governing his trade. If he is not-

Would the hon. member allow me a question? Will he contend that all traders, even those under a license from the minister, always know the regulations prescribed by the minister as to the packing and marking of the goods?
Certainly; especially in the case of export business. My hon. friend referred a few minutes ago to the export of raw opium, and I am certain that no exporter-
I am referring to subsection (c) of section 2.

My impression is that anyone who wants to trade legally in these drugs will take good care to * obtain the proper license and keep himself fully posted on all the regulations, because it is a very limited trade, and from its very nature should be so, as it is in the interests of the community that the trade should be restricted.
You are L* favour of prohibition.
So I say that instead of decreasing the minimum it should be restored to the original figure of $500, as we know, every magistrate will apply the minimum penalty in every case.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the subsection carry?
No.
We object to the clause carrying now, and as it is six o'clock we ought to rise automatically.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would ask the consent of the House to dispose of this subsection, as other business will be taken up after eight o'clock.
What is it?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Public Bills and orders. As I cannot be here to-night I would like to make some further progress if my hon. friend wishes to propose an amendment.
That does hot dispose of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. But this has been under discussion on two former occasions and I would like to get it disposed of now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall subsection 2
carry?

Mr. J. E. ARMSTRONG (East Lambton) moved the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Railway Act, 1919. He said: This Bill is the same as the one which I placed before Parliament last year, with the exception that the words "on a regular route '' are struck out of the second clause, and clause 358 of the new Consolidated Railway Act which passed this House last session has been reconstructed so as to conform with the principles contained in this Bill. The object of the Bill is to place the boats on our inland waters and coastwise trade under the control of the Railway Commission as regards rates, tolls, tariff agreements and arrangements, time of call and duration of stay, and all matters pertaining to the carriage of goods. Last year the opponents of this measure spent a great deal of time in opposing the matter of minimum rates; but they will find, that that subject has been eliminated from the
Bill. They will understand that this Bill does not interfere with boats on our inland waters and coastwise trade making minimum charges.
I may be asked why these boats should be placed under the control df the Railway Commission. The reason is that the Railway Commission is a thoroughly organized, independent body of men, capable of dealing with this very subject. That board has been in existence for the last sixteen years, and I think it would be wise to place on Hansard this record. I have here a statement prepared by Mr. Cartwright, secretary of the commission, as follows:

Mr. Speaker, I was calling attention to the fact that these boats are able to carry enormous quantities of grain, and I was about to make a comparison with the sailing vessels of the past. The Grant Morden can carry as much in a few trips as a sailing vessel in days gone by could carry in five years; and while of course the rates then were much higher than they are to-day, they were only just abbut twice as high as the rates the Canada Shipping Company are charging from Port Arthur and Fort William down to the port of Montreal. Just look at these excessive rates and see what they mean. I feel safe in making the statement that these steamship lines on our inland waters and those that are engaged in ocean traffic are exacting from the farmers of the western provinces at least ten cents a bushel more than they ought to exact from them. Ten cents a bushel on 300,000,000 bushels of grain means $30,000,000. I have made the statement that these Boats were able to carry gram, and as a matter of fact did carry grain, at the low rates of two-half, three and four cents a bushel from Port Arthur and Fort William to Montreal in 1909, and now the rates are eleven and twelve cents, and there is no likelihood "of their being lowered. I wish to say something in regard to package freight, and I shall mention my own county of Lamb-ton. In 1909, 1910, 1911 and 1912 the people in this country were anxious to develop the fruit industry, and 300,000 fruit bearing trees were planted. The fruit growers shipped their product successfully and had control of the markets of the Sault and those at Port Arthur and Fort William. But what happened? When the merger was formed, up went the rates in connection with package freight, and these fruit growers were driven out of the markets I have mentioned and the people from Michigan wpre able to come in and take these markets away from them. The same may be said in regard to the largest vegetable growers' association in the Dominion, which is located in Lambton, and also of a number of manufacturers and shippers in that district. These exorbitant freight rates had

been exacted to such an extent that they effectually drove out the trade during the years following those I have mentioned. The freight rates were increased from 20 cents to 76 cents per hundred pounds, and when I called attention to this fact in Sarnia the other night, Mr. Peter Paton, who represents the steamship interests in that town, made this reply: "Well, we did not want to stop to take on these goods." I want to say that carload after carload was waiting for shipment, and they were left to rot on the docks at the port of Sarnia simply because the boats would not call. This gentleman made the statement: "Oh well, we could make our connections at Port Arthur or Fort William to better advantage." Mr. Speaker, what they did do was to sail by and make more millions by neglecting this port, and the same thing has happened on lake Ontario. Mr. Paton opposed me the other evening in the city of Sarnia, and I have a copy of the speech which he delivered on that occasion and as reported part of it is as follows:
Mr. Armstrong took a flyer at my old company, the Canada Steamship Lines. I am not going to dispute a single word of it. He stated their statement is published, and it is a fact that they have made profits that are more than enormous, but it must also be remembered that the Canada Steamship Lines is purely and simply a war baby, nothing more or less. It got its opportunity during the war, the same as the munition makers, and of course took advantage of it, and they did make all the money that Mr. Armstrong says they made, and with regard to their capital, it is also as he states.
But if Mr. Armstrong knew more about that company or knew much about it prior to the war which was declared in 1914 he could tell you with truth that on that day the Canada Steamship lines was bankrupt beyond control; In fact, I doubt very much if at the end of that season we could have paid our current accounts.
He looks upon the Canada Steamship lines as a war baby. Let us look at this organization. In 1912-13 the merger was formed. I had better read from the annual statement as prepared by the Canada Steamship lines. This is the annual statement for 1919 appearing in the March issue of the Canadian Railway and Marine World:

What does that mean? It simply means that this merger that started out with a cash capital, as far as I can learn, of $6,000,000 to-day has assets amounting to over $50,000,000. How did they make that money? They made that enormous sum of money out of the pockets of the people of Canada by exacting from them excessive freight rates; there is no question about that. When Mr. Paton talks about this company as a war baby, I would like to call the attention of the hon. the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) to the need of taking a greater toll than $1,200,000 out of a company that can purchase boats and add to their assets to the amount of over $5,000,000; that can set aside for depreciation and repairs $4,500,000 and that claims to have assets of $44,500,000 and a surplus of $6,764,000. This merger was only enabled to take that enormous sum out of the pockets of the people of Canada by reason of having these largely increased freight rates. Mr. Paton has called attention to another matter. He says:
Not so many years ago several boats ran between Toronto and Montreal, calling at Bow-manville, Cobourg, Port Hope; Oshawa, and way ports. These ports have no coasting service now.
Why? Simply because they could make more money by passing them by.
He says that:
In the year 1908 there were three or four companies carrying package freight between Montreal and Port William, and competition became so keen . between these water lines that they went to the Government and asked that the rate should be put under the jurisdiction of the board of railway commissioners, and the reply they received was: "No, we prefer water competition."
They had water competition in 1908 but I do not think there is a man in this House who will dare to say. that we have any water competition on our inland waters or along our coasts to-day. Then there is something else that I should put on record. Mr. Gildersleeve, who represents the Northern Navigation Company, which is part of the Canada Steamship lines, addressed a letter to the president and members of the Sarnia Chamber of Commerce and he made use of these words:
In 1918 the Canadian Pacific railway, which has a through railway line between Eastern and Western Canada, approached the Canada Steamship lines and Grand Trunk railway and said: "if you will withdraw your boats trading from Sarnia to Port Arthur, we will withdraw our boats trading from Port McNiehol to Port Arthur and there will only be operated the All Water line from Montreal, Toronto, and Hamilton to Port Arthur, and the All Rail line between Eastern and Western Canada, and instead of your water line making its differential rates under the lake and rail rates, which they now do, you will take your differential rate under the all rail rate, which between the East and Port Arthur is much higher than the lake and rail rate. This arrangement "will give you (the Canada Steamship lines) sufficient extra earnings to more than pay the interest on the investment which you have in the Northern Navigation Company and as we will carry the freight all rail that now goes lake and rail we can more than afford to pay interest on our boats which have been trading from Port McNiehol to Port Arthur.
Had this idea been received favourably by the Grand Trunk railway and the Canada Steamship lines, the lake and rail rates would have been withdrawn, and the public would have paid higher freight rates.
I am placing that on record so that the members can see how these large corporations attempt to deal with each other in the way of exacting from the public enormous tolls. What happened? The Chamber of Commerce in Sarnia had been sending protests against this Bill. When I had the privilege of placing before them my material in connection with it, and after the Dominion Marine Association had sent up Mr. King, their most prominent lawyer, to that city, for an extraordinary meeting the representatives of that organization were good enough to send me the following telegram:
Sarnia Chamber of Commerce goes on record as strongly in favour of the Armstrong Bill, holding 97 for the bill, 70 against. When you consider that officials of Northern Navigation Company have been persistently canvassing the membership in opposition to this Bill this defeat in their home town speaks volumes.
(Sgd.) George French, Manager Lambton Growers Association.
I had the privilege of addressing the London Chamber of Commerce. For years past we have been receiving protests from the London Board of Trade and Chamber of Commerce against this measure. Last year for instance after a protest had been sent to Ottawa, I re>
ceived the following letter from Sir Adam Beck, dated September 27, 1919:
London, Sept. 27, 1919. Mr. J. E. Armstrong, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Canada.
My dear Mr. Armstrong,-
I attended the Chamber of Commerce executive yesterday in this city, of which I

happen to be a member, and the matter that you are so enthusiastic about, and that you have striven so long to bring about, was discussed in a letter from the Dominion Marine Association re the Armstrong Bill which was read ; resolutions from Manufacturers' Associations and various Boards of Trade and Chambers of Commerce were also read opposing the Bill. I urged that the board do not interfere, that I was satisfied that it was a most desirable one, and that the rates of lake transportation should be regulated and controlled. However, I was defeated by a vote of four to three. I do not know who or what is behind the movement, but I imagine railways and others are.
I wish you every success and hope the Bill will pass. I know you have been at it for many years, so good luck to you.
I remain,
Tours sincerely,
A. Beck.
I merely place this le*ter on record to show that only small groups in these Boards of Trade get together and send in protests, and that members should not pay too much attention to the statements made by such organizations. The public cannot organize in respect to matters pertaining to the carrying of products on our waterways. Eight millions of people scattered throughout this country are not able to organize but if we had a tribunal like the Railway Commission to stand between .the producers and consumers of Canada, you can depend upon it we would be in a very much better position than we are today with iespect to lake freights.
Let us consider some of the statements that have been made in regard to freight rates on water carriers. Majors Lewis of Toronto, who was at the Sarnia meeting, said that freight should be carried by water for one-tenth as much as by rail. Mr. Joseph E. Ransdell, president of the National Rivers and Harbours Congress, made the following statement:
As to the relative cost by the two methods, there can be no difference of opinion. The Interstate Commerce Commission reported that the average cost of moving freight by rail in 1906 was 7.48 mills per ton per mile. The statistical report on the lake commerce for 1906 by Colonel Davis, U.S.E.C., shows it cost to move over 51,000,000 tons through the Sault Ste. Marie canal last year .84 of one mill per ton per mile or one-ninth of the average rail rate.
Prom the best information I can get, after a careful study of the subject, I am convinced that waterway, transportation in this country, under favourable conditions, costs only about one-sixth as much as the average cost by rail. The above remarks apply to the lakes and rivers.
The Interstate Commerce Commission in an investigation they made two years ago, on the actual cost of moving a ton of freight a mile by water and by rail showed a ratio of one to ten in favour of water; 100 miles of rail to 1,000, miles of water.

Senator Townsend, in a speech made to the Lake Carriers' Association in Detroit on January 22, 1914, made use of this statement:
The lake rate on freight passing through the Soo locks in 1907 was eight-tenths of one mill per ton-mile, while the average rail rate of the United States in that year was 7.82 mills per ton-mile. In other words, the rail rate was more than nine times higher than the lake rate.
Here is a further statement:
On the railways, from Buffalo to New York, the lowest rate which has ever prevailed, has been 4 cents a bushel for wheat, equal to 3 mills per ton-mile. Competent authorities state that, under the most favourable conditions, the lowest rail-rate possible is 25 mills per ton-mile, or 35 a bushel, but such rate has never yet been reached. Comparing this lowest possible rate of 25 mills per ton-mile, with the lowest lake-freight rate previously given .275 mills, it will be seen that on this basis one ton can be carried 900 miles on the lakes at the same price as for 100 miles on the railways.
My object in placing these statements on record is that members may realize and appreciate the fact that with the enormous expenditures that have been made in improving our waterways, lake vessels ought to be in a position to carry the freight offering at an altogether less rate than they are carrying it at to-day.
Well, these gentlemen say, "Storms on the lakes interfere with our trips." But what about the operation of our railways? It is estimated that during the winter season the railways of Canada are only able to handle about sixty per cent of the business they are able to carry during the spring, summer and the fall months. When you take into consideration the amount of money invested in Canadian railways, the enormous sum spent in repairing rolling stock, and in improving stations, and the vast army of men employed by those railways as compared with the small number that find employment on lake vessels you cannot come to any other conclusion than that losses in operation of shipping on our lakes and on our coasts are not to be compared with the great losses on our railways.
Now, let us take into consideration the development in the carrying capacity of lake vessels. Not many years ago a vessel that could carry one hundred thousand bushels of grain was regarded as having reached the maximum; but to-day vessels are in operation that can carry five hundred and seven hundred thousand bushels of grain. This greatly reduces the overhead charges.
Another matter to which I wish to invite attention is the exorbitant insurance rates

charged by the insurance companies that are acting in conjunction with the vessel men. While in Winnipeg not long ago my attention was called by shippers of grain in the Northwest to the fact that it was impossible to get a boat from this merger without insuring in the Interlocking Insurance Company the grain that went to that vessel. The grain men claimed that the extra amount of insurance which they would then have to pay would usually amount to thirty or forty per cent more than the rates charged by American companies. We have 8,500 vessels on the Canadian register employing forty-five thousand hands. _ The Government appointed a grain commission to grade the farmers' grains, and grain elevators were built in the Northwest to accommodate that grain. The farmer knows exactly what he pays when he goes to the grain elevators with his grain; and when it is en route to the elevators at Port Arthur and Fort William; but after the grain leaves those elevators and is placed in the hold of the eastbound vessel, he has no conception of the rate he is charged from the time the grain leaves port until it reaches its destination. The vessel men are free- to make whatever charge they please; they can exact any toll they wish in the form of freight rates on grain products. They are a law unto themselves. We have built grain elevators at Port Arthur, Fort William, Port Colborne, Montreal, Quebec and St. John for the purpose of aiding the vessel men and the latest appliances have been installed for the handling of grain. Boats carrying three or four hundred thousand bushels of grain can call at one of these elevators and be loaded or dischaiged in a few hours. All these facilities can be considered as aids to navigation. Furthermore, the United States last year placed an embargo against Canadian vessels doing a coastwise trade on their shores.
This Parliament placed a similar embargo on American boats doing a coastwise trade around our shores. What happened? Immediately afterwards the freight rates on grain from the West jumped to twelve cents per bushel as against the rate in previous years of three or four cents per bushel, notwithstanding the fact that our customs .regulations surround ship-owners with all kinds of safeguards, and the Department of Trade and Commerce assist them not only in the home market, but in foreign markets as well.
It is necessary to bear in mind that the cost of transportation enters into the price of everything that is bought and sold; of
everything that we eat and wear; of our homes-in their construction, furnishing and maintenance. This cost must be paid, and it is paid by the producer and by the consumer; the middleman and the manufacturer are not worried very much about these transportation charges.
It is true that the Board of Trade of Winnipeg has protested against this measure. But let us for a moment examine the organization in Winnipeg that is interested in the transportation of grain and other products on these waters. Take the Grain Exchange, for instance. The members of that exchange.are not worrying about the freight rates that the farmers in the West are paying, for whatever Tate is charged between Fort William and Port Arthur and the grain markets of the world is deducted from the amount that the farmer receives. Liverpool is looked upon as the most important grain market in the world, and it is there that the prices for grain are fixed, and the freight rates are alway deducted from those prices.
When we take into consideration the fact that 125,000,000 tons of freight originated on our inland waters last year, and the enormous amount of business that is involved in the handling of this great volume, we realize what a wonderful country we have. Our fertile fields, our exhaustless mines, our vast forests, and manufacturing plants combine to make the territory served by our great inland seas not only the most productive on this continent, but the most productive in the world.
Ocean-going vessels will soon be passing up to the head of the lakes, and many of our inland poTts are looking forward to that day. We must see to it that our Great Lakes are not exploited for the benefit of the few. In this connection I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Railways to the fact that the time is coming when we should place on these waters some of the ships composing our National Merchant Marine, so that we may be able to know exactly what it does cost to transport freight from, say, Port Arthur and Fort William to Montreal. If our National Merchant Marine have only been able to make $1,500,000 of a profit in the past year, compared with the tens of millions of dollars profit made by the Canada Steamship Company, then it is time that we placed our boats o'n more profitable'routes. It may be interesting to hon. members to know that the Canada Steamship Company last year made a greater profit than that made by all the gold and silver mines of this country.

Unless this Bill becomes law we may depend upon it that excessive freight rates will continue. In 1912 the Saskatchewan Government appointed a Grain Commission to investigate grain rates on the ocean as well as in Canada, and while I have not the time to devote to matters connected with that report, I cannot refrain from reading a statement which is contained in the final pages of it. The Commission reported that:
The people of Canada pay more freight on the grain to reach Liverpool than do the people of any other country in the world.
That statement is based on the rates in force in 1912, which were, to say the least, reasonable. I wonder what that commission would say to-day if they were investigating current rates. The rates that are being charged on Canadian grain to-day are more than the Argentine rate, although
6,000	miles away, and more than Australia and New Zealand, although 12,000 miles away.
Last year. our export and import trade amounted to $2,235,000,000. It is estimated that $1,200,000,000 of that sum represented the freight carried by water. This shows what a few cents per bushel or per hundredweight would amount to on such an enormous volume of' traffic. Canada, in the years to come, with its greater population and consequently greater production, will do a still greater business. The representatives of the Department of Agriculture advised me last year they estimate that $640,000,000 worth of agricultural products alone were exported from this country in that year.
This question is a national one. The principle of the Bill is sound and should appeal to the man who" tills the soil, who develops a mine, who runs a factory, or who carries a dinner-pail. Reduced freight rates will mean increased profits to the producer and lower prices to the consumer. During the next decade our greatest increase in production will be in the grain belt of our great West, 2,500 miles from the sea. It is true we have 40,000 miles of railway to transport our products to the sea, but it is also true that we need to develop our great water facilities. Our Canadian waterways have been the chief factor in building up the towns and cities along their shores, for they are nature's own highways. We have 2,200 miles of waterways leading into the very heart of this continent, the first '1,100 miles from the Gulf of St. Lawrence to Montreal having sufficient dcnth 
to 'accommodate boats drawing 30 feet of water, while on the other 1,200 miles boats drawing 14 feet of water can proceed in perfect safety.
When we open the barriers of the river St. Lawrence, an opportunity will be afforded to ocean-going vessels to pass through another 1,200 miles of water to the head of the Great Lakes. We want to see to it that we have control over these boats before we attempt to spend any more money on the development of these great waterways. No individual nor corporation would dare to undertake the expenditure that Canada has undertaken in that regard. Canada has assumed these responsibilities, and what has she received in return? Increased rates and an unregulated, irresponsible mercantile marine. We must either regulate and control this organization, or open the door to foreign vessels to come in and trade along our coast. Why control our railways and not our waterways?
I had promised the hon. member for Toronto Centre (Mr. Bristol) that I would endeavour, to the best of my ability, to prove to him that the boats in the United States are under absolute control, and I expect to be able to prove it I have here the issue of February, 1920, of the Canadian Illustrated Monthly published by the Canada Steamships, Limited, and I am sure my hon. friend will not find fault with statements contained in that publication. I quote from this publication the artiele headed: "The future policy of the United States Shipping Board," by Hon. John Barton Payne, Chairman United States Shipping Board:
In 1917, the United States Shipping Board Emergency Fleet Corporation launched 106 ships, totalling 708,970 deadweight tons. Of these if delivered complete 49 vessels, amounting to 302,115 deadweight tons In 1918, the Emergency Fleet Corporation launched 812 ships, amounting to 4,244,126 deadweight tons, and delivered to the Shipping Board 532 of these ships completed, representing a tonnage of 3,026,006 deadweight. In 1919, we have launched 1,065 ships, representing 5,982,277 deadweight tons, and actually delivered 1,181 ships with a tonnage of 6,385,123 deadweight. There remains of the War Construction programme, 524 ships of 3,661,767 deadweight tons. These will he completed and delivered by August, 1920.
Besides this, we purchased or contracted with Japan for the building of 45 ships of 372,023 deadweight tons. The total of these Japanese ships actually received and in service is 18, and 148,323 deadweight tons.
These activities and the taking over of German and Austrian cargo tonnage have given the United States 8,700,917 deadweight tons of steel ships, 1,799,123 deadweight tons of wooden ships, 63,000 deadweight tons of composite

and 10,000 tons of concrete ships, a total tonnage of 10,573,040 deadweight, excluding the 3,661,767 tons to be completed in 1920.
We have lost-
And this is what I want to call to the attention of the House as some hon. gentlemen have been claiming that the United States have not control over boats on their inland waerways or coastwise trade:
We have lost, reconveyed to former owners or sold 194 ships, representing 1,274,371 deadweight tonnage. Some of the ships now in operation we will sell for use by foreign flags, but the fleet as a whole, representing 1,688 ships of 9,298,669 deadweight tons will be operated under the United States flag as a permanent merchant marine, and will be available to serve the trade routes to South America and other countries.
I have here the report of the President of the United States Shipping Board Emergency Fleet Corporation for 1919. I do not dare to take up the time of the House in calling attention to many of the statements that are contained in this report, but these are some of the subjects discussed:
New trade routes and freight rates. Reductions in Atlantic rates. Sale of ships.
They have been able to sell only very few of them.
Continue to build ships. The Government have directors on corporation board. Bill to operate and dispose of vessels. Rates, tolls and arrangements. Countries to which these vessels are allowed to go. Exports and imports. Rates on established trade routes. Coastwise trade permits on the lakes.
I shall have to deal with this last to some extent because some hon. gentlemen are constantly saying that the United States have no control over the boats on their inland waters. The report, General Order No. 1 says:
To Managers and operators and officers of Division of Operations:
A decentralized plan of organization for the division of operations will become effective as of May 1, 1919.
General offices, Washington, D.C.
Districts with headquarters and assistant directors or district agents as named will be as follows:

There shall be for each district:
1.	An assistant director or district agent, with a staff adequate to care for activities of the district. Where necessary, agencies directly under the districts will be created.
2.	An assistant comptroller or district auditor and staff sufficient to meet the volume of business of the district, with agency auditors at agencies where necessary.
3.	An assistant treasurer or cashier for each district or agency where necessary.
All instructions, assignments, etc., to be directed and issued by the general office, through assistant director of district agent.
This is signed:
J. H. Rosseter, Director of operations.
There are other directions with regard to the Assistant Directors on the Great Lakes, and this is the final statement:
Great Lakes District.
Cleveland:
Assistant Director, J. L. Crosthwaite, Perry-Payne Building.
Chief Inspector, construction and repair, J. N. MacRae, Perry-Payne Building.

I have been placing these on record merely to show that the United States have control, not only of their coastwise trade, but of trade on their inland waters. To go still further, I quote a statement from the New York Journal of Commerce of April 19, 1919, as follows:-

Is any control of rates
shown by the document the hon. member has read?

If the hon.
gentleman had kept his seat until I was through with this article, I am sure he would have been satisfied that the United States have absolute control. This is an article from the United States Journal of Commerce of April, 1919. I can produce similar documents, but this will surely be sufficient to convince the hon. gentleman:
New Great Lakes Freight Rates. Charges on coal, ore and grain agreed on. Conference in Washington between Shipping Board and Grain Corporation officials and shipowners and shippers fruitful.
On ore, 80 cents per ton; on coal, 42i cents per ton, and on grain from Lake Superior to Lake Erie and from Lake Michigan to Lake Erie, April and May loading 34 cents per bushel and 3 cents per bushel respectively; June, July and August loading, 3 cents and 3 cents respectively ; September, October and November loading, 3J cents and 3 cents respectively, and December loading including winter storage on vessels 5 cents and 5 cents respectively. The grain rates to Georgian Bay and Goderich were fixed at 4 cent per bushel; to Port Huron, i cent, and to Collingwood, i cent per bushel, under the Lake Erie rate. The rate to Detroit was made the same as to Lake Erie ports.
Surely that is sufficient to convince the hon. member. But if not, I will give him more definite information. Here are two letters I received from the Division of Operations of the United States Shipping Board Emergency Fleet Corporation:

Perky-Payne Building, Cleveland, Ohio, October 28, 1919.
Prom: H. L. McDonald,
Asst. Director of Operations,
U. S. Shipping Board,
Cleveland, Ohio.
To: Hon. J. E. Armstrong, M.P.
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir,-
Replying to your letter of October 25, relative to the rates on grain established for lake boats during the past two years.
The rates established during the last two years have been made by the United States Grain Corporation, which is part of the Government Food Administration.
And in the other letter he gives the rates, similar to those I have already quoted. Is that not sufficient to convince the hon. member? Oh, but these gentlemen will say that the United States has given up the fixing of ocean rates. I have here a copy of the Shipping Act of the United States which contains the most drastic kind of legislation in regard to the control of shipping. Over there they have also control over ocean rates and terminal charges. I have also other booklets here. I have only time to read the headings - Ocean Rates and Terminal Charges; Stowage Factors for Ship Cargoes; Rules of Practice, United States Shipping Board. There is also a large document entitled " Trade and Shipping between the United States and the Principal Regions of the World in 1914 and 1918, prepared by the Division of Planning and Statistics, United States Shipping Board." I have also here a complete list of tariffs, showing the rates that are charged by the United States Shipping Board to all parts of the world. Here is the United States Bulletin with the latest rates available between the United States and the principal ports of the world; another booklet entitled " Steamship Fuel Stations in Foreign Countries and Non-Contiguous United States Territories, prepared by the Division of Planning and Statistics, United States Shipping Board."
Lest some hon. gentleman will say tonight that the United States has _not control over ocean-going boats, I will read a paragraph from the Magazine of Wall Street, dated April 17, 1920:
The Shipping- Board has been showing a tendency to greater activity now that it is in more powerful hands. The Jones Bill for the control of shipping provides for greater powers to the board, allowing it to go into new construction with the proceeds of the sale of the war-built ships, giving it possession of the War Department docks and terminals, and giving it authority to make regulations in regard to shipping. Already a more active regulation of shipping rates has been put into force by the

board on the basis of existing legislation, but its powers in this respect will be strengthened.
I do not know what further evidence hon. gentlemen require to convince them that the United States Shipping Board has absolute control over the boats not only on the inland waters and in coastwise trade, but over ocean-going vessels too. Gentlemen have been coming before the Railway Committee year after year, making statements, and they have been repeated on the floor of this House, to the effect that these rates were only effective during the war period; but the statements 1 have placed on record show that as recently as a very few days ago the United States Government had absolute control over their boats no matter where they were, and that they are going on extending their control in every conceivable way. Canada is practically the only civilized country in the world that has not control over her shipping and yet some hon. gentlemen would have us go on in the same way and let the men who are interested in these great shipping combines in our country make their tens of millions of dollars out of the people as they have been doing in the past. I think it is up to the members of this House to take an active interest in the matter and to deal with it definitely to-night. Do not let the present state of affairs continue from day to day and from year to year, and have Canada looked upon as a country that is unable to deal with an important question of this kind.
I hope 'that the Minister of Railways will not ask me to send this Bill to the Railway Committee. It has been before the Railway Committee before, and year after year I have gone before the committee and endeavoured to convince them that this Bill was in the public interest. I am surprised that hon. members on both sides of the House continue to oppose this measure. It is a measure of national importance. We want 'to remember the fact that the northern half of this continent is ours. It is ours to maintain, it is ours to develop -and it 'is ours, if we will, to destroy. The foundations of a great nation have been well and truly laid. We have built
40,000	miles of railway, and have spent over $400,000,000 in developing our waterways. We have absolute control over our railways as regards their rates, tolls, tariff arrangements and agreements and everything connected With those matters, but we have no control over the -boats that ply on our inland waters, in our coastwise trade, or across the ocean. Justice will be the basis of commission control. Do not wait until next year. "Do it now," is a

good motto. The principle of the Bill is sound. The restrictions provided in the Bill a.re fair and reasonable. The interests of the producer and consumer are reasonably safeguarded. The marine interests -will be accorded fair treatment by an independent tribunal, while just and equitable consideration will be accorded to all who use our navigable waters.
I hope that the members of this House will not allow this Bill to be sent to the Railway Committee. You must rremem-ber that the men who appear before the Railway Committee are either representing the large shipping interests in this country, or are directly concerned in those interests. The men who are opposed to this measure are the shipping interests and the large manufacturers who are receiving special treatment at the hands of these shipping combines. Who are the men who are supporting this legislation? Year after year I have been [DOT]'putting on Hansard articles in support of this legislation. The Retail Merchants' Association of Canada, at the last meeting ptf the Dominion Board held in Ottawa in January last, passed the following resolution:
That this association strongly approves ot the proposal to place coastwise and lake shipping under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners, as is provided for in the proposed amendment to the Railway Act.
And that the Dominion Board instruct the Dominion Executive Council to use all the moans at its command to secure the passage of the proposed legislation.
I have the following letter from the Canadian Council of Agriculture:
613 Boyd Building,
Winnipeg, November 18, 1919. J. E. Armstrong, M.P.,
Petrolea, Ont.
Dear Sir:-In accord with the request of your letter of October the 18th dated from Ottawa, I beg to inform you tbat the Canadian Council of Agriculture at its meeting last week considered the question raised in your Bill amending the Railway Act. The following resolution was passed by our council:
" That this council is of the opinion that the lake shipping and coastwise traffic in Canada be brought under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners."	.
Yours very truly,
N. P. Lambert, Secretary.
Then I have the following communication from the Legislature of the province of British Columbia:
April 2, 1919.
Sir,-I have the honour to forward to you, herewith enclosed, for your consideration, a Minute of the Executive Council of the province of British Columbia approved by His Honour the Lieutenant-Governor on the 26th
ultimo recommending that lake and river transportation rates of the Canadian Pacific Railway system in British Columbia be placed under the oonttrol ot the Railway Commission of Canada
These are only a few of the representations that have been made to me from time to time in support of this measure. It is obvious that the small shipper and producer is not able to come before the Railway Board or the Railway Committee to urge legislation of this kind, for the reason that if he did the shipping interests would see that he did not receive much consideration. These men know it. On the contrary, you will find coming before that committee representatives of the shipping interests with all their powerful organization. There is not a port of any importance in this country that l}as not a thorough organization of shipping interests who are doing their utmost to defeat this measure. I therefore appeal to hon. members to see that this Bill goes into committee to-night, so that we may have it passed at the earliest possible moment, because I think I have made it perfectly clear that it is eminently in the public interest.

(Comox-Alberni): I simply rise, Mr. Speaker, to ask a question of the hon. member. I have heard a great deal about rivers and lakes, and about Ontario and the Canada shipping lines, etc. I want to assure my hon. friend that I do not own a dollar's worth of watered or any other kind of stock in any steamship company. I should be glad if my hon. friend could suggest some remedy for our trouble in British Columbia. The people in the territory which I have the honour to represent are crying for ships and more ships, and if there is so much profit in steamship companies I cannot understand why those people have not been able so far to get ships for their purposes. We have four corporations in British Columbia, and many people in my part of the country have been pleading with me for four or five years to induce the steamship people to put boats on to get freight delivered to various islands and to convey mails. TJp to the present time, however, I have not been able to induce these four companies to do anything. Hon. members from British Columbia will appreciate this statement. We should consider this question from an intelligent standpoint, and I would like my hon. friend to tell me, if there is so much profit in these steamship companies and corporations, how it is that on the Pacific coast we cannot get even a small boat to take freight and mail to these various places.
The best answer I can give the hon. gentleman is to refer him-
