-to the statement I have already read.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The
hon. member has already exhausted his right to speak and unquestionably he is not in order in replying to questions asked by any other hon. member. Only by unanimous consent of the House could he now answer a question. The House is not in committee and the hon. member (Mr. Armstrong) will have an opportunity of answering all questions wrhen he exercises his right to close the debate on the second reading.
May I be privileged to say that the Provincial Government of British Columbia passed unanimous resolutions which I read a few moments ago in support of a measure such as I am now advocating.
We have very few lakes and rivers where steamship companies can operate in British Columbia.

The matter which the hon. gentleman has brought to the attention of the House not only this year but for the last six or seven years is of course one of national importance, and if the facts as stated by him were accurate in every particular there could be no doubt that he has made out an overwhelming case for his Bill. But so far as I am personally concerned I have listened to the same statements from him, not merely on this occasion, but also some years ago when the hon. gentleman for the first time introduced this legislation, and when he was given a committee of the Senate and the House of Commons to hear every one in reference to the subject, and the whole matter was explained very carefully by the ablest men in the shipping business; and I suppose when all is said and done they were the most competent to give an opinion.
From their point of view.

It was then pointed out' what the effect of this legislation would be on the shipping trade on the Lakes, and I think that my hon. friend was shown very clearly that the statement that there was no competition .so far as grain was concerned was an absolute absurdity. And I

will tell you why. The grain is the chief product that comes down from the Canadian West and its price is of vital importance not only to farming interests but to every one in the country. It comes to Port Arthur. How much of that grain goes by the Canadian route and how much by New York? And what is the competition that exists between the American boats taking grain to Buffalo from Port Arthur and the Canadian boats taking it down to Port Col-borne? I am not referring at all to rail competition. But when I tell you that the American boats sometimes beat the Canadian boats to the extent of carrying nearly 75 per cent of the grain of the West you will readily see that it is because they are able to give lower rates. Now, why are they able to give lower rates than - the Canadian freighters when it is a case of competition, as it usually is for grain? The matter is simple. The price of wheat is fixed in''Liverpool so far as Canada is concerned, and if a man has grain in the Canadian West he has either the Buffalo-New York route to Liverpool or the Port Colborne-Montreal route; and I am sorry to say that the New York route is nearly two cents cheaper per bushel than the Canadian route for the reason that at New York you get most of the tramp ships of the world. New York, of course, is the greatest seaport in the United States and it is one of the greatest in the world. The tramp comes to New York, takes grain to Liverpool, carries a cargo of manufactured products to South America, comes up the coast with a cargo from South America to New York, and gets a cargo of grain again, and so is always kept loaded. The tramps going by the Canadian route up the St. Lawrence are faced with the dangers of navigation and their rates of insurance are therefore higher than on the New York route, and besides this they frequently have not- cargoes. It is only when cargoes are scarce in New York that you can get tramps coming up the St. Lawrence. So the New York rate is lower. In the early spring and fall you have at Port Arthur the great competition of the big American boats running on the Port Arthur-Buffalo ro.ute, and these large American freighters take 500,000 bushels or more. What other advantage has the American freighter over the Canadian? It has this advantage, that the coal trade and ore trade of the Lakes originate in the United States. It is not possible for the Canadian boat to carry coal from port to port on the United States coast, but it is perfectly possible for the big American freighters to take coal

and ore from the United States to Canada. When the grain trade for Canadian boats is slack and the boat is laid up you have the American boat busy in the ore and coal trade. My hon. friend prefaced his speech throughout Canada by speaking of the enormous earnings of the Canada Steamship Company, the .watered stock and other matters of that character.
I have here the first annual statement of the Canada Steamship lines issued in December, 1914. The company was formed on December 15, 1913. Mark the date-December 15, 1913, and not December, 1912. The war broke out in July, 1914, and for the first year of the company's operations I have the statement showing that they made a loss of $59,000. My hon. friend talks about the company raising the rates. I:f the rates had been raised, they had not been raised very successfully if they resulted in such an adverse balance sheet as that. My hon friend made the statement that the Canada Steamship lines started with a capital of $6,000,000 He is out just $10,000,000, because they started with a capital of $16,000,000 and their assets were $26,000,000 His statement of the capitalization is quite correct; that is $12,500,000 of preferred stock, $12,000,000 of common, and $9,000,000 of bonds. The assets as valued by appraisal companies at that time and accepted by London bankers were $26,000,000. That is in the annual report of the company and yet my hon. friend, when he was in London the other day, and a long way from here, discusses that matter in this way:
I have facts under my hand that no man dare to dispute. I have the material to back up any statement I make to-day. The Canada Steamship Company formed a merger in 1912-
That is not accurate.
-with the Richelieu Navigation Company.
That is not accurate either.
Their boats were taken in and the actual capital invested did not amount to $6,000,000. I made this statement on the floor of Parliament, and I made it in Winnipeg. They floated a company for $12,500,000 of preferred stock, $12,000,000 common stock, $7,000,000 in bonds-
And so on.
That of course is quite correct, but you will see how close he is to the assets of the company.

May I ask the
hon. gentleman a question?

You may ask anything
you like, with pleasure.
I made a similar statement in Sarnia and Mr. Peter Paton who represented these gentlemen-

Mr. Paton was not a
director of this company and never was; he was an' agent and employee and what statements he made I do not know.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must point
out to the hon. member (Mr. Armstrong) that he did not ask a question.

I have answered his
statement. I am speaking from the balance sheet of the company. A public man in making statements of that kind must assume his responsibility for them and I propose to put the statement of my hon. friend where it belongs. My hon. friend quoted from the annual statement for the year 1919, and stated that the sum of $5,619,247 represented the net additions to the fleet for the year. I want to say that in 1914 the company made no money because the war was on. What happened was this: The British Government appealed to Canada Steamship Lines and other ship-owners in this country to come to their aid with shipping and do everything they could to assist shipping on the high seas because of the number of boats that were being sunk by torpedoes. The Canada Steamship Company took 26 ships off the lakes and spent about $100,000 on each of them to enable them' to pass the Lloyds inspection for ocean business. Eight of these boats were torpedoed and the others lasted through the war. Shipping went up in value from 200 to 300 per cent and these boats that went on the high seas were eventually sold for from two to three times their book value; in fact there were three boats of this steamship company that were sold for $2,000,000 which were valued on the books at a total of $450,000 for the three. There has been a great increase in the assets of the company but that great increase was not derived by taking excessive rates out of the farmers of the West but it was derived from the enormous increase in the value of ships as a result of which boats on the high seas were worth from three or four times their original value. My hon. friend spoke of the Shipping Board, the Wheat Board and some other board in the United States fixing rates. Everybody knows they did fix rates and everybody knows that the Wheat Board of Canada fixed rates during the war. What rate did they fix? They fixed a rate of 14 cents during the latter part of the war and since the rate fixings ceased, as my hon. friend says, the rate

is 12 cents. I do not know what it is today because the rate varies from day to day and hour to hour in the busy season. My hon. friend is concerned this year about the maximum rate. I do not know how you are going to work out a maximum rate with American shipping coming .into Port Arthur when we are not able to put a maximum rate on ships coming from the United States. Suppose you were to put on a maximum rate the only result would be that the American boat which is not under our control will get the business above the maximum rate and the Canadian will lose the profitable trade. Then you have this curious state of affairs-suppose there were no American boats and you set a maximum rate; the steamship companies having fixed this maximum rate-

Are the
American ports closed to Canadian ships?

Do you mean:	Can a
boat run from Canada to Buffalo?

Yes.
Mr. BRISTOL. Yes, certainly. All the American ports are closed to Canadian ships in the coastwise trade but in the fall our government has frequently allowed American ships to come into our coastwise trade notwithstanding the fact that we are trying to build up shipping and the shipbuilding industry in this country. Coming back to this question of the maximum rate, what happens is this? Towards the end of the season there are several countries, such as Greece and Italy and others, seeking our grain. They are on the Winnipeg Exchange bidding against each other and the broker who must cover himself has to get his rate to the port of destination before he can fix the price he should pay for his grain. If you have a maximum rate you either have to give it to the first comer or you leave it to a shipping clerk to allot the space and the individual or the Government that wants the grain most and is willing to pay the best price to the farmer for his grain, and pay the shipping company whatever rate the broker and the shipping company agree upon, cannot get the shipping space. It is not the shipping company that fixes the rate now; it is competition that fixes the rate. I think that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) who is a great believer in free trade will thoroughly appreciate what competition means in a matter of that kind. England, the country where the hon. gentleman was born has abandoned rate fixing absolutely 
and at the present time there is free competition upon the high seas. But, during the war, England controlled rates. By taking possession of the merchant marine of Great Britain in 1917 as she practically did, and paying the ship owners twelve or fourteen shillings per ton she made a billion or more sterling for the British Treasury because when she charged her rates to France, and Italy she charged them enough to pay all expenses, and properly so, and British shipping was one of the great bulwarks that helped England to win the war.
Now coming back to the question of competition I want to say further that the United States Government have abandoned -my hon. friend should know the fact because I have it direct from Washington -these rate regulations that he speaks of. My hon. friend has been referring to April of last year; I am talking of April this year.
What I read was under the date of April 17.

Yes, but April, 1919. A despatch on the subject reads as follows:
Competition Restored.
Shipping Board Vessel Operators Make Own Rates.
Washington, March 3, 1920.-Competition in ocean shipping rates was restored to-day by an order of the Shipping Board withdrawing all freight tariffs heretofore published, and leaving the matter of rates in the hands of the individual operators of Shipping Board vessels.
Heretofore the rates for Shipping Board vessels have been fixed by the board, and they were changed several times to meet competition with British shipping. Recently officials came to the conclusion that in order to promptly meet cuts in rates by foreign ship operators and also by private American lines, the question of rates should be left with the 160 or more operators of Shipping Board craft.
Now coming back to this allegation that the Canada Steamship Company "took it out of the poor farmer." In the first year of their operations they met with a loss of $59,932. The next year and the three following years they were operating under war conditions and the wheat board fixed the rates and if the rates were fixed too high this is not attributable to the Canada Steamships or any other shipping company but to the Government board. This year they are up against American competition the same as they always were in the past and the rates are lower than during the war.
My hon. friend has sought to score a * point by reason of the large expenditures made by the Government of Canada on aids to navigation. My hon. friend should re-

member that all the other civilized nations of the world spend money for this purpose, and it is not charged to the account of the ships of that country hut is for the benefit of ships of all countries. No vessel that is under British control pays anything extra by reason of the fact that the waters through which they pass are equipped with lighthouses, bell buoys and other aids to navigation. These facilities are free to all vessels. When it comes to harbour improvements or matters of that kind the reason they are undertaken is because everybody knows that water transportation is cheaper than rail transportation. Therefore every city and town in the country that can possibly have water transportation is going to secure every possible aid to navigation so that ships can pass freely to and from the port. They do not ask where those vessels are registered, they are only too glad to have them. In basing his argument on the expenditures for this purpose my hon. friend might as well complain of the expenditures for lamps on the streets of a city, and matters of that kind, facilities that are provided so that pedestrians may safely traverse the streets. Everybody in this world is under more or less regulation, and there should be a certain amount of intelligent regulation in a matter of this kind. But if there is open and free competition, and if the result of that open and free competition is fair dealing all round it is surely better to leave matters in that condition than to attempt to fix a maximum rate which, as I pointed out, leads to a very anomalous and impossible position.
I will make a further statement in this connection: During the war Sir Norman Hill, one of the greatest shipping authorities in England, came out most strongly against a maximum rate, not only on the grounds I have indicated, but also on the ground that it led to this result: a shipping clerk has the matter under control, and if half a dozen people want the accommodation, and there is a maximum rate in effect, it led to favouritism. The shipping clerk favoured his friends rather than the person, or the country, that most needed the shipping space. The result was to put upon this shipping clerk, or some other official of the kind, the responsibility of saying from hour to hour, and from day to day, during the period when the demands for shipping were most urgent, who should get the shipping space that was available.
Will my hon. friend tell us what the shipping rates were on wheat last fall?
I could not tell my hon. friend. I do not keep track of matters of that kind.
I thought my hon. friend was representing the Canada Steamships.

I am not acting in that capacity here. I am a director of Canada Steamships, but I do not know anything about their rates. When my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) made the statement he did as to the capital invested in the business and as to its financial position I thought it proper to call attention to the facts. And let me say that he is mistaken as to the extent of this company's control of steamers. Canada Steamships have twenty-five per cent of the lake vessels, and ten per cent of the total of the Canadian Merchant Marine. Of course men like Mr. Playfair who are strongly opposed to Canada Steamships, and have large steamship lines of their own, would offer them the strongest competition they can put forth, quite apart from the American competition, which is, of course, the greatest of all.
If there is any question any hon. gentleman wishes to ask me I shall be only too willing to answer it now.
On the question of rates, I think I have shown clearly that there is the freest and greatest competition in the world.
I want to say a word or two>
in reply to what my hon. friend said with respect to bulk freighters. I say without any fear of contradiction that bulk freighters are not undeT the United States Government control at all, and their operations are not regulated unless they are running between railways on a lake and rail route. If they are they come under the Railway Act just the same as the vessels which belong to the Canadian Pacific and run on a lake and rail route. However, the American bulk freighter that carries the ore, the grain and the coal on the Great Lakes is a competitor for any grain that comes out of the Canadian West, and will be as long as the two countries are located side by side.
With respect to the question of an increase in rates, I want to say that not only has the cost of building ships gone up enormously, gone up to the extent of about two hundred per cent over the cost of a few years ago, but wages have gone up from one hundred and fifty to three hundred per cent. Coal, which only used to cost $1.30

per ton at the mine, to-day costs $3.25. Furthermore, the cost of oil, rope, and all accessories that are used in connection with ships have gone up from two hundred to three hundred per cent. I would ask my hon. friend to consider whether the extent of increase of these costs is at all comparable with the increase in the price of farm products. For example, wheat at one time was worth only ninety cents a bushel. I do not know what the price of wheat is to-day, but I do know that the price went as high as $3. I hope the farmer will always get a fair return for his work, because I think no -man earns his money harder than he does, and farming is a basic industrial industry. But when it comes to the question of shipping rates, you have here as free competition as you can get and the rates are always lower than those charged by the railways.
My hon. friend made another statement. He said that it cost more for grain coming from the Canadian West to Great Britain than from the Argentine Republic and from Australia to Great Britain. That may be, I cannot dispute the accuracy of the statement, but I would point this out:	The
route from the Argentine to Great Britain is entirely by water, or practically so, and the same is the case -with shipments from Australia, as compared with a long rail and lake haul in Canada, and of course dt is the long rail haul that puts up the price enormously on the grain of the Canadian farmer. I would appeal to my hon. friend to treat the shipping companies more fairly. Do not keep attacking a company from yeaT to year unless it is doing something wrong; do not make hugely exaggerated statements as to profits which do not exist and never have existed. Do not try to excite a prejudice against this great enterprise, but rather endeavour to treat it fairly and try to build up the shipping interests, which are of such great value to the country. It is in accordance with the law of supply and demand: That the more -ships you have the lower rates you are going to secure. And if you deter people from building ships by your constant attacks on the business of shipping on the Lakes and elsewhere, and if you threaten them with what you are going to bring about in the way of control you certainly are not going to help the industry or the country either.
Then my hon. friend speaks about the question of ports of call. He says that the fruit-growers in Lambton have been greatly handicapped by the character of the service given by the fast express boats tuh-

ning between Sarnia and Fort William, and which could only stop at the Soo long enough to put off small quantities of freight, but not long enough to unload large quantities of fruit and make their railway connections. Of course, any boat is glad to take freight, but if it is running on a passenger service, connections have to be made, and they could not be made if my hon. friend's fruit was handled. I suppose as the result of not being so handled that fruit had to be shipped by rail. But where boats vary in size from 100 tons to 14,000 tons, and where the facilities for loading and unloading also vary at the different ports of call, and where even the character and volume of the labour obtainable is also a varying quantity, it is impossible to make rates on a mileage basis which will be uniformly fair. That is because the profit made by a ship depends on the quickness with which you can unload one cargo and take on another. In other words, at Port Colborne you may be able to unload your cargo of grain in twelve hours and take on another load, but if your boat is kept there three or four days while other boats are being unloaded you are losing money. The same thing applies at other ports.
As a matter of fact the rates on our inland waters and even on those of the United States are fixed on the Atlantic ocean. When the Government began to build a National Merchant Marine'I have no doubt that the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Bal-lantyne) had in view giving the farmers of this country the benefit of those ships during the grain season in order that they might get lower ocean rates, because there is where the cut has to be made if we are going to reduce rates below their present level. The competition between New York and Montreal has gone on for a long period of time, and the basis of our deepening the Welland canal has been to improve the route from Montreal so that grain would not go to Buffalo but could come down in bulk and not have to be trans-shipped at Port Colborne from a big freighter of 500,000 bushels to a small freighter of 100,000 bushels. No doubt when that work is completed it will materially help the rate so far as Montreal is concerned as against New York. But while there are enough shipping companies on the Atlantic ocean to form what they call the Atlantic conference for the control of freight rates 'on the high seas between Liverpool and New York or Liverpool and Montreal, I can assure you, Mr. APRIL 27, 1920
Speaker, that so far as lake transportation is concerned, there will be a very bare living for any boats on the Great Lakes. For that reason the Canada Steamship Company has gone on the high seas to endeavour to protect itself from the Atlantic conference and to be able to carry their freight straight from the West to Liverpool. I believe that in the future as they become more powerful they will be able to compete on fairly even terms with the Atlantic conference, and by building more ships and treating our shipping in a generous fashion we will be able to reduce rates and make the general rate position more favourable for the people of this country.
As regards passengers and matters of that kind, I may say that the Canada Steamship Company has carried over a million and a half passengers during the past year without an accident, for which the company is very grateful. But I am not able to see, with the free and open competition that prevails so far as Port Arthur and Fort William are concerned, how the
10 p.m. Bill of my hon. friend is going to help the situation in any possible way. On the other hand I am satisfied it will prove unworkable and a distinct injury to the transportation interests of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this Bill mainly because the hon. member who has introduced it has made one or two statements which I think ought to be set right before the House. He intimated that there was an organized lobby against this Bill. I wish to disassociate myself from any such influence.
I beg to differ !rom the hon. gentleman. I never made use of any such statement, Mr. Speaker.

Well, I am bound to accept my hon. friend's correction, but I know that on several occasions to-night he stated that undue influence had been brought to bear on various organizations throughout the country, and as a result of that undue influence telegrams and letters of objections had been sent here.
Hear, hear.

He also referred in most emphatic terms to hon. gentlemen who had on previous occasions opposed this Bill before the Railway Committee.
Another reference I wish to correct is that to small groups-I took his words in this connection-of Boards of Trade control-110
ling these Boards of Trade in their representations. I have in my hand, Mr. Speaker, [DOT] a resolution which I desire' to place before the House showing clearly the attitude of the Vancouver Board of Trade, which consists of perhaps nearly 2,000 members, and is composed of a large number of bureaus representing the retail and wholesale merchants, the shipping interests, and so forth. When my hon. friend introduced this Bill last year I had every desire to see it receive the most careful attention, and while at the time I doubted the wisdom of the measure, I sent the Bill to the Vancouver Board of Trade, with the request that they give me the benefit of their views. After the session closed I addressed the Board of Trade briefly, pointing out the arguments of my hon. friend as well as I could, and asking them to give his Bill very careful attention. They referred the Bill-not to th,e Shipping Bureau, as might have been the natural course to follow, but to the Wholesale Bureau. The wholesalers naturally represent the large shippers, that is, the element or group of citizens who use the shipping facilities to the largest extent, and if those gentlemen did not know of any grievance, or if they did not approve of the Bill, their attitude was certainly worthy the attention of this House.
The Wholesale Bureau went into the matter with very great care, and my colleagues and I attended a number of meetings at which it was discussed in great detail. They brought in a report, and with the permission of the House I will read it as it clearly sets forth their views. It is embodied in a letter from the secretary of the Vancouver Board of Trade addressed to me in which he states:
I beg to give you herewith a copy of. the report of the Wholesale Bureau of this board on the Armstrong Bill which was unanimously adopted by the board at the regular monthly meeting held on the 10th inst. (February).
Now comes the resolution:
That whereas Mr. J. A. Armstrong, member of Parliament for Lambton, Ontario, proposes to again introduce in the coming session of the Dominion House of Parliament a Bill known as the Armstrong Bill,
And whereas, this Bill, in brief, provides for the operation of steamboats on the inland and coastal waters of Canada, under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners,
And whereas, the adoption of this Bill by the Dominion Government would eliminate free competition which now prevails, and would result in a higher cost for transportation,
And whereas, there would be a tendency, if this Bill was passed, to eliminate all competition, due to the fact that the operation of steamships would be under the control of a board,



Therefore be it resolved that the Wholesale Bureau of the Board of Trade reports to the council that they are opposed to the Armstrong Bill, No. 8, in its entirety.
This report, Mr. Speaker, was submitted to the council of the Board of Trade, and later to the whole board and unanimously adopted. I wish to emphasize the importance of this, because I can assure the House that the subject matter was given the most careful consideration.
Mr. hon. friend has stated that the object of the Bill is to bring the steamships of our inland and coastal waters under the Railway Commission, which, according to him, is a sound principle. I wish to bring to the attention of the House one or two thoughts in connection therewith. The principle upon which the railways were placed under the Railway Commission was that a railway is given a special franchise, and that its trains run over a given route that cannot be changed. It is desirable that any enterprise which receives a monopoly should be subject to restriction. That is a sound principle, and that is the principle which my hon. friend says applies to this Bill. Let us see if it does. In connection with water transportation, any vessel may enter into competition with any other vessel. This is the vital point; it, in fact, answers the whole contention and, in my opinion, disposes of the whole controversy. Let me fake this up first in connection with coastal trade. Any Canadian or British vessel can enter into coastal trade in competition with any other vessel. As regards ocean trade, all vessels enter into competition, the only distinction being the freight charges. I want the House to consider the effect of control, and with the permission of the House I will apply, as an illustration, operations with which I am very closely acquainted, namely, the Canadian Pacific steamship service on the Pacific coast. The Canadian Pacific run a line of steamships from Vancouver and Victoria north to Prince Rupert, calling at pe 'haps twenty or thirty places along the route Some of these points of call are very unimportant, some being what may be called in railway language, flag stations,- that is, if there is no signal out, the vessel will not stop unless it has passengers or freight for such a point. We shall assume that a tariff is filed under this Bill; that a fixed rate is made for this service, and that the company is compelled to call at given times at these various points, because that is really what the Bill intends to give power to the board to enforce. In the fall season, we have a big salmon pack on the Pacific 
coast and there are canneries which may turn out thousands of cases of salmon to be loaded. A vessel coming from Prince Rupert to Vancouver might stop at one cannery knowing that the salmon was ready, and it might spend four or six or eight or ten hours at that point loading that large cargo. Then, it continues its voyage, somewhat behind its scheduled time, it is true; but it passes up other points, knowing that another vessel will be coming along the same or the next day, and, perhaps, having no more room for freight and no freight for those points. If this legislation should pass, it is probable that the inhabitants of some of these small places will insist upon this vessel calling regularly; and if that is insisted upon, it cannot possiby maintain its schedule. Should it endeavour to maintain its schedule, it would have to stop at this large cannery of which I have spoken for only an hour or two hours, and it could load only such freight as it could take on in that time, whereas, under present circumstances, the vessel will stop and take on the full quantity of freight. That is only one illustration of the difficulties that would arise.
This is another illustration which I think is important. If you place restrictions on a transportation company-and again I use the Canadian Pacific as an illustration-if you . compel them to file a tariff and to observe a regular schedule, you have an obligation to protect them against competition. The last clause of the Bill provides that:
No such water carrier shall engage in the business of transportation, whether of freight or passengers, until such carrier shall have submitted to and the board shall have approved its standard freight or passenger tariffs.
You have an organization with a regular line of steamships with millions of dollars invested, working out a fixed schedule under the direction of the board. Along comes a small vessel which wants to enter into competition with this line.; but before it can carry a pound of freight, before it can enter into competition, it must come to Ottawa, or wherever the board may sit, file a tariff and have it approved. We shall assume that this splendid existing organization has a tariff of an imaginary figure of 100, and we shall assume that the small vessel that is poorly equipped, not so luxurious nor efficient, comes along and files a tariff of 75. Is not the first company going to oppose approval being given to the second tariff? That is certainly what will happen. And, as I say, if you impose

restrictions and conditions upon the first applicant, you have an obligation to protect him in the tariff that you compel him to operate under. In railway matters, a railway is not allowed to lower its freight rates until it receives the permission of the board; and why? Because there may be some unfair competition with a tariff already filed by another line:	That is the
principle adopted in connection with railway transportation. As regards transportation on our coastal waters, absolute freedom of competition is the rule; any vessel at all may enter into the business. If a large quantity of freight is offering, vessels jump in and get a part of it.
I will give another illustration of how this legislation would affect our coastwise trade adversely. The heaviest traffic occurs in the summer months, when you have the tourist traffic, the heavy movement of height, such as mining and logging machinery, and all that sort of thing; and in the fall there is the heavy salmon pack. Those are the large items of freight we have on the Pacific coast, plus the tourist traffic, and to handle it all requires all the vessels that we can put into operation. Late in the fall, maybe about November, that business will drop off, and the result is that vessels are pulled off various routes; some are tied up for the winter and others are put on other routes. They are changed around as the trade changes and as conditions and the freight offering demands. Under this Bill, that could not be done; a company would have to come to the Board of Railway Commissioners and get permission before they could pull vessels off.
This is another illustration of the utter impracticability of this legislation. Just a few years ago one of the Grand Trunk Pacific boats ran ashore and was wrecked. As this boat was on a very important route, what did the company do? They took another boat off its existing route and put it in the place of the boat that was wrecked, allowing the remaining boat to take care of the business on the other route. That could not be done under this legislation without an order of the board, so that you would be tied hand and foot. Thus, from almost any angle at which you choose to look at this question, you will find that the inevitable result will be to handicap the operations of the water-borne trade and to increase the rates.
My hon. friend (Mr. J. E. Armstrong) quoted certain rates in 1912 on the Great Lakes, ^nd I would call the attention of the House to this fact that nearly all of my 110i
hon. friend's arguments were based on the movement of grain on the Great Lakes. He quoted a rate of 24 cents on grain in 1912, and he gave it at that part of his speech as an illustration of a splendid rate, a rate that should be maintained, if possible, right along. Forgetting that he had advanced that argument, about half an hour afterwards my hon. friend quoted from a grain commission in Saskatchewan, and he read from that grain commission a complaint, that the farmers were losing money in the Great Lakes in carrying grain from Fort William east.
I am sure the hon. gentleman has no intention of misquoting me. The 24 cent rate was a rate that was charged in 1908, and it was 1912 when the Saskatchewan Grain Commission was appointed.
Virtually, the same rates obtained in 1912.
No.

Three cents or thereabouts. This is the point I wish to make: Suppose we did control the rates on the Great Lakes from Fort William to Port Colborne, or any other point in Canada, would it make one whit of difference in the rates that now exist in competition with American vessels? Canadian vessels cannot carry grain at a higher rate than competing American vessels. We know that one of our handicaps to-day is the enormous amount of Canadian grain that is passing through Buffalo, and one of Canada's problems is how to get this grain moving through Canadian ports, Montreal for instance., But we are fearfully handicapped by. nature; that is the long and the shoit of it, and it is nature and competition that have fixed the rates in the past.
The House should not be misled by the high freight rates that have obtained on the Great Lakes during the past few years. Any one who has given any study to freight rates at all knows that in all parts of the world shipping rates have gone up to an abnormal extent simply because of the exigencies of the war. Here was a cargo of freight that was urgently needed at a given point. Perhaps it was munitions of war. The. shipper of that cargo or the nation receiving it would pay an enormous sum to get it delivered, not because of the value of the goods, but because of the necessities of the case. That applied to the whole shipping world, and the

condition was, of course, aggravated by the sinking of so much tonnage.
Another point to which I wish to draw attention is this: My hon. friend said-I took careful notes, and if I misquote him it is rather because he was unhappy in his delivery than that I was inaccurate in my notes-that before we undertake this enormous expenditure in the development of our canals we must control our steamship freight rates. iMy hon. friend does not correct me, so I assume I have quoted hini accurately. Now, Mr. Speaker, what are we developing this great canal system for? It is so that the water-borne traffic of the world can get up to the head of the Great Lakes. Will my hon. friend say that he is going to control the rates of that class of shipping?

Why not?
Mr. STEVEEJN8: You cannot do it unless you shut that shipping out.
I say-

My hon. friend cannot control shipping rates on these vessels without shutting them out. Let me make that more clear. I say that we are going to spend these huge sums on our canal system in order to invite the shipping of all countries of the world to come up to the head of the Lakes; in other words, to make Port Arthtur a seaport instead of a lake port. If that is not the object we should not have started the undertaking. If it is our object, while you may control in an arbitrary, and I think an unjust, manner the rates of Canadian lake shipping, you certainly cannot control the rates on French, and British and Norwegian shipping that comes from France and Britain and Norway to the head of the Lakes, because those are foreign ships and the freight originates in a foreign country. My hon. friend ought to know that, even if he does not appreciate it now. A reference has been made to a resolution passed by the British Columbia Legislature. My hon. friend, when he read that resolution, was facing the other way, and I did not hear him very clearly, but I think the resolution referred to the Canadian Pacific lake and river steamship service. My hon. friend will correct me if I am wrong.

Not definitely, if I remember correctly. .
[Mr. Stevens.!
Would my hon. friend kindly send me the resolution?	[DOT]

My material has
gone up to Hansard.

I will stake my reputation on the statement that it referred to the Canadian Pacific lake and river steamship service. Now under the existing Railway Act, freight which is carried by water and rail, that is, where the routing of the freight involves both, is now under the control of the Railway Commission. While I did not have the honour of being sent a copy of this resolution, in the face of the fact I have just mentioned I cannot for the life of me understand why such a resolution was passed. The whole idea was, as near as I can gather, that in some mysterious manner we were going to lower freight rates by passing this Bill. If it would by any possibility lower freight rates, I would give my hon. friend my support; but I am convinced, after a most careful study of the -question, that the result would be to raise rates rather than lower them. I will read the resolution. It is from the Acting Under-Secretary of State for the province of British Columbia, and is as follows:
That in the opinion of this House it is desirable that the. rates of lake and river transportation systems owned and controlled by the Canadian Pacific Railway in British Columbia should be under the control of the Railway Commission of Canada.
These rates are already under the control of the Railway Commission with the exception, perhaps, of the rates from some small point of call from which a steamer will carry freight to another local point on the lake, but where the freight is carried through, and ninety per cent of it is, the rates are under the control of the Railway Commission.
I should like to call attention for a moment to the Bill itself. The first clause of the Bill deals with traffic accommodation. I shall not weary the House by analysing the Bill in detail. I think I have already pointed out the general principles sufficient, in my estimation, to warrant the House in rejecting this Bill. In the first clause of the Bill you will find numerous instances of this kind; I shall cite only one. We are to give to the Railway Board, mark j'ou, control of traffic accommodation. Now, any hon. member of this House, or any citizen who has given any thought at all to water transportation knows that a large number of coasting vessels have very poor accommodation. They have, perhaps, ordinary cabin accommodation for passengers, but they do not aim to carry passengers; that is

not their object. Being within the terms of the Canada Shipping Act, however, they do occasionally carry passengers, although their main business is the carrying of freight, and they enter into that freight business in a manner which I might call general in its form; that is, they have no particular routes to follow. They are coastwise tramp steamers, if I might use that term-one of the most useful instruments of transportation; they are one of the main factors in keeping down freight rates, and passenger rates too for that matter. Now under this Bill the privileges, the liberty and freedom of movement of this class of -vessel, which as I have said is one of the main factors in reducing freight rates, would be entirely eliminated, or so restricted as to make it unprofitable for these vessels to operate.
Before I sit down let me say this: Through lake-and-rail freight on the Great Lakes is already under the control of the Railway Board, so there is nothing^new so far as that is concerned. Let me say also, so far as the United States is concerned, that none of the bulk cargoes are under any control whatsoever as to rates in the United States. Let me repeat: No ship of Am-can registry carrying a bulk cargo on the Great Lakes is under any control whatsoever as to rates. In view of these facts I feel that the passage of this Bill would be inimical to the interests of the public at large, and that it would tend, if anything, to increase freight rates, and to restrict the freedom of movement and liberty of ships.

I do not feel, Mr. Speaker, that I have sufficient knowledge of the subject matter of this Bill to address the House at any great length. I am impelled to vote against [DOT]the Bill by reason of the fact that this important Montreal institution is opposed to itv I was also impressed by the argument of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). He evidently has been studying the literature which has been supplied to us from time to time by the owner of the launch Narbethong. Unfortunately I have not the time to give it as close scrutiny as the hon. member. As for the Bill, it has been before the House ever since I have had the honour to have a seat in this Chamber, and I understand that for many years before I came here this legislation was trotted out by the hon. member for East Lambton. There is one thing for which the hon. member can be commended with regard to this Bill, and that is, his persistence; he does not know when^ he is beaten. He brings this Bill before the House year after year in the hope that it imay receive a better fate than it had the year before. It has now become a hardy perennial, and we should all be disappointed if the hon. gentleman did not bring it before the House in due course in the same way as the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) introduces his flax resolution. Coming from a city which .ships as much by water as any other city in the Dominion, I think I would be derelict in my duty if I did not raise an objection to this Bill. I do mot think that St is necessary that I should take up much time of the House, because the absurdity of the arguments of the hon, member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) is apparent on their face, and hon. gentlemen who. halve followed him have shown that his contentions are based more on private .considerations than on any regard for the public interest. I have before me a large number of telegrams expressing disapproval of the Bill in as strong term3 'as it is possible to use. I

shall not Tead these telegrams, but I may mention the sources from which they come: Walter Woods & Company, merchants; C. W. Kirkpatrick, publicity agent; W. B. I also have a letter which I am asked to read to the House. It is from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and although I regret to take up the time of the House, I feel bound to place this communication before hon. members. The letter reads as follows:
As a matter of easy reference I am quoting hereon our telegram of protest sent you on March 9th last asking your very best assistance towards Withdrawal or defeat of the Armstrong Bill having to do with control of water carriers within the Dominion.
"Since 1914 Mr. J. E. Armstrong, member of Parliament for East Hamilton, has continued his harassing efforts to amend seotion 358 of the Railway Act asking that water carriers be placed under jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. This effort continues notwithstanding the unanimous dissent of each joint committee and the non-support of a single member of the various joint committees beifore whom lengthy and expensive evidence has been submitted from time to' time protesting against the objectionable efforts of the proposal. It appears unneasonaJMe that the business interests of Canada Should be forced; year after year into defending a position based on the judgment of any single representative. This company again state our belief that such legislation could only interfere with trafUc and discourage the reconstruction of our new lake freight carrier lines. We trust that in the interests of Canadian shipping generally you will make every effort towards withdrawal of Mr. Armstrong's amendment and defeat should the amendment go before the joint committee and House. We would refer you to the evidence on file."
As has already been explained this continual effort on the part of Mr. Armstrong is causing shippers generally throughout the Dominion both annoyance and anxiety, the latter because we on the outside realize fully the uncertainty of the political arena at all times as well as

the susceptability of certain political interests to coincide in a trading way with the proposers of measures about which they frequently understand very little and the only fear we have in connection with this Bill is that it may be brought up at some time when the House is largely occupied by the opposition possibly to the Farmers' party and others of the same nature and through general misunderstanding, and possibly with the spirit of good will to the proposer, be carried through.
We are advised through the Canadian Manufacturers Association that this Bill comes up on Monday next and at a special meeting of the local executive of that Association a resolution was passed empowering the writer to act on behalf of all members of the association, all of whom have jointly filed their protests from time to time, this by urgently placing before yourself and Mr Mewburn the necessity of continued opposition if protection against the measure is to be assured.
We fully appreciate that it is not opposed by the Government as the Government and that every member has an open voice. Under such circumstances we believe that we must ask a full rally of all members who are thoroughly interested in the desires of the industrial and commercial interests of Canada.
Therefore may } suggest that in the event of this Bill when before the House looking dangerous that some decided demand or request be made for the production of all opposing evidence that has been submitted under great expense by shippers from year to, year as the Bill appeared before various joint committees and was decisively defeated at each successive hearing, the only assenting voice that of the proposer, Mr. Armstrong. Mr. Armstrong is not a shipper and as far as can be ascertained does not represent shipping interests to any degree whatsoever, but on his own statement we believe that the entire effort on his part is based on personal grievance; the instance that of leaving a oar of fruit some years ago by one of .the water carriers either through oversight or impossible loading.
I am decidedly opposed to any regulation of our waterways likely to place them on the same basis as privately owned railroads, and possibly to give the railroads undoubted control of the waterways under operating agreements with some one, or as the oase may be several steam boat lines.
It seems to me that everything that can be thought bad for lake and river commerce is in this proposal, and as far as I can see this is without one good redeeming point. It would mean that our free waterways are gone' forever to monopoly of joint rail and boat Interests. The independent could never exist without separate docks and separate railway terminals.
Under regulation every railroad could refuse to become a party to any tariff but those of one line, perhaps their own. This would of course mean that all independent boat lines would be prohibited the use of railroad docks arid terminals, and it is needless to say that without these facilities no line in Canada could exist.
It could not even help the interest asking for this regulation, as no power can compel boats to oall at any docks, and tariffs issued would not include some now depending upon competition for service.
The independent carrier would be a thing of the past, as he could not contract with any shippers without first issuing tariffs, and it is

pointed out that this would, he a long process if they were not acceptable to the railroads.
In other words, they would only reach from water point to water point, without any assurance of being able to reship a carload.
If this is good legislation, may I ask for what purpose the Water Boards of Toronto and Hamilton are striving to create free docks or wharves, and this under Government assistance, so that monopoly of our waterways cannot come about. It may be pointed out that we at the present time in Canada have one line of 'boats only, but even so this is bad enough. However, this condition can always be treated by competition if conditions become unfair, and I am very glad, to say that as far as I know no unfairness exists at the present time on this score.
Therefore I sincerely believe that the regulation of these routes or placing the control of operating boats under regulation wili be directly detrimental to the development of Canada commerce.
1.	By preventing individuals from operating steamship or steamboat companies. The railroads, where they are directly competing with such water transportation, will promptly reduce their rates to such a point as to make it unprofitable for steamboats or steamships to operate. In the United States the railroads have years ago paralleled all the river routes, with the result that there is not a first-class steamboat line on any river in the United States to-day, meaning by this such as used to operate on the Ohio and Mississipi.
2.	The development of commerce along rivers and lakes depends upon competition and this not only between competing boat lines, and of course it is obvious that with rules and1 practices regulated by commission there could be no occasion, and in fact, no room for competition. Regulated transportation may be and is all right within privately owned railroads as a matter of fairness to such railroads, but railroads have not as yet bought up the great waterways in Canada. These belong to the people and the people and the railroads should' utilize them to the best advantage and with mutual freedom.
There is no question but that the legislation asked for if carried through will interfere with the growth of the Canadian Merchant Marine, and will in time eliminate every particle of water service to the package freight shipper on the Great Lakes, and I think you will agree must certainly mitigate against the new Ham-

On every occasion when I have heard my hon. friend from Fast Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) speaking in this House I have observed that he has simply used the argument that the steamboat companies should be placed under the Railway Board. The only reason he can give why this should be done is that the Railway Board is a very important body, that it has had to deal with many important cases, that it has discharged its duties with ability and that no person on the floor of this House has ever found any fault with any action it has taken. I think it is up to the hon. member -for East Lambton to show that *these steamboat companies have been exercising their privileges in a way they should not do or that they have been overcharging. He has not been able to do that; and I doubt very much if he will be able to do so, and without presenting any evidence of that kind he is endeavouring to accomplish something with the assistance of this House that should not be allowed here. The hon. gentleman, however, should have gone further and stated that although the commissioners controlled the freight rates to Fort William, the Canadian Pacific were charging, at this very time he. made those statements, fifteen cents a bushel for whea$ from Regina to Fort William, a distance of 777 miles. I also find that the vessels he referred to which took the grain from Fort William to Montreal, a distance of nearly one thousand miles, carried the grain for seven cents a bushel. Now just think of the Canadian Pacific getting fifteen cents a bushel for carrying wheat a distance of something near 777 miles, and the steamship companies, that he complained of, carrying -wheat for nearly one thousand miles at seven cents a bushel. Surely this is pretty good proof that there is no cause to complain against the steamship companies. In the circular the hon. member had sent out to the members of Parliament, he makes the statement, that he thinks the rate of freight charged by steamship companies, should be one-third less than the rate charged by railway companies. Let me read you a letter that I received from Mr. Payne, a government official here at Ottawa:

" You have asked me to give you some comparison of railway freight rates by water. .	.
.	.	.	. The Canadian Pacific rate on wheat
from Regina to Fort William is 24 cents per 122 pounds, which would be the equivalent of $4.80 per ton. The distance Is 777 miles. By dividing the mileage into the freight charges per ton I find that the rate is .618 cent, or a little over six-tenths of a cent per ton-mile. By the same process, and using the same factors, the rate per ton per mile last year on waterborne wheat from Fort William to Montreal was .309. This is exactly half the railway rate. During the war; as you know, freight rates on the Great Lakes have been greatly increased. In 1915, for example, the rate to Montreal was but .132 per ton per mile. Even in 1918 it was as low as .158 from Fort William to Buffalo. Speaking broadly, it might be assumed with some degree of soundness that freight rates on our inland waterways are about one-third of the railway rates."
Now let me compare the position of railway companies with that of steamboats.
(Steamship companies have no monopoly. They are given no franchise, receive no assistance in the way of grants or subsidies, the water routes are open to all vessels, and the greater the number of vessels competing for business the lower will be the rates. If vessels are placed under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission they will be required to file tariffs.
I submit that fixed rates for vessels are neither feasible, desirable, or necessary.
Fixed rates in the case of vessels are not feasible on account of:	1. Variation in
carrying capacity; 2. Variation in speed; 3. Variation in cost of insurance; 4. Variation in cost of operation at different seasons of the year. (A fair rate in summer might be a ruinous rate in November). 5. Variation in cost of operation because of:
(a)	Different depths of water In different
years.
(b)	Different depths of water at different times in same year.
(c)	Difference in loading facilities at different elevators, wharves or ports.
(d)	Difference in unloading facilities at different elevators, wharves or ports.
Fixed rates in the case of vessels are not desirable because they would:	1. Result
in an elimination of competition: 2. Place Canadian vessels at a disadvantage in competing against U. S. A. boats whose rates in ordinary times are regulated only by the lawr of supply and demand; 3. Result in vessels lying idle when set rate was unprofitable; 4. Discourage the building of further vessels.
Fixed rates in the case of vessels are not necessary, because to get business now boats now must: 1 Underbid the rail rate; 2 Underbid or meet rate charged by boats
already under Railway Commission; 3 Offer fair rates or other boats will be built.
Another objection to our boats being placed under the Railway Commission is in the fact that if our boats were placed under the Railway Board, and the Railway Board fixed a tariff, all the American boats would have to do would be to come in here and go one or two cents less. That would take trade away from our boats here, which would be most injurious to Canadian interests.
-My hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) stated that the bulk freight rates in the United States were under the control of the Interstate Commerce Commission. I do not know where the hon. gentleman got his information, but it is certainly incorrect. I have before me a letter which was addressed to Mr. Francis King, counsel for the Dominion Marine Association, from the United States Shipping Board at Washington, which distinctly states that coal, ore and wheat are not under any restriction whatever, and the carriers are at liberty to charge what they like -for these commodities. I have another letter from Buffalo on the same subject which says:
March 17, 1920.
Referring to your inquiry of March 3, and answering your question as to whether American bulk freight rates are under any Government control, we beg to state that Amerioan bulk freight rates are not under any legal or Government control; but rates charged by the boats are (based on the natural law of supply and demand. Bulk freight cargoes such as iron ore, coal and grain are carried for the most part in vessels which are not common carriers', but are commonly known as tramp ships; and bulk freights when carried in such vessels are not under the jurisdiction of the Interstate Commerce Commission or the United States Shipping Board. Neither are bulk freight cargoes such as iron ore, coal or grain, even when carried in what are classed as package freighters where the carriage is limited strictly from port to port and is not part of the through rate.
Another letter from Buffalo, dealing with the same matter, says:
Buffalo, N.Y., March 16, 1920.
The undersigned are managers of a fleet of steel bulk carriers ; and we assure you that the statement that American bulk freight rates are not under any legal control, -the rates charged by the boats being based on the natural law of supply and demand, is correot.
I do not think the hon. gentleman will dispute the correctness of the foregoing statements; they come from authorities that cannot be questioned.
With respect to the finances of Canada Steamships I have a statement of its financial operations before me, and when the

hon. gentleman attempts to satisfy the House that this company has made an enormous amount of money out of carrying freight that assertion is not correct. The Canada Steamship Company purchased a great many vessels when they entered thi3 merger. The value of these vessels has since increased very materially, and they are worth nearly double as much to-day as they were at the time the merger took place. The freight rates between Canada and Liverpool did enable the company to make some money; but out of the profit of two millions and some odd dollars which they realized last year, less than one-third of the amount was derived from freight earnings in Canadian waters. If these earnings form less than one-third of a total of approximately $2,000,000, I do not think anybody can say that the public have been robbed to any very great extent.
There is another point to which I desire briefly to refer. The cities of Quebec, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, Hamilton, London, Winnipeg, Calgary, and Vancouver-although I did not know until to-night the extent of the opposition in Vancouver-are strongly opposed to this Bill. I think I am safe in saying that eighy-five per cent of the total freight handled by water is carried in and out of the cities referred to. If this be true surley it is fairly strong evidence against the Bill. Take the city of Hamilton which I have the honour to represent. Two or three years ago I had occasion to look up the amount of freight carried in and out of Hamilton by water, and hon. gentlemen will be surprised when I tell them that at that time we shipped twelve times the tonnage of that of the city of Toronto, although the latter city is five times the size of the city of Hamilton. Surely there is no hon. member who will deny that in view of that amount of freight shipped by Hamilton we should have some knowledge as to how the steamship companies deal with their customers. Not one of the cities which I have mentioned but is decidedly opposed to the hon. gentleman's Bill. Under the circumstances it is surprising that the hon. gentleman should take up the time of the House year after year in seeking to have this legislation passed when the public- of Canada are almost unanimously opposed to it. In view of the fact that the cities referred to carry eighty-five to ninety per cent of the total freight that is handled by water, and they are satisfied with the terms they are getting, why does the hon. member want to have the privilege which those cities now enjoy taken away from them? I appeal to this 
House that unless some evidence can be shown that these steamboats have been overcharging, this Bill should not be allowed to pass.

I rise, Mr. Speaker, for the purpose of presenting a resolution from the Chamber of Commerce of the riding that I represent. I followed very closely the argument of my hon. friend from East Lamlbton (Mr. Armstrong), and while I desire to give him credit for all that he desires to achieve by means of this Bill, I am bound to confess that I feel now very much as I did last year, that it would not be in the interests of this country to pass such legislation.
I was a member of the special committee to which the Bill was referred a year ago, and we had before that committee representatives from all the interested parties; we had the consumer, the shipper, the manufacturer, and the steamship man. After the evidence and representations that were then placed before that committee, I could come to only one conclusion,-that if this legislation as proposed were enacted the outcome would simply be wholly contrary to what apparently my hon. friend desires.
Let me say, Sir, that I am not interested in any steamship company, nor do I represent in this House any shipping concern, and if the Canada Steamship Company or any other shipping company should come to this House looking for special legislation that I feel would be for the purpose of increasing their revenue at the expense of the people, I would oppose them. But, Sir, I am interested in the consumers, and I believe that the shippers of this company, if they are privileged to have a continuance of the competition that we now have on the Great Lakes, will of necessity have the benefit of lower rates of freight.
The hon. member for East Lambton paid particular attention to the Canada Steamship Company. If he can show, as he says he can, that the Canada Steamship Company, or any other steamship company, has been exacting unjust tolls from the people of this country it is up to the Government of which he is a supporter to impose such taxation as will return this excess to the people to whom it belongs. That is the remedy in my opinion, rather than an attempt to stifle competition on the Great Lakes.
The riding that I represent, Mr. Speaker, is situated on the Detroit River, and is largely a manufacturing district in which is situated the city of Windsor and the towns of Walkerville, Ford and Ojibway.

We have a progressive Board of Commerce of 1,000 members with a transportation section,-and let me say that the members of that section do not represent any shipping interests; on the contrary, they represent the men who are shipping freight by water transportation. And after considering this Bill they brought in a unanimous report condemning the measure as not being in the public interest. It was fully
11 p.m. discussed at a general meeting, and as a result I was instructed to present the resolution and to oppose the Bill. With your permission, Mr. Speaker,
I will now read the resolution:
Whereas, the Armstrong Bill, which has been rejected by the House at Ottawa at previous sessions has been again introduced at the present session and proposes to put water rates from port to port in Canada under the control of the Railway Commission; and
Whereas, in the opinion of this Chamber of Commerce, the operation of steamship business being under entirely different conditions than rail transportation, does not lend itself to the same regulations prescribed for rail carriers.
Therefore be it resolved that this Chamber of Commerce places itself on record as opposing the passage of the Armstrong Bill and wishes the member of this constituency to so represent their views before the committee. Border Chamber of Commerce,

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to assure the hon. member for Lambton East (Mr. J. E. Armstrong) that my opposition to this Bill is not inspired by the combined interest of the steamship companies and the manufacturers to whom they grant special advantages, as was suggested in his speech. I am merely expressing the unanimous opinion of the business men, traders and merchants of the city and district of which I am one of the representatives. Last year, when the proposal of my hon. friend was defeated in the House, one morning paper said afterwards that those of us who had voted against it had voted against public opinion and public interest. It is precisely because public opinion in the district from which I come is unanimously opposed to this Bill that I am going to vote against it. I will not take up the time of the House by reading letters and telegrams which I have received, but I may say that the persons who have spoken or written to me about this Bill are unanimously opposed to it. I will read merely the letter of the Quebec Board of Trade, and to save time I will translate it from the French:
Mr. Ernest Lapointe, M.P., Ottawa,
Dear Sir:-We are informed that Mr. Armstrong comes back with his famous Bill to place the inland navigation companies under the control of the Railway Commission. The Quebec Board'of Trade, like most of the other associations of the same kind in the Dominion, is strongly opposed to the adoption of this Bill, because its effect would be to deprive our merchants of the benefit of competition, in summer, in freight transportation between the railway companies and the inland navigation companies. Furthermore, there does not seem to be any serious or good reason that militates in favour of such a radical change in the situation.
The council of the Board of Trade of Quebec hopes that you, with your colleagues of the Quebec district, will act in the same way as last year, so as to postpone the adoption of this Bill to the Greek Kalends.
Your obedient servant,
T. LEVAS'S'ETJR, Secretary.
From one letter which I have received from a steamship company, which is not the Canada Steamship Company, nor under the control of that company, but which is the Gulf of St. Lawrence Shipping and Trading Company, Limited, I read the following extract:
In our case, we wish to add three or four big vessels to our fleet, and we would not be able to raise the necessary capital if the Armstrong Bill was adopted.
All I wish to add is this. The waterways are natural facilities, they are the gift of

nature, and when Parliaments or men want to interfere with them, that interference should be only in such a way as to increase the facilities instead of restricting them. The case of the steamships is different from that of the railways. First, nobody comes to Parliament to ask for permission to use the waterways, and furthermore, as the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. T. J. Stewart) read from a document, there are all sorts of differences between vessels in matters of speed and loading capacity, differences in loading facilities at wharves and elevators and variations in the seasons, all of which make fixing freights for steamships less feasible than fixing rates for railways. We have enough restrictions in this country at the present time; we have enough beaurocracy; let us keep the air and the water free. I believe in the law of supply and demand; and if commerce by water is profitable, we may be sure that we shall have a sufficient number of steamships to carry the trade. The hardy seamen who built up the trade of the maritime powers were not prevented or restricted by any such restrictions as those which my hon. friend wants to force on Canadian seamen.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a few words on this very important Bill. I agree with the statement of the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) that the waterways and rivers and lakes are natural; that they were given to us by Divine Providence. But he knows very well that the Government of Canada, representing the people of Canada, have spent over $400,000,000 on our waterways, and that without such an expenditure, there would be very little traffic on our inland waters to-day.
That was done for the benefit of the people of Canada.
To build up trade.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I think it is well that I

should say a few words before the debate closes. The Bill which is now before the House, as the discussion this evening has abundantly shown, is a very important one, and there seems to be a difference of opinion on both sides of the House. The Bill is isimilar to one which was before a special committee last session, when we heard evidence for at least a day, if not longer. At that time the evidence showed that the subject matter of the Bill was considered of great importance, but it was decided not to take any action in regard to it. If this Bill were to be considered during the present session I think it would have to go before the Railway Committee again for further consideration, for I have had many letters and telegrams from various individuals asking to be given an opportunity of being heard in connection with it if it were decided to proceed with it. I was struck with one or two points in the discussion this evening, and one of them was in reference to vessels in their relation to the Railway Commission. Last session we included in the Railway Act the same clause that had been in the Act prior to the revision that took place last year. If I remember correctly, we added a word or two to the previous Act, and I shall read the clause with regard to water traffic as it now stands in [DOT]the Act. Section 358 reads as follows:
Traffic by Water.
S58. The provisions of this Act shall, in respect of tolls, tariffs and joint tariffs, so far as deemed applicable by the board, extend and apply to the traffic carried by any railway company by sea or by inland water, between any ports or places in Canada, if the company owns, charters, uses, maintains or works, or is a party to any arrangement for using, maintaining or working vesselB for carrying traffic, by sea or by inland water between any such ports or places.
In my judgment, in view of the foregoing clause, almost all vessels are virtually under the Board of Railway Commissioners at the present time; if any person wishes to apply to the board for an adjustment of freight rates. The Canadian Pacific railway own and operate a number of steamers between Port Arthur and the Georgian Bay ports.
There is no doubt whatever about those that are owned and operated by the Canadian Pacific. There is no doubt they charter a number of vessels to carry grain between Port Arthur and Georgian Bay ports. There is no doubt whatever but that they would come under this Railway Act. Taking that into consideration, it covers nearly all the vessels that are operating between our Canadian ports.
The same thing applies to the Grand Trunk and the Canadian National railways. Hon. members who come from Ontario know that the Grand Trunk has an agreement with, I think, the Northern Navigation Company for the operating of a line of steamers between Sarnia and upper lake ports. Vessels that are chartered by the Grand Trunk will also come under this Railway Act. The Canadian Government in connection with the Canadian National railways have built a great many steamers. There are twenty odd steamers that are of the Welland canal size that will likely within a very reasonable time operate between Port Arthur and Montreal. They are now operating on the ocean; they were sent to the ocean when they were constructed because of the urgency in getting foodstuffs to our soldiers overseas and also to those countries that were in such desperate need of food. There were also sent to the ocean other vessels operated by private corporations in order to carry the products of this country to foreign countries. A number of them have been plying between the West Indies and Canada, and it was very important that these vessels should operate , there in order that our food and manufactured products might be taken to the West Indies and that in return we might get sugar and the products of those islands to supplement the food supplies of the people of Canada. I mention that to show that these vessels are only temporary on the ocean. As soon as the tonnage can be produced these vessels will be operating between Port Arthur and Montreal, and they will be placed under the Board of Railway Commissioners.
The Canada Steamship Company has been referred to. I know for a fact that probably one hundred vessels were sent to sea when the war was on. That probably reduced our Canadian tonnage below what it had been prior to that time and it has not been replaced. In addition to having the advantage of these vessels under the Board of Railway Commissioners and being in a position to control rates, if the board can do so on account of this clause, let me also say that the people of the West have always had and now have competition in so far as freight between Montreal and Port Arthur is concerned. There is some arrangement by which the rates from Halifax and St. John in winter, and Quebec, and Montreal, New York, Boston and other Atlantic ports in summer, are the same to ports in England. Therefore the only place where there could be any possible chance of taking advantage of competitive or controlled rates would be

between Port Arthur and Montreal. Hon. members know that there is a water route between Port Arthur and New York. Large steamers go to Buffalo;. the grain is transshipped there and sent on to New York and the rate from Port Arthur to New York is ^always up against the rate from Port Arthur to Montreal. The result is that our farmers in the West always have a competitive rate. Shippers in purchasing the grain of the West know that it is absolutely impossible for the Canada Steamships lines, or the several other steamship companies having large steamers in Canada, to prohibit grain from going other than by the Canadian route.
I feel that that is a protection that will always justify leaving these vessels open to competition. However this is a big question and one that has merits on both sides. My hon. friend from East Lambton has taken a keen interest in it for several years. No one can blame him for taking an interest in it or for believing as he does and trying to have his idea crystallized into law. Others are opposed to the idea just as much as he is in favour of it. The question is so important that I feel it would not be fair to those who have so much money invested to let this matter go without giving them a full opportunity of placing before the members of this House through a committee the position they would take in connection with this Bill. I know there are a number of other members who w'ould like to speak on this very important matter but the hour is getting late and they feel it would be impossible for them to do justice to the subject or to say what they wish to say. I would like to say more than I have in the few minutes I have spoken. But as the hour is getting late I would beg leave to move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
Rt. Hon. Mr. DOHERTY moved the adjournment of the House.
